articles.title: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says
articles.excerpt:
Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good ph...
articles.body_text:
Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.

“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”

After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”

Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.

The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.

Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.

Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.

“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”

Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.

Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.

Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.

He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.

“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”

The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.

Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.

“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

articles.title: Team USA hero Connor Hellebuyck discusses the difference between playing hockey in US and Canada
articles.excerpt:
Former NHL player Viktor Stalberg recounts a wild week in Russia's KHL in which he was nearly waived, traded, and then suddenly not traded by a hockey coaching great.

The NHL was rocked by a massive ...
articles.body_text:
Former NHL player Viktor Stalberg recounts a wild week in Russia's KHL in which he was nearly waived, traded, and then suddenly not traded by a hockey coaching great.

The NHL was rocked by a massive trade on Friday that saw the Winnipeg Jets deal three-time Vezina Trophy winner, Olympic gold medalist and soon-to-be Medal of Freedom recipient Connor Hellebuyck to the New Jersey Devils.

The goalie hasn't played so far this season after asking for a trade over the summer, but now that it's done, he's gearing up to hit the ice and has addressed the New Jersey media for the first time.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"Sitting at home for so long was getting to me. For myself, I’m just really excited to play hockey again," Hellebuyck said on Saturday, per the Associated Press. "I’m joining a very skilled group. They brought me for a certain specific role. I’m really excited to fill that role, not only on the ice but off the ice as well."

SOCIAL MEDIA REACTS TO EXCRUCIATINGLY AWKWARD MOMENT BETWEEN DEVILS JACK HUGHES AND ESPN ANALYST

New Jersey Devils general manager Sunny Mehta and goalie Connor Hellebuyck pose for a photo at the latter's introductory press conference. (Photo by Rich Graessle/NHLI via Getty Images)

The Devils are off to a good start this season with a 7-4-0 record after Saturday's win over the Los Angeles Kings, during which netminder Jake Allen was between the pipes. Adding a goalie of Hellebuyck's caliber to the lineup could mean that goals will be at a premium for any team that plays the Devils.

But for Hellebuyck, it will be different playing in New Jersey compared to a Canadian market like Winnipeg, something he was asked about.

UTAH'S MACKENZIE WEEGAR REACTS TO AMERICAN PLAYERS SEEKING TRADES OUT OF CANADA: 'IT’S A BIT UNFORTUNATE'

"I mean, it's a catch-22; some people love that," he said of playing in markets where people bug players about hockey while they're trying to grocery shop. "Sometimes you just want to be left alone. Canada loves their hockey, and I felt that to the bone, and I loved my time there, and I've loved the people I've met. Made a lot of good friends and built good relationships there."

"So, I can't say that one is better than the other," he continued. "I know that I've enjoyed both and I've experienced both. It's just one of those things that's part of hockey culture... they love their hockey, and we love our hockey in our own way, and that should be celebrated."

Devils goalie Connor Hellebuyck speaks at his introductory press conference on Saturday. (Rich Graessle/NHLI via Getty Images)

It was quite the diplomatic answer, and we'll see how it goes in just a few weeks when Hellebuyck and the Devils visit Winnipeg on November 10.

articles.title: Raiders mourn Super Bowl champion Pete Banaszak, key figure in iconic 'Holy Roller' play
articles.excerpt: Chicago Bears legend coach Mike Ditka passes away at 86. Fox News contributor and sportscaster Jim Gray speaks on Ditka's passing, calling Ditka 'America's coach.' Ditka led the Bears to the 1985 Supe...
articles.body_text:
Chicago Bears legend coach Mike Ditka passes away at 86. Fox News contributor and sportscaster Jim Gray speaks on Ditka's passing, calling Ditka 'America's coach.' Ditka led the Bears to the 1985 Super Bowl triumph.

Former Oakland Raiders standout Pete Banaszak, a 13-year veteran who helped the franchise win its first Super Bowl, died at 82, the team announced.

"The Raiders Family mourns the passing of Pete Banaszak, whose toughness, competitive spirit, and dedication embodied a legendary era of Raiders football and made him a cherished member of the Silver and Black," the team said in a statement released Saturday.

The Raiders also remembered the late running back's deep pride in his Polish heritage and extended their condolences to his loved ones.

"A Wisconsin native, Banaszak was fiercely proud of his Polish heritage and was inducted into the National Polish-American Sports Hall of Fame in 1990. The deepest condolences of the entire Raider Nation are with Pete's wife Sue, daughters Rebecca and Amy, grandsons Luke, Austin, and Connor, and all of his loved ones."

RAIDERS LEGEND GIVES BLESSING TO FIRST OVERALL PICK FERNANDO MENDOZA TO WEAR NO. 15: 'HE'S PERFECT'

Oakland Raiders running back Pete Banaszak is in action during the 1971 NFL season. (Malcolm Emmons/USA TODAY Sports)

Banaszak was primarily a reserve during his career, starting just 36 of the 173 NFL games he played. Even so, he made the most of his opportunities and etched his name into Raiders lore during his 13 seasons with the famed Silver and Black.

Banaszak made his final appearance with the Raiders in 1978. His best season came in 1975, when he rushed for a league-high 16 touchdowns and a career-best 672 yards in his 10th year with the franchise. Those 16 rushing touchdowns remain a Raiders single-season record.

Oakland Raiders running back Pete Banaszak (40) carries the ball against the Chicago Bears during an NFL game at Soldier Field on Nov. 7, 1976, in Chicago, Illinois. Banaszak played for the Raiders from 1966-78. (Focus on Sport/Getty Images)

CRAIG MORTON, QUARTERBACK WHO LED THE BRONCOS TO THEIR FIRST SUPER BOWL APPEARANCE, DEAD AT 83

Banaszak crossed the goal line twice in the Raiders’ Super Bowl XI victory over the Minnesota Vikings. The win marked the first time the franchise won the Vince Lombardi Trophy.

Banaszak also played a key role in one of the NFL’s most famous plays, the "Holy Roller." In Week 2 of what would be his final season, the Raiders trailed the Chargers 20-14 with seconds remaining when Ken Stabler fumbled while seemingly being sacked. Banaszak recovered and batted the ball forward, giving tight end Dave Casper a chance to make the recovery in the end zone. The extra point secured Oakland’s improbable 21-20 win.

Oakland Raiders running back Pete Banaszak follows Marv Hubbard against the Denver Broncos at the Oakland Coliseum on Dec. 19, 1971. The Raiders defeated the Broncos 21-13. (Darryl Norenberg/USA TODAY Sports)

Banaszak finished his storied NFL career with 3,772 rushing yards, 1,022 receiving yards and 52 touchdowns. He is also credited with six touchdowns in the playoffs.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Man arrested after fire engulfs Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest mountain retreat in the Bavarian Alps

articles.body_text:
‘The Katie Miller Podcast’ host Katie Miller discusses a study showing the decline of traditional nuclear families in major U.S. cities and reports of child marriages in Germany on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

A man in Germany was arrested on suspicion of arson this week after he allegedly set fire to a mountain retreat built for Adolf Hitler.

The fire broke out at the Eagle’s Nest in the Bavarian Alps on Friday evening, and firefighters battled the flames against strong winds.

The 33-year-old suspect is a German citizen who showed signs of mental illness and was taken to a psychiatric facility, authorities said.

WORLD-FAMOUS CATHOLIC SHRINE TORCHED, 'DEVIL IN A SKIRT' SCRAWLED ON VIRGIN MARY STATUE

The Eagle's Nest, built for Adolf Hitler in the Bavarian Alps, burns early Saturday. (Bergerlebnis Berchtesgaden via AP)

But they aren’t ruling out a political motive for the arson due to its notorious history.

He was seen heading down the mountain on a motorcycle.

The Kehlsteinhaus, as it’s called in Germany, is more than 6,000 feet above sea level and accessible by an elevator during the day for tourists.

The building has operated as a seasonal restaurant and tourist attraction since 1952, and has an exhibit on its history.

MASSIVE FIRE DESTROYS 400-YEAR-OLD FOOD MARKET, LEAVING HISTORIC LANDMARK IN RUINS

A man in Germany was arrested on suspicion of arson this week after he allegedly set fire to a mountain retreat built for Adolf Hitler. (Bavarian Red Cross via AP)

He did frequent his Berghof residence in the same area, which was blown up after the war.

"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, told reporters at Eagle’s Nest. "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."

This 2007 photo shows the Kehlsteinhaus, or Eagle's Nest, built for Adolf Hitler in 1938 near Berchtesgaden, Germany. (Geir Moulson/AP Photo, File)

He added: "It is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Sacha Baron Cohen says 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' is his last in this style of comedy, calling them too risky
articles.excerpt:
Comedian Adam Carolla says he was troubled by what he saw during COVID, when some performers appeared less willing to question authority or push against conventional thinking.

Sacha Baron Cohen is do...
articles.body_text:
Comedian Adam Carolla says he was troubled by what he saw during COVID, when some performers appeared less willing to question authority or push against conventional thinking.

Sacha Baron Cohen is done starring in over-the-top comedies.

In a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter, the 55-year-old actor confirmed that his new movie, "Ali G: Who Iz I?," will be his last in the risky, character-driven comedic style that made him famous.

"I want to do stuff that challenges me," he told the outlet. "So again, I’m not doing 'Borat 3,' which also would be incredibly challenging. Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more."

The actor has said he was done with this style of comedy in the past, but decided to make this movie because he is "terrified of where our society is headed" and thinks of his comedy as a way to comment on it.

Cohen says he is not going to make any more comedies like "Borat." (Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)

SACHA BARON COHEN’S RIPPED NEW LOOK FOR MARVEL ROLE HAS FANS DOING A TAKE

He explained that through his films, he can "show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence." He added that at the end of the day, he also "wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made."

"These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI," he said. "If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble, and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy."

Cohen's early breakthrough came in 2000, with "Da Ali G Show," and he later gained international recognition with the release of "Borat" in 2006.

He followed that up with "Bruno," "The Dictator," "Who is America" and "Borat Subsequent Moviefilm," as well as some dramatic roles in "The Trial of the Chicago 7," "Les Misérables" and "Disclaimer."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Cohen made a name for himself playing characters such as Borat and Bruno. (Steve Granitz/WireImage)

Throughout the interview, Cohen explained that these comedies "are dangerous to make" and are "incredibly demanding" on the body, but that he and his crew "try to limit the risks and keep everybody safe."

He described the final scene of his latest project as "an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations" with a lot of different elements, filmed as "a continual shot."

"There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert," he said. "On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, 'You will go to hospital if you make this movie,' because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, 'You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.'"

The "Balls Up" star explained that he hired "an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France" to be next to him throughout filming and that, despite the precautions, "a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Cohen said a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration while filming ""Ali G: Who Iz I?" (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)

Despite how it may seem, Cohen assured fans he "will never do a scene if I think I’m actually going to die."

"I was about to do a scene [in 'Borat 1'] and we had a cop who had his gun on his thigh and I said, 'Why is your gun on your thigh?' He goes, 'Well, I need to be really fast to draw in this area.' I said, 'Well, how close are you to me?' And he said, 'I’ll be with you within three minutes.' I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Cohen was nominated for Academy Awards for writing the two Borat movies. (Rick Rycroft-Pool/Getty Images)

On the other hand, however, Cohen agreed to film a scene at a gun rights rally for the second "Borat" film, knowing there was a chance he could be shot, but said, "I felt it was an important film to be made."

His risk-taking ways have paid off, as he received two Academy Award nominations for writing "Borat" and its sequel, in 2007 and 2021 respectively.

He also received an acting nomination for his role in "The Trial of the Chicago 7."

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: UCF Knights pull off stunning upset over undefeated BYU in mind-boggling overtime thriller
articles.excerpt:
UCF's Landen Chambers rushed for a short TD, tying the game vs the BYU Cougars.

It has been a wild couple of weeks in college football, but what happened on Saturday in Orlando — a UCF Knights double...
articles.body_text:
UCF's Landen Chambers rushed for a short TD, tying the game vs the BYU Cougars.

It has been a wild couple of weeks in college football, but what happened on Saturday in Orlando — a UCF Knights double-overtime win over the BYU Cougars — might be the craziest thing yet.

After a big win over Notre Dame and Top 10 teams dropping like flies last weekend, the BYU Cougars found themselves coming into Week 8 at No. 2 in the nation.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

On Saturday, they headed down to Orlando, Florida, to take on Scott Frost's UCF Knights.

BYU QB BEAR BACHMEIER SAYS NOTRE DAME 'DISRESPECTED' HIM AND HIS FAMILY FOLLOWING UPSET WIN OVER IRISH

Tyren Hornes #2 of the UCF Knights reacts in the first half of the game between the UCF Knights and BYU Cougars. (Photo by Dustin Markland/Getty Images)

The 3-3 Knights have struggled in the Big 12 since joining the conference, but tend to be better at home in the friendly confines of the Acrisure Bounce House.

The Cougars opened the scoring when quarterback Bear Bachmeier hit wide receiver Kyler Kasper for six.

But UCF managed to hold them through the rest of the first quarter and then answered with a touchdown of their own in the second, when Knights running back Landen Chambers broke through a notoriously solid BYU defensive line on the goal line.

After forcing BYU to punt, UCF managed to drive deep into Cougar territory, but failed to get into the endzone. They settled for a field goal attempt on fourth-and-goal. While kicker Will Stone got the job done to give the Knights a 10-7 lead, the decision to play it safe drew boos from the home fans.

They may have had a point because Bachmeier lowered his head and burst into the end zone on the following possession.

UCF ended the half with another red zone drive coming off of an interception, only this time they didn't have to settle for a field goal.

QB Keyone Jenkins found Chambers through the air for six.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

That plus an extra point meant that UCF took a 17-14 lead to the locker room at halftime. This was the third time they led or were tied with a ranked opponent at the half this season, but went on to lose both games.

In the second half — with rain falling — BYU scored on their first drive, but UCF answered right back to regain their three-point lead.

BYU settled for a field goal to tie the game at 24-24.

Central Florida quarterback Keyone Jenkins throws a pass during the first half against BYU. (AP Photo/Phelan M. Ebenhack)

A couple of drives later, a short punt gave UCF good field position with 8:50 left in the game.

What followed was an 11-play drive that set up a fourth-down play on the goal line.

The Knights held the Cougars deep in their own end, but they flipped the field with a booming punt ahead of UCF's final drive of regulation. Johnson then led the offense downfield and into kicker Will Stone's field goal range.

On second-and-ten, it appeared that Jenkins had fumbled and it was recovered by BYU; however, upon review, it was overturned and ruled an incomplete pass. On top of that, BYU defensive tackle Keanu Tanuvasa was assessed an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty that gave the Knights a fresh set of downs and moved them up to the BYU 28-yard line.

Central Florida running back Landen Chambers (11) runs for a two-yard touchdown in front of BYU safety Raider Damuni (3). (AP Photo/Phelan M. Ebenhack)

After a few plays to bleed time off the clock, UCF brought out the kicking unit on third down, but the kick was blocked and recovered behind the line of scrimmage. With Stone's helmet coming off and no flag on the play, the half came to an end because of a ten-second run-off, and it was off to overtime.

UCF won the toss and elected to get the ball second.

On third-and-13, Bachmeier hit Legend Glasker to put the Cougars ahead.

But it didn't last long because on UCF's first play, Jenkins scrambled for his life, then found receiver Josh Derry in the endzone.

Stone returned and kicked a field goal, but BYU's Kendal Wall was called for roughing the kicker, giving the Knights a fresh set of downs, and it only took two plays for Jenkins to hit tight end Grayson Brousseau — who grew up fifteen minutes from Provo — for the touchdown, and then was successful on the mandated two-point attempt.

In their second OT possession, BYU's undefeated season and No. 2 ranking came down to a single play, and UCF managed to hang on for the biggest win over a ranked team in program history.

That throws a huge wrench into the rankings and playoff picture, and it had the potential to rejuvenate UCF's season as they go to 4-3 with a signature win under their belt.

Kalani Sitake's Cougars will now look to bounce back on Halloween against the Arizona State Sun Devils, while the UCF Knights will move on to face Baylor.

articles.title: Obama slams Trump’s ‘cruelty and corruption’ at Ohio rally for Democrats
articles.excerpt:
Barack Obama has criticised the “cruelty and corruption” during US President Donald Trump’s second term, as the former president campaigned for Democratic candidates in two Midwestern states.

Obama d...
articles.body_text:
Barack Obama has criticised the “cruelty and corruption” during US President Donald Trump’s second term, as the former president campaigned for Democratic candidates in two Midwestern states.

Obama delivered scathing criticisms of Trump on Saturday during a midterm election campaign rally in Ohio, slamming his successor’s foreign policies.

“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” the 65-year-old Democrat said. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for,” he added, referring to the US-Israel war on Iran.

Obama urged Ohioans to vote against the Republican administration, saying: “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough’.”

The former president also addressed the recent controversy in Ohio’s gubernatorial race surrounding an attack advertisement by Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy against Democrat Amy Acton.

“In recent days, we’ve seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to,” Obama said of Ramaswamy. “I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behaviour are so low that somebody could run an ad like that.”

In the advertisement, Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, disputes her daughter’s account of a childhood involving homelessness and ⁠⁠⁠⁠sexual abuse by her stepfather, urging Ohioans not to vote for her.

Acton says she has not seen her mother since 1978. Acton’s brother has supported her account of being sexually abused by her stepfather when she was a child. The stepfather, who died in 2004, was charged with rape.

Obama backed Acton, saying that she has “spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she’s experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness.”

The former president shared the rally stage with Acton and Ohio’s former Democratic senator, Sherrod Brown, who will attempt a comeback against incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted.

Trump defended the Ramaswamy advertisement on Saturday, when he cast his ballot early in Florida.

Polls give Democrats a slight lead in both Ohio races, but results are expected to be close.

Later on Saturday evening, Obama headed to Michigan, where he condemned critics of Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, suggesting that they are using the 41-year-old politician’s name and Muslim faith to tear him down.

“We have seen this movie before. I starred in it,” Obama told a rally in Detroit. “I’ve got a long-form birth certificate to prove it.”

He added, “Abdul is as Michigan as it gets.”

The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a “radical”, declaring that “Abdul shares my values”.

Obama remains the Democratic Party’s best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. And he is taking his star power on the road in the final days of the midterm elections, which will help determine the balance of power in US politics on November 3.

Obama will headline a Democratic Party rally in Georgia next week with Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms.

articles.title: Ukraine's Starlink restored as Elon Musk claims Kyiv violated terms of service 'to kill people'
articles.excerpt:
Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on the fallout over Starlink satellite system restrictions in Ukraine on ‘Special Report.’

Elon Musk on Saturday continued to d...
articles.body_text:
Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on the fallout over Starlink satellite system restrictions in Ukraine on ‘Special Report.’

Elon Musk on Saturday continued to defend Starlink after Ukraine faced more than a week of speed restrictions that disrupted its war effort against Russia, saying SpaceX has done more to defend the country than any other private company "by far," while accusing the country of using the technology in violation of its terms of service "to kill people."

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X, claiming that Ukraine had "violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He explained that Starshield is a different system controlled by the U.S. government.

ELON MUSK BLAMES TRUMP, US MILITARY FOR SPACEX RESTRICTIONS UKRAINE WARNS COULD HAVE DEADLY CONSEQUENCES

Elon Musk on Saturday continued to defend Starlink, while accusing Ukraine of violating the company's terms of service "to kill people." (Getty Images, File)

"Starlink remains critical to the defense of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now," he wrote in response to an X post that stated Starlink is "not a weapons system."

"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," he added.

Musk said that Starlink was crucial at the beginning of the war because it was the only means of communication that couldn’t be "destroyed or jammed by Russia.

"SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR," he claimed. "That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict. May you burn in hell. End of story."

Last week, Musk blamed the issue on the U.S. military.

"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the SpaceX, Tesla and X CEO wrote in a post.

UKRAINE SHOWED TRUMP HOW EASILY AN ENEMY COULD CRIPPLE AN AI POWERHOUSE

Last week, Musk blamed the issue on the U.S. military. (Getty Images, File)

A source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital that Ukraine received no advance warning before the restrictions took effect overnight, despite relying on the service under arrangements contracted through the U.S. government until May 15, 2027.

Ukrainian forces discovered the change after experiencing connectivity problems and contacting SpaceX customer support. They were told Starshield service would be restricted on platforms traveling at speeds of 100 mph or higher, the source said.

Musk did not say whether President Donald Trump, War Secretary Pete Hegseth or another U.S. official personally authorized the new restriction or explain why it was imposed.

Trump told reporters on Saturday that he had spoken to Musk about the issue, but wouldn’t elaborate.

UKRAINE REGAINS CRITICAL STARLINK SERVICE AFTER RESTRICTIONS DISRUPT DRONE OPERATIONS

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the U.S. "betrayed" him with the recent Starlink satellite system restrictions. On Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Elon Musk about the issue. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images; Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)

Ukraine's Ministry of Defense announced Saturday that it had regained broader access to Starlink, with connections remaining stable at speeds of 250 mph.

It remains unclear what led to the slowdown in service, with Ukraine having accused both Trump and Musk of being behind it, and comes after renewed hope for Ukraine and Russia to reach a resolution in the war.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Hegseth have denied that the U.S. government was responsible for slowing Ukraine's Starlink service.

Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told "Fox & Friends" this week he would be open to ending the war by freezing the fighting along the current front lines.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House, SpaceX, along with the War and State departments for comment.

Fox News' James Cirrone contributed to this report.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Barack Obama rallies Michigan crowd for El-Sayed, saying he’s ‘fighting for real change’
articles.excerpt:
Former president speaks to rapturous crowd of thousands in support of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate

Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting for change,...
articles.body_text:
Former president speaks to rapturous crowd of thousands in support of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate

Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting for change, real change, that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket”, as he threw his weight behind the Democratic Senate candidate and the rest of the ticket on the first day of early voting in Michigan.

Obama said in front of thousands of onlookers at Cass technical high school in Detroit that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American”.

The former president headlined the rally for El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate, and secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, the party’s candidate for governor, at an evening event to “get out the vote”.

He accused Donald Trump of “enriching himself and his family”, and said the administration had set a “culture … at the top” of taking favors. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this,” he said.

The rally came on the first day of Michigan’s early voting period, with the general election on 3 November. It was also Obama’s first weekend of in-person campaigning during the midterms, which started in Cleveland, Ohio, earlier in the day to stump for the former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton earlier in the weekend. He issued similarly scathing remarks aimed at the White House and the GOP.

The Detroit stop is Obama’s first public show of support for El-Sayed, who emerged from a bitter August primary in which the former president stayed on the sidelines. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health official, beat the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens who was riding on the backing of the Democratic establishment and pro-Israel organizations.

Obama was on the offensive against the administration, mocking the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, as “laser-focused” on the “jawline and testosterone levels of our troops”, asking: “How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?”

On tariffs, Obama said Trump was toughest on “that well-known evil empire”, referring to Canada, a few minutes’ drive from Detroit across the bridge. “These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup,” he said.

He even took a jab at Trump’s attempts to renovate the White House. “He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of the many renovations in Washington, including the White House ballroom and the Rose Garden. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Questions had hung over whether Obama would back El-Sayed at all. El-Sayed, a champion of Medicare for All, had at one point called the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature domestic achievement, an incremental fix. The two men spoke by phone after the primary, and El-Sayed has since called Obama a mentor figure.

El-Sayed has the most ground to make up in Wayne county, where Detroit is the county seat, after Stevens beat him there by about 51% to 45% in the August primaries. Obama last campaigned in Detroit – which is more than three-quarters Black – in October 2024 for Kamala Harris, and Harris herself appeared with El-Sayed in Detroit last month.

Republicans have not held a Michigan Senate seat in 25 years, but the party sees the seat as one of its better pickup chances nationwide. El-Sayed faces Mike Rogers, a former congressman endorsed by Donald Trump who lost a 2024 Senate matchup against Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point. The Cook Political Report rates this race a toss-up.

Slotkin, a featured speaker at the rally, told the crowd that “Michigan believes in electing fighters”. And when it came to any disagreements she may have with El-Sayed, she said: “It’s OK because we agree on so much more.”

“We’re putting a check and balance on Donald Trump in the White House,” she said.

A Marist poll of likely voters statewide conducted in mid-October put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, within the margin of error. RealClearPolitics’s average had El-Sayed ahead by about 2.6 points in a similar timeframe.

Trump has attacked El-Sayed throughout the campaign, calling him a “jihadist”, pointing to his middle name and alleging that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed strongly denies, and has created one of the most viral moments of the year. El-Sayed has also faced a barrage of criticism from the establishment wing of the Democratic party over his appearances with leftwing streamer Hasan Piker.

Trump is due in the state himself on Sunday, when he will hold a rally for Michigan Republicans in Port Huron, on the Canadian border. The city said it will be the first presidential visit to St Clair county.

If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim and first Egyptian American in the US Senate. Benson faces the Republican congressman John James; a James win would make him Michigan’s first Black governor.

Turning to the disagreements between them, Obama acknowledged that some people had pointed out that El-Sayed “didn’t like some things you did as president”. “We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue,” he said. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.”

“We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society,” Obama said, “and that the system’s not just run for those at the top.”

articles.title: LaNorris Sellers' acrobatics, late fumble recovery help give South Carolina walk-off win over Tennessee
articles.excerpt:
Kansas's Bryson Hayes takes it to the HOUSE for 95-yard kickoff return TD, tying game vs Kansas State

LaNorris Sellers' Heisman candidacy may be out the window, but whatever pose he pulled off will l...
articles.body_text:
Kansas's Bryson Hayes takes it to the HOUSE for 95-yard kickoff return TD, tying game vs Kansas State

LaNorris Sellers' Heisman candidacy may be out the window, but whatever pose he pulled off will live in South Carolina lore for quite some time.

The quarterback barreled, twisted and turned through Tennessee defenders to tie the game late, and the Gamecocks then turned an ensuing fumble into a walk-off field goal in their 27-24 victory over No. 11 Tennessee.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

With roughly three and a half minutes to go at the South Carolina 38, the Vols went for it on 4th and 1 but were stuffed. South Carolina then moved down the field on a drive that resulted in a touchdown you have to see the believe.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers escapes a tackle attempt by Tennessee defensive back Qua Moss during a college football game between Tennessee and South Carolina at Williams-Brice Stadium in Columbia, South Carolina, on Oct. 24, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

On 3rd and goal from the 4, Sellers scrambled right and was at first stuffed at the 3. But he kept churning his feet and was nearly down at the 1. Yet just as he was about to be down, he laid out for the end zone and scored. The PAT tied the game at 24 with 1:17 to go.

Tennessee had a chance to make magic of their own, but instead, on just the third play of their drive, George MacIntyre lost a fumble, and the Gamecocks recovered at the Vols' 34 with 33 seconds left.

Four plays later, Malik Orsan drilled a walk-off 48-yard field goal as time expired, and the South Carolina faithful stormed the field.

South Carolina had been 1-28 when trailing by seven or more points in the fourth quarter under Shane Beamer. It is also back-to-back wins against ranked teams for the Gamecocks after a massive upset in Gainesville against Florida.

LaNorris Sellers #16 of the South Carolina Gamecocks celebrates after a touchdown during the first half of a football game against the Tennessee Volunteers at Williams-Brice Stadium on Oct. 24, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Getty Images)

Sellers was South Carolina's leading rusher, going for 96 yards on 18 carries and scoring twice. South Carolina had gone up 14-0 in the first quarter but let Tennessee fight back.

South Carolina is now 4-3 on the season and 2-3 in SEC play. For Tennessee, it's their second loss on the season against six wins (3-2 in conference). The loss will almost surely knock them out of potential College Football Playoff seeding — but the first CFP poll isn't until Nov. 3.

South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers looks to pass the ball during the first half of an NCAA college football game against Tennessee on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (AP Photo/Artie Walker Jr.)

In any case, Tennessee will have some making-up to do, and that will start in two weeks against No. 12 Kentucky back in Knoxville. South Carolina will host Oklahoma next week.

Four people have been injured after a driv...
articles.body_text:
Offenders still at large after shots fired from vehicle outside licensed premises in Loganholme

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Four people have been injured after a drive-by shooting outside a venue hosting a boxing event.

Police said they responded to reports of shots being fired from a vehicle outside a licensed premises in Loganholme, south of Brisbane, at 8.15pm.

“The involved vehicle was witnessed leaving the scene,” police said.

Four injured people were taken to hospital, police said, and their condition was being assessed.

Speaking Sunday morning, Logan’s mayor Jon Raven described residents in the area as frightened.

“This has sent a shockwave through Logan. We’ve never seen something like this in Logan before,” Raven told the Today show.

“Our hearts go out obviously to the victims and the staff and the people at this boxing event.

“I’ve been to one of these events before, they’re really family-friendly environment, and I know there’s lots of children who were there, and this will impact them for the rest of their lives.”

The deputy commander of Queensland Police, Chris Stream, described the scene as “confronting”.

“A number of people had suffered gunshot wounds,” he told Today.

Fitzys Loganholme on Bryants Road was scheduled to host the Logan City Titles Fight Night on Saturday.

Logan City Titles shared a statement on social media on Sunday morning.

“We are heartbroken about the incident that occurred at the fight night,” it said.

“Logan City Titles was a family event, an event for our community, showcasing local talent, hard work and everyone’s skills inside the ring.

“These types of incidents have no place in the boxing community or any part of the broader community.”

The offenders are still at large but police said they did not believe there was an ongoing threat to the public.

Police were urging anyone with information about the incident to contact them.

articles.title: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
articles.excerpt:
Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November

Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the poss...
articles.body_text:
Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November

Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.

The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU.

Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.

In an interview with the Sunday Times he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”

The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.

The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.

“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times.

“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.

“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.

He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.

The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.

In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics.

Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.

Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.

It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.

Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.

But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.

Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.

The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”

Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.

“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

articles.title: Storm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rain
articles.excerpt:
Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday

Amber weather warnings have come into force as the worst of Storm Boelo could be set to hit parts o...
articles.body_text:
Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday

Amber weather warnings have come into force as the worst of Storm Boelo could be set to hit parts of the UK.

Storm Boelo’s winds will peak from Saturday evening, leaving areas in the warning zone, including Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, braced for gusts of 60-70mph and even 80mph in exposed coastal spots, the Met Office said.

The forecaster’s amber warnings came into force on Saturday at 9pm.

Maximum gust speeds of 75mph have already hit South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland on Saturday, according to the Met Office, which has also issued several yellow warnings for rain.

Storm Boelo follows Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, which brought strong winds to parts of the UK on Friday.

Gusts of 76mph were recorded at St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph at Aberporth in south-west Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.

Heavy downpours since 8am on Saturday have already seen rainfall totals of 72mm in White Barrow, Wiltshire, along with 43mm in both Cwm Dyli, just south of the Snowdon range in North Wales, and Inveruglas on the west shore of Loch Lomond, Scotland.

Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday where the National Grid said power had been restored to 131,225 properties by Saturday at 7pm.

An amber wind warning, the Met Office’s second most severe, is active across Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm on Saturday to the same time on Sunday.

A further amber warning runs from 9pm on Saturday to 10am on Sunday in the north-east of Northern Ireland.

Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, will bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and people should stay indoors as much as possible, the forecaster said.

The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings which extend south into parts of England and North Wales and cover the whole of Northern Ireland.

The Environment Agency had issued 58 alerts for spots across England where flooding is possible by 8pm on Saturday, as well as 12 warnings stating that flooding is expected.

Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.

“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.

“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts.

“People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”

People should secure loose items outside, plan ahead if they are travelling and keep an eye on the latest forecast and warnings, he advised.

Storm Boelo has already caused widespread disruption.

Boelo’s strong winds disrupted flights at Dublin airport, where as of 4pm on Saturday, nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines because of weather issues.

It also reported that six inbound flights performed go-arounds – five of which landed on the second attempt, with the other diverting to another airport before returning a short time later.

Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, in a call for those living near rail lines to secure their garden furniture firmly.

Visit Liverpool announced that the region’s River of Light event, featuring illuminated artwork, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”.

London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations this Sunday were also cancelled on independent health and safety experts’ recommendations in light of the storm.

Other attractions closed on Sunday include Edinburgh Castle and the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire, which was due to host its Fountains by Floodlight event.

articles.title: Gunmen kill at least 10 people in eastern Nigeria, police say
articles.excerpt:
Gunmen have killed at least 10 people in an attack ⁠⁠on a village in eastern Nigeria, police said, as the country continues to battle banditry and armed groups in several parts of Nigeria.

Nigerian p...
articles.body_text:
Gunmen have killed at least 10 people in an attack ⁠⁠on a village in eastern Nigeria, police said, as the country continues to battle banditry and armed groups in several parts of Nigeria.

Nigerian police said on Saturday that 10 bodies had been recovered as of Friday evening after a large group of gunmen on motorcycles attacked Binnari village in Taraba State.

According to police, the attackers also looted food from shops.

Survivors told the AFP news agency that at least 20 people were killed, while human rights group Amnesty International said in a statement on Saturday that the death toll was 40.

Amnesty International also said that while police ⁠had earlier confirmed the killing of 10 people, more bodies were recovered later on Saturday.

The gunmen opened fire just after Friday prayers, residents said.

“After the attackers left, we counted more than 20 bodies, and some people were still missing,” Binnari resident Sa’idu Nuhu told AFP.

Resident Isiyaku Musa also gave a death toll of at least 20.

Malam Abubakar Saifullahi, a community leader, told AFP that the attackers arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece, before raiding the village.

“They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions. They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack,” Saifullahi said.

Amnesty International criticised the Nigerian authorities, saying they “continue to leave rural communities in some parts of the north at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly committing atrocities with impunity”.

Banditry has become a growing issue in northwest and central Nigeria, with powerful gangs battling overstretched police and military across hard-to-reach, rural locations.

Taraba, a central-eastern state, also faces the non-ideological threat of “bandit” gangs.

Bandits raid villages, kidnap people for ransom, and levy “taxes” on farmers or miners in rural areas of Nigeria with little state presence.

Nigeria has also been fighting an armed rebellion since Boko Haram’s 2009 uprising.

Separately, on Saturday, the Nigerian military said it had killed 15 “terrorists” in northeastern Borno state in an air strike.

articles.title: Obama compares Trump's White House renovations to 'Saddam Hussein opening a Cheesecake Factory' at Ohio rally
articles.excerpt:
Former President Barack Obama returned to the campaign circuit Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, during a midterm rally in Ohio for U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton.

F...
articles.body_text:
Former President Barack Obama returned to the campaign circuit Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, during a midterm rally in Ohio for U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton.

Former President Barack Obama mocked President Donald Trump's White House renovations Saturday, comparing the historic residence to a Cheesecake Factory run by Saddam Hussein while campaigning for Democrats in Ohio.

Obama delivered the jab during a Cleveland rally supporting Democrat gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, criticizing Trump's priorities just 10 days before the midterm elections.

"I mean, I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations," Obama said. "He should be on HGTV."

OBAMA CLAIMS HE OCCUPIES 'A SUITE' IN TRUMP'S MIND, QUESTIONS THE PRESIDENT'S FOCUS ON AMERICANS

Former President Barack Obama speaks during a campaign rally at Cleveland Public Auditorium on Oct. 24, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. Obama took a swipe at President Trump's White House renovations Saturday, despite documented practical uses for the upgrades to the property. (Jeff Swensen/Getty Images)

Obama rattled off Trump's ballroom project, Rose Garden makeover and South Lawn helipad before taking aim at the president's affinity for gold décor.

"He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama quipped.

The renovations, however, include several functional upgrades to the White House grounds.

TRUMP DEFENDS US INTERVENTIONS ABROAD AHEAD OF 'BIG DECISION' ON IRAN: 'SETTLING YEARS OF UNFINISHED BUSINESS'

Tables and chairs in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Friday, Aug. 8, 2025. Trump ordered updates to the Rose Garden in March. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The Rose Garden's former central lawn was replaced with limestone paving in 2025, creating a patio for outdoor events, speeches and entertaining, while the traditional roses were retained around the perimeter.

Trump also unveiled an upgraded granite White House helipad featuring the presidential seal in September. Official White House photographs show Marine One landing on and departing from the new facility during a Sept. 21 ribbon-cutting ceremony.

The administration's ballroom project is intended to provide permanent, secure space for large official events, addressing a longstanding reliance on temporary tents for major White House functions. A National Park Service environmental assessment notes that the need for expanded event space was identified in a White House planning document dating to 2000.

Obama's swipe at Trump's White House makeover comes as his own presidential center in Chicago has faced criticism over its imposing, granite-clad tower, which some critics have dubbed the 'Obamalisk,' along with ballooning construction costs and years of delays.

The Obama Presidential Center's projected price tag has surpassed $1 billion, nearly triple its original $350 million estimate, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting. Subcontractors have alleged they are owed millions for their work, while taxpayers have been saddled with hundreds of millions of dollars in associated public infrastructure costs separate from the center's construction budget.

Obama's criticism extended beyond the presidential residence to Trump's handling of the conflict with Iran, which the former president blamed for higher energy costs.

"Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for and nobody voted for," Obama said.

He also defended the nuclear agreement negotiated during his presidency.

TRUMP RIPS OBAMA'S 'STUPID' IRAN DEAL, CLAIMS FORMER PRESIDENT THOUGHT 'HE COULD BRIBE THEM'

Trump gave a tour of the White House Ballroom construction to the press on  (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"Iran didn't have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place that everybody knows kept them from getting nukes," Obama claimed.

Trump withdrew the United States from the 2015 agreement in 2018, arguing that its temporary nuclear restrictions were insufficient and that it failed to adequately address Iran's ballistic missile program and support for regional militant terror groups.

The agreement offered Tehran sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear restrictions and international inspections. Inspectors reported some Iranian compliance before the U.S. withdrawal, although Iran subsequently expanded uranium enrichment beyond the deal's proposed limits.

Obama also accused Trump of pursuing policies that increased consumer costs, criticizing immigration enforcement as he urged Ohio voters to hold Republicans accountable.

Acton faces Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the governor's race, while Brown is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

The former president carried Ohio in both 2008 and 2012, but the state has backed Trump in his three presidential campaigns.

Fox News Digital contacted the White House for comment on Obama's remarks.

Fox News Digital's Michael Dorgan contributed to this report.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

articles.title: How have Democrats’ policies shifted since the last major US election?
articles.excerpt: Two years after United States voters delivered a stunning rebuke of the country’s Democratic Party by electing Republican President Donald Trump to a second nonconsecutive term, some of the party’s mi...
articles.body_text:
Two years after United States voters delivered a stunning rebuke of the country’s Democratic Party by electing Republican President Donald Trump to a second nonconsecutive term, some of the party’s midterm candidates are reassessing stances on a host of hot-button issues.

Whether they have dialled it back on issues like transgender rights or ramped up efforts to oppose Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Democrats in some of the toughest midterm battleground races are responding to voter concerns – or even breaking outright with party leadership.

Those shifts have resonated with some voters, while others have been alienated as the party tries to find its footing in Trump’s second term and wrestle away control of both houses of Congress from Republicans.

But in the time since Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, Democratic divisions have only grown deeper. Establishment and self-described moderates within the party have struggled to hold back a rising tide of progressive populism as voters increasingly demand stronger, bolder policies.

That movement, powered by groups like the Democratic Socialists of America, has forced a reckoning over what it means to be a Democrat in Trump’s second term, leading to significant differences among candidates on policies that often depend on where they are running.

Here’s how – and why – the party has shifted:

The most notable shift among Democrats has, arguably, been on Israel.

Three years after Israel launched its genocidal war in Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians following Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attacks, polls have suggested that Americans hold increasingly negative views on Israeli military actions.

A Pew Research Center survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 60 percent of US adults had an unfavourable opinion of Israel. That number is significantly higher – 80 percent – among US Democrats.

In response, some longtime Democratic supporters of Israel – including Senator Chris Coons, who is likely to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee if Democrats retake control of the Senate next month – have shifted, as voters, especially younger ones, demand greater accountability from the US ally.

The moderate Delaware Democrat told Politico in an interview this month that he wants a “thorough reexamination” of the US-Israeli relationship and is even willing to impose sanctions on Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

It is a marked change in tone after Harris rejected calls to feature a Palestinian American speaker at the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago.

Earlier this year, 40 Democratic senators voted in support of a motion that disapproved proposed military sales to Israel. Only seven Democratic senators voted with Republicans to block it.

But as a new Congress may include even more progressive voices demanding the US rethink its relationship with Israel, those calls would likely be met with stiff resistance from some in the Democratic leadership, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.

The New York Democrat, who would likely become majority leader if Democrats retake the Senate, has said that the US “commitment to Israel’s security and defense must be ironclad”.

Following years of attacks from Republicans, Democrats in tightly contested US House or Senate races have downplayed – or outright dismissed – support for the transgender community, mostly when it comes to the participation of transgender students in school sports.

In Ohio, Democratic Representative Marcy Kaptur ran an advertisement featuring her saying, “Boys should not play in girls’ sports”. And in North Carolina, Representative Don Davis released a television commercial in which the Democrat says there “should always be a safe and fair space for women and girls in sports”.

Next door in South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews, a doctor, said in a newly released advertisement that she opposes “biological men playing in women’s sports”.

Trump’s return to the White House was fuelled, in part, by a now-famous advertisement in the 2024 campaign that highlighted Harris’s support for transgender Americans.

“Kamala is for they/them,” a narrator said in the advertisement, referring to gender neutral pronouns used by some in the transgender and nonbinary community. “President Trump is for you.”

But the reassessment of transgender rights after the commercial’s airing is not taking place in every part of the party.

On Thursday at a “Students vs Billionaires” town hall in Portland, Maine, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez addressed concerns from a transgender college student who told the New York progressive that they felt “abandoned” by Democrats.

“They’re wrong”, Ocasio-Cortez said about some members of her party. “First and foremost, I want to just let you know how shameful and sorry I am that there are people out there that scare so easily after an election”.

The congresswoman added, “The moment you compromise the rights of a trans person in America, you compromise the rights of every citizen.”

During former US President Joe Biden’s term, Democrats encountered near-daily attacks from Republicans on the country’s immigration system.

US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) recorded more than 8 million encounters at the US-Mexico border between 2021 and 2025, fuelling concerns among some voters that the Biden administration had ignored the issue.

In Texas’s closely watched Senate race, candidate James Talarico has positioned himself as a “border security Democrat”, advocating for stronger border enforcement and comprehensive immigration reform.

Third Way, a US-based organisation that pushes for moderate policies, said stances like Talarico’s resonate better with voters because they have taken a proactive, rather than a reactionary approach.

“I remember very clearly when Harris came out and spoke at the DNC in 2024; she… said we need order at the border and to have a strong immigration system”, Third Way’s senior political adviser, Lucas Holtz, told Al Jazeera.

“The problem is, after that, the Harris campaign really did not stick with that line in the sand… They stopped taking a stand on these issues, and more voters thought that she was too far to the left.”

“[Talarico] is making the case in a lot of his ads that the Biden administration failed on securing the border… It’s putting Republicans on their back foot in some of these races.”

But among progressives, Trump’s response to the nation’s immigration issue has also prompted a strong swing to the left.

After several high-profile incidents earlier this year – including federal immigration agents in Minneapolis, Minnesota, shooting dead US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti  – calls to abolish, or drastically overhaul, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have gained momentum.

Left-leaning political groups and politicians have united behind a message of “abolish ICE”, which would dismantle the federal agency and end its enforcement authority.

As cost-of-living issues remain paramount for voters, Democrats of all stripes have coalesced behind the need for more government intervention in the country’s healthcare system.

But how exactly the party addresses rising medical costs remains up for debate.

Some progressives, including Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, have championed policies like Medicare for All, which would expand the nation’s federal health insurance programme for seniors so all US citizens would be guaranteed healthcare.

Others running in more conservative states, like Andrews, have called for the return of Affordable Care Act subsidies that lapsed during Trump’s second term, as well as limits on health insurance companies’ profits.

Polling released by the independent health organisation KFF suggested that 66 percent of US adults now support Medicare for All, a 13-point increase from October 2020.

“Everybody’s going to have their own approach to this, but by and large, all Democrats want to move to a universal healthcare system in the best way possible”, Holtz said.

“We’re in agreement that we need to do better than what the Trump administration has done.”

articles.title: Indiana outlasts Michigan in overtime for first win at Big House since 1967

There have been few reasons to celebrate in Ann Arbor over the three seasons since Michigan won the Colleg...
articles.body_text:
Indiana Hoosiers got a clutch 4th-down stop that sealed OT win over the Michigan Wolverines.

There have been few reasons to celebrate in Ann Arbor over the three seasons since Michigan won the College Football Playoff national championship.

On Saturday, the Wolverines’ misery continued as they failed to reach the end zone when they needed it most and suffered their third loss of the season, a 13-6 overtime defeat to defending national champion Indiana.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Indiana quarterback Josh Hoover scored on a 4-yard touchdown run in overtime, then the Hoosiers’ defense stopped Michigan on its ensuing possession to secure a 13-6 victory. The win also prevented Indiana from suffering its first two-game losing streak in three years under coach Curt Cignetti and marked the Hoosiers’ first victory at Michigan Stadium since 1967.

OLE MISS AND TEXAS COLLIDE IN MASSIVE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SHOWDOWN WITH ARCH MANNING'S SEASON AT STAKE

Indiana kicker Paddy McAteer misses a field goal at the end of the first half of a college football game Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (AP Photo/Lon Horwedel)

Tommy Carr started at quarterback for the Wolverines, while Bryce Underwood sat out. However, Carr, a freshman, didn’t fare as well as he did last week, when he came off the bench to help Michigan defeat Penn State.

Carr lost a fumble on an ill-advised pitch in the first quarter and was picked off in the second half. He took sacks in the second and third quarters that led to missed field goals, including a 32-yard kick after advancing to the Indiana 1.

Indiana Hoosiers QB Josh Hoover (10) during a college football game between the Ohio State Buckeyes and Indiana Hoosiers on Oct. 17, 2026, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Indiana. (James Black/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Michigan reached the Hoosiers 3 in the final minute of regulation when Carr was sacked for a fourth time, leading to a 26-yard field goal as time expired.

Michigan Wolverines Tommy Carr (14) runs during the third quarter against the Indiana Hoosiers at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on Oct. 24, 2026. (Gregory Shamus/Getty Images)

Hoover struggled, too, until making a 21-yard pass to Brock Schott on the first snap of overtime that set up his touchdown.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Carr finished with 167 passing yards, an interception and a fumble. His brother, Notre Dame quarterback CJ Carr, attended the game while his team had the weekend off. Indiana returns home next week to face Minnesota, while Michigan will look to rebound against Rutgers.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.
