articles.body_text:
Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday to vote for their next president.

They are choosing between Brazil's current left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin.

As Americas correspondent Ione Wells reports from Rio de Janeiro, voters are choosing between two very different candidates.

articles.title: Packers activate Josh Jacobs; running back set to play in first game since domestic violence arrest
articles.excerpt: In an explosive sports talk interview on player safety, Craig Carton and former NFLPA executive director DeMaurice Smith break down the Philadelphia Eagles and NFL's controversial handling of quarterb...
articles.body_text:
In an explosive sports talk interview on player safety, Craig Carton and former NFLPA executive director DeMaurice Smith break down the Philadelphia Eagles and NFL's controversial handling of quarterback Jalen Hurts

Fresh off the commissioner's exempt list, Josh Jacobs will play in his first game on Sunday since his arrest on charges of domestic violence earlier this year.

The Green Bay Packers running back landed on the list following the alleged incident, missing the team's first six games.

But the team activated him on Saturday, and he will likely be the team's lead back in their NFC North matchup against the Detroit Lions.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs (8) reacts after running for a touchdown against the Carolina Panthers during the second half of an NFL football game Sunday, Nov. 2, 2025, in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (AP Photo/Morry Gash)

The league continues to investigate Jacobs' situation despite Jacobs' plea of no contest to both misdemeanor battery and misdemeanor criminal damage to property. Jacobs being removed from the list doesn't hinder the investigation, the NFL has noted, but he is allowed back with the Packers.

Jacobs was placed on the commissioner’s exempt list Aug. 30, three days after charges were filed against him. His status on the commissioner’s exempt list prevented him from playing or practicing, but he still could prepare himself in other ways.

"He could go to meetings," head coach Matt LaFleur said earlier this week. "He could lift with our strength coaches and condition with them. He couldn’t go to any of the team activities – the practices and what not."

Green Bay (4-2) has won three straight, but is averaging just 59.8 yards rushing per game – 16.2 fewer than anyone else. The Packers also are last in the league in yards per carry (2.9). MarShawn Lloyd, Kaleb Johnson and Pierre Strong Jr. all have been given chances to establish themselves. None have been productive.

Jacobs ran for 929 yards and 13 touchdowns while gaining 4 yards per carry last year. That followed a 2024 season in which he rushed for 1,329 yards and 15 touchdowns while making the Pro Bowl.

Jacobs spoke with reporters earlier this week, expressing remorse for his actions.

Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs (8) against the Cincinnati Bengals on Sunday, October 12, 2025, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis. (Reuters)

TRUMP SAYS NFL 'COULD'VE PROBABLY POSTPONED' PARIS GAME AS FRANCE PROTESTS STRETCH POLICE THIN

"Excited to be back with the team, with the guys," he said during his media availability. "I want to say thank you to the organization really for supporting me throughout this whole process and how everything played out.

"With that being said, I can't really get into a lot of things, like specifics of things, but obviously I'm remorseful, and sorry for putting this (team) in this situation.

"Sometimes, when you go through life, situations occur, and a four-second, three-second decision can alter your life honestly. With that being said, still a human being, man, still trying to learn, still trying to grow from the whole process. Actually learned a lot throughout this whole process, legally and just personally."

Jacobs also filed a civil suit last week calling for an injunction and a protective order surrounding evidence, specifically surveillance footage of the incident, which would restrict access to records of the case.

Josh Jacobs of the Green Bay Packers stands for the National Anthem before an NFL wild card playoff game against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field in Chicago, Ill., on Jan. 10, 2026. (Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images)

The Packers and Lions kick off at 4:25 p.m. ET.

OutKick's Scott Thompson and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democratic senator accused of 'political malpractice' after job ad ignites firestorm over DEI language
articles.excerpt: Fox News contributor Mary Katharine Ham discusses Sen. Ed Markey's, D-Mass., internship posting encouraging 'underrepresented candidates' to apply and argues its DEI-focused language comes close to vi...
articles.body_text:
Fox News contributor Mary Katharine Ham discusses Sen. Ed Markey's, D-Mass., internship posting encouraging 'underrepresented candidates' to apply and argues its DEI-focused language comes close to violating hiring laws on 'The Will Cain Show.'

A Democratic senator’s internship job posting was deemed "political malpractice" by an essay in The Atlantic on Friday that argued diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) language can fuel the White identity politics that Democrats oppose.

The commentary by Conor Friedersdorf, headlined "The DEI Language That’s Doing More Harm Than Good," pointed to a social media post from Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., in which he sought interns for his Boston office.

In the post, Markey wrote, "BIPOC, LGBTQ+, working class, veterans, and other underrepresented candidates with Massachusetts ties are encouraged to apply."

TRUMP ADMIN'S PUSH TO SCRAP DEI IN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT TAKES LANDMARK STEP WITH NEW HIRING RULE

Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., at the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, June 4, 2026.  (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The senator’s call for applications sparked criticism online, with critics suggesting Markey was openly discriminating against White men while attempting to appear inclusive.

The Atlantic essay noted that Manhattan Institute senior fellow Christopher Rufo alleged Markey’s internship posting was an open violation of civil rights law and called on the Justice Department to pursue federal charges.

Former Trump Justice Department appointee Theo Wold also weighed in, writing that the goal of the Democratic Party is to make sure White men "have no opportunities to find gainful employment."

Friedersdorf called the senator’s wording "political malpractice," arguing that language that fuels White identity politics is harmful to Americans of all races, even when the intent is good. He added that Democrats should instead adopt rhetoric that clearly commits to equal opportunity.

"White identitarians would exist even in a world without bias of any sort in recruitment or hiring –– but using language that fuels White identity politics, as Markey’s language did, is political malpractice that’s bad for Americans of all races, no matter how well intentioned it might be," the author wrote.

Fox News Digital reached out to Markey's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

NEW YORK TIMES SUED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OVER ALLEGED 'DEI-RELATED' EMPLOYMENT DISCRIMINATION

DEI symbol, Diversity, equality, inclusion, DEI text appearing behind torn paper. (Getty / Stock photo)

The article went on to argue that Democrats were more likely than Republicans to support policies that promote diversity in employment opportunities, which Friedersdorf said have prompted credible allegations of discrimination from White men.

Friedersdorf added that members of Generation Z are even more likely to perceive discrimination against young, White men, and that generational differences can further exacerbate the sentiment.

According to the article, in 2019, about a third of young men said men face some discrimination in America. By 2025, that figure was reportedly 51%.

AOC SAYS ‘WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY,’ BUT DEMOCRATS STILL OWE VOTERS AN EXPLANATION

Sen. Ed Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts, and his wife Susan Blumenthal attend a primary election night watch party at the Omni Parker House in Boston, Mass., on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026.  (Mel Musto/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

However, Markey’s call for applications — and the outrage it sparked — drew the attention of Democratic political strategist Kaivan Shroff, who told Fox News Digital the post may have done more harm than good when it comes to Democrats’ public pledge for equality.

"Markey’s post is exactly the kind of virtue signaling that feeds the outrage cycle without actually doing much for diversity," Shroff said. "If your office genuinely wants a broader applicant pool, you should already have relationships with colleges, community groups and organizations that can get the posting in front of those candidates."

Shroff added that the senator's post appeared to be more about "announcing your values than doing the harder work of diverse recruiting."

"So there is also a basic competence question here," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "A Senate office should not need social media language that makes half the country wonder whether they are less welcome in order to find diverse applicants. That also makes the post look like a substitute for the infrastructure you should already have."

The essay concluded by pointing to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., as a model. Her office’s intern job posting describes it as an equal-opportunity employer and encourages "all individuals from all backgrounds" to apply — a notable difference from Markey’s own solicitation.

Warren’s approach was echoed by Shroff, who noted how Democrats have increasingly turned social flashpoints into easy lay-ups for their opponents.

"The larger political mistake is that Democrats keep handing the right these easy cultural fights for almost no substantive benefit," the Democratic strategist said. "Most people understand the argument for widening opportunity and even rebalancing past unfairness where possible."

"What they resent is language that makes it sound like to lift up one group or groups you have to put down or exclude another and that is just unproductive — and incorrect," Shroff added. "Politics is all about addition and not subtraction, so it’s a wrongheaded approach."

Julia Bonavita is a media and culture writer for Fox News Digital, and a Fox Flight Team drone pilot. You can follow her at @juliabonavita13 on all platforms and send story tips to julia.bonavita@fox.com.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula, Bolsonaro draw thousands to election-eve rallies
articles.excerpt: Brazil’s presidential candidates Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro have rallied thousands of supporters in a final show of campaign strength in advance of the country’s closely contested ...
articles.body_text:
Brazil’s presidential candidates Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro have rallied thousands of supporters in a final show of campaign strength in advance of the country’s closely contested run-off election.

Donning a red hat, Lula addressed hundreds of supporters at Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach on Saturday, waving a Brazilian flag from a campaign truck as crowds gathered on the final day of campaigning.

“The people must choose either someone who kisses the national flag or someone who kisses the American flag”, the 80-year-old told the crowd as he referenced his opponent’s ties to US President Donald Trump.

Lula is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term in Sunday’s run-off, which will task Brazilians with determining whether to stick with their incumbent left-wing leader or join a broader regional shift towards the right.

Bolsonaro, a senator and son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, secured 47 percent of the vote in the first round, narrowly ahead of Lula’s 45 percent.

Recent polling shows Lula and the younger Bolsonaro remain about even on the eve of the pivotal election.

A CNT/MDA survey released on Saturday revealed Bolsonaro would receive 46.3 percent of the vote compared ⁠with 45 percent for the left-wing ⁠Lula. Last week, ⁠the poll showed a slightly closer race with Bolsonaro leading ⁠Lula 46.8 percent to ⁠45.9 percent.

The poll’s margin of error was 2.2 ‌percentage ‌points.

On Saturday, Bolsonaro’s supporters, including hundreds of motorcyclists wearing Brazil’s yellow national football shirts, gathered in the southeastern state of Minas Gerais.

One of those supporters, Ebert Dorigo, accused Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT) of encouraging dependence on government welfare, arguing a change in direction was needed for the country.

“The values we uphold are nation and family. Our country is divided today because, due to welfare-based policies, some people … haven’t grasped that improvement and achievement come only through hard work,” he told the news agency AFP.

The bitter campaign has exposed deep divisions over economic policy, crime and Brazil’s political future, which Bolsonaro has pledged to tackle with hundreds of thousands of more spots in prison and cuts to government spending.

His father, who served as president from 2019 to 2022, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after losing that year’s election to Lula.

The two candidates struck a calmer tone during their final debate on Friday, although they traded accusations over the country’s economic difficulties and their respective records.

For some voters, however, the choice has been a difficult one.

“If there were any other candidate, that would be a better option,” Gabriela Ribeiro Viana, an event organiser, told AFP. “But we’re stuck choosing between the worst, the horrible, and the lesser evil”.

articles.title: David Spade and Dana Carvey call out Hollywood for focusing too much on race and gender
articles.excerpt: David Spade, Dana Carvey, and Tim Dillon spoke about how the entertainment industry in LA has been in crisis for years, to the point that people and projects are fleeing to other states. ("Fly on the ...
articles.body_text:
David Spade, Dana Carvey, and Tim Dillon spoke about how the entertainment industry in LA has been in crisis for years, to the point that people and projects are fleeing to other states. ("Fly on the Wall" podcast, April 8, 2026)

David Spade and Dana Carvey call out Hollywood's focus on race and gender.

In a recent episode of their "Fly on the Wall" podcast, the two comedians questioned Hollywood's emphasis on race and gender, with Spade arguing that the industry should "stop separating us like that" by highlighting those distinctions.

"On race, let me just say at any of these award shows, I saw a clip the other day saying, 'And this gentleman won, and he's the first black director to win for this documentary,' I wish they would quit saying that because I think everyone we can't all be equal to you," Spade said. "'Oh, the first in 30 years to have a black actor win this.' If you just say we're all actors . . .now this is my point of view, that it just makes it more even and not, we're all just the same. We're all acting."

Carvey then joked that when he won his Emmy Award, they announced that he was the "198th straight white male that has won this award."

Spade called out the focus on race and gender in Hollywood during a recent podcast episode. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Netflix)

ISSA RAE SAYS DEI HAS BECOME A 'BAD WORD' IN HOLLYWOOD AS EXECUTIVES OF COLOR 'TIPTOE' TO KEEP JOBS

Spade also pointed out that while he was working on the hit NBC show, "Just Shoot Me," from 1997 to 2003, they would inform him anytime they would be working with a female director that week.

"I [would] go, 'That's fine. Just is it a director? Yeah. Okay, we got it.' Like you don't even have to say that," Spade said. "Female director. It feels like a little, not condescending, but a little diminishing. That's a good word. It's a little 5%. Instead of going, 'We don't have a regular director,' you know what I mean? So, I was a big proponent of fighting that."

Carvey agreed with his co-host, mentioning that "female director" is "a funny thing to say."

In a previous episode of their podcast released in March, Spade gave his candid opinion on the state of Hollywood under the leadership of Governor Gavin Newsom and Mayor Karen Bass, "the Hollywood industry is dying" and that he's "just trying to put the blame somewhere."

Spade previously spoke about the state of Hollywood. (Phillip Faraone/VF25/Getty Images for Vanity Fair)

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"Dude, I'm so old," he said. "I was on the lot at, uh, CBS Radford when we were doing ‘Just Shoot Me.’ … And also they were doing 'Seinfeld,' and I'd see him on his bike. It was the greatest lot. Of course, just filed for bankruptcy, the lot. Terrifying in LA Thanks, [LA Mayor] Karen Bass. Thanks, [Gov.] Gavin [Newsom]."

The mayor's press office responded to Spade's claims at the time, telling Fox News Digital in a statement, "Mayor Bass has championed the entertainment industry because it’s a bedrock of our middle class.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"This year alone, she slashed filming fees at Griffith Observatory and reopened the LA Central Library to film production for the first time in over a decade," the statement added. "Under her leadership, more than 3 million square feet of studio and creative office space have been approved, and over 120 sound stages are now under construction across Los Angeles."

In April, Spade and Carvey revisited Hollywood's struggles when comedian Tim Dillon joined their podcast as a guest.

Spade asked for Hollywood to become more of a priority when it comes to California leadership. (Gonzalo Marroquin/Getty Images for Netflix)

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

During the episode, Spade recalled how he "got in trouble" for his previous comments, clarifying, "I wasn't really mad at Gavin Newsom and Karen Bass."

"I was just saying, ‘Could we make it a slightly more of a priority? I don't know what we're spending the money on that's flowing in, because it's a lot flowing in, but it goes out so quickly. I want to sort of reserve a little piece of the pie to like focus, like let's try to get this back,’" Spade said. "That's all."

Although Spade softened his criticism of California's leadership, Dillon argued that Bass and Newsom "seem to think everything's kind of going well," adding, "When someone thinks things are going well, it's very hard to make them understand" that people are leaving.

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Healey’s first budget to include big devolution package to boost growth
articles.excerpt:
Chancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’

Andy Burnham has promised that local leaders in England will no longe...
articles.body_text:
Chancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’

Andy Burnham has promised that local leaders in England will no longer have to come “cap in hand to Westminster” ahead of a fresh drive to devolve spending power in next week’s budget.

In his statement on Wednesday, the chancellor, John Healey, will include plans for a new £1.5bn borrowing facility, to be drawn up in collaboration with mayors over the next two years.

Regional mayors have long complained that they are constrained by their limited borrowing power – in contrast to local authorities in the US and some European countries, which commonly issue their own bonds.

The borrowing plan will form part of a big devolution package aimed at boosting regional economic growth. This will also include the allocation of an initial £285m “good growth” funding next year, to be spent on local leaders’ priorities – which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.

Amid fears in the Treasury about whether some local authorities have the capacity to administer increasingly large budgets, Healey will also announce £150m of support to help them scale up and build expertise.

Hailing the plans, Burnham said they would mean local leaders would no longer need to come to the Treasury for approval for each individual project. “I’m calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country. When I became prime minister, I said that if a decision can be made closer to home, it should be.

“Today we’re putting that into practice, shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best.”

The £285m in “good growth” funding is intended to tide local authorities over until a new system comes into force in 2028 whereby some income tax revenue will be handed directly to their areas to give them longer-term security – an idea first mooted by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, earlier this year.

More details of how this will work will be announced at the budget. Local leaders are expected to be allowed to keep some of the additional revenues created by a stronger local economy, giving them an incentive to back pro-growth policies.

Tax and spending in the UK is more centralised than in many other leading economies, and Burnham experienced the constraints first-hand as mayor of Greater Manchester.

Healey said: “Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas.”

The package has been drawn up in collaboration with No 10 North, which has been holding a weekly “situation room” meeting with local leaders, to ask them about the barriers to promoting economic growth.

This resulted in an announcement this week that the Treasury has called the “green book”, which gives guidanceon which projects taxpayers should fund. Under the new rules, projects that can be combined to boost growth – a housing and a transport scheme, for example – can be considered together.

A government white paper on “rewiring the state”, due to be published after the budget, will set out more details of how the civil service will be reshaped, as more powers are passed down from Whitehall.

Alongside the devolution plans, Healey’s first budget is expected to include support for poorer households hit by rising energy costs; and modest tax rises, including on banks. The chancellor has repeatedly said he wants to offer a “breathing space” to households and businesses that have struggled as the war in the Middle East has driven up bills.

These higher costs have also pushed up the interest rates on government borrowing, making it harder for Healey to balance the books.

He will set out how he plans to fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced in the dying days of Keir Starmer’s premiership.

However, Healey is not expected to say when the UK will commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence – an issue that was central to his resignation from Starmer’s cabinet. This is likely to be delayed until a spending review due at some point next year.

articles.title: Iran blames US for deal failure, urges new try amid fear of new attacks
articles.excerpt: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has blamed Washington for the unravelling of an interim deal aimed at ending the war with the United States and Israel, amid growing fears that the fighting could r...
articles.body_text:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has blamed Washington for the unravelling of an interim deal aimed at ending the war with the United States and Israel, amid growing fears that the fighting could resume imminently.

In comments broadcast by Iranian Press TV on Saturday, But Pezeshkian also said that both sides should return to the deal and “conclude it”.

His remarks come amid growing fears that military action could resume as soon as this weekend, after US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he “may do another little Epic Fury”, using the codename of the US-Israeli war against Iran that started on February 28.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has warned that even limited strikes would trigger a response “several times greater”, according to comments reported by the semi-official Fars News Agency.

Iranian Armed Forces Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi said on Saturday that the US military would not be allowed in the Gulf “under any circumstances and at any time”. Abdollahi said Trump could only “dream” of seeing US forces enter the Gulf, adding that he would take his dream to the grave.

Trump has suggested he could take further military action against Iran, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he remains committed to overthrowing the country’s government.

Both leaders face elections, with Israelis set to choose their next government on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trump’s Republican Party faces crucial midterm elections on November 3, with Democrats potentially winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Such an outcome would be a major blow to Trump, who still has more than two years left in his final term in the White House.

Iranian government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said on Saturday that Tehran would not “wait for permission to defend itself”, adding that the country “seeks peace but will respond to any aggression with severe consequences”.

“Our position is clear: we do not flee from dialogue for peace, and we do not hesitate in defending the country. Those who harbour the illusion of destroying Iran must correct their calculations,” Mohajerani wrote in a memo.

Her comments came as Iranian judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The pair discussed how to tackle corruption and pursue compensation for Iranians affected by the US-Israeli war, among other issues.

Khamenei replaced his father as supreme leader after the latter was assassinated during the opening strikes of the war on February 28. He has not been seen in public since assuming the position in early March.

Parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf was reported to have met Khamenei earlier this week.

articles.title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
articles.excerpt:
Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protestors during skirmishes

Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were follo...
articles.body_text:
Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protestors during skirmishes

Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.

After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.

But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.

The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.

Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them

Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.

President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.

Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.

Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.

In the southern port of Marseille, protesters erected makeshift street barricades and set them alight late on Saturday

In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.

Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.

In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.

"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.

Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.

The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.

"We really want a change in France," a teenage protester told the BBC

Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.

"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.

Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.

"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."

He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".

Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of Orléans which proceeded peacefully.

Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.

In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.

In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.

Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.

Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.

One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.

The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.

The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

articles.title: Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden
articles.excerpt:
Houthi fighters have launched a series of attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in Aden.

In a Facebook post on Saturday, the Yemeni governme...
articles.body_text:
Houthi fighters have launched a series of attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in Aden.

In a Facebook post on Saturday, the Yemeni government’s Transport Ministry denounced what it described as the Houthis’ targeting of Aden International Airport with two ballistic missiles, calling it the “fourth such attack this month”.

The airport attacks pose “a threat to the safety of civil aviation” and have “humanitarian and economic repercussions for citizens” who rely on it, the ministry warned.

Yemeni authorities said that the coastguard headquarters and a second building were also hit.

The Houthis claimed attacks on the al-Nasr camp and Aden’s naval military base.

Yemen’s army said a Houthi missile killed three people when it malfunctioned and fell on a family home in Houthi-held Sanaa on Friday. The army said it was one of a number of missile malfunctions seen in recent weeks by the Iran-backed group.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV said on Saturday that Saudi coalition air strikes killed several civilians in Sanaa and in the port city of Hodeidah. The claim could not be verified and Riyadh has not commented on the alleged raids.

Also on Saturday, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said on X that the Houthis had launched two ballistic missiles towards Mecca and Medina, warning of “the fall of shrapnel” following their interception.

Images shared on X by the Saudi Press Agency appeared to show a large, blackened missile-shaped object that had landed somewhere in Saudi Arabia.

Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, Secretary-General of the Gulf Cooperation Council, described the Houthi attacks as “heinous”, which embody “a blatant disregard for the lives and security of civilians” in a statement shared on Saturday.

The Houthis said the claim that they targeted the two cities – the holiest in Islam – was a “huge lie”. They said their targets were three Saudi airports, oil infrastructure, and an airbase.

The Houthis have persistently targeted Saudi energy infrastructure and airports across the country with long-range strikes since a fragile ceasefire agreed in 2022 fell apart in July.

Intense fighting is continuing on Yemen’s front lines as the Houthis battle forces of the internationally recognised government for control of key areas.

On Saturday, Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said that government forces had carried out more than 700 “targeting operations” over the last 24 hours across Yemen, “neutralising” 300 Houthi fighters and disabling military vehicles.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.

Operations targeted field command centres, Houthi gatherings, weapons depots, and supply lines in Taiz, where intense clashes have been ongoing for days, the spokesman added.

articles.title: Beverly Hills school board candidate under fire over messages mocking trustee's visit to Jewish holy site
articles.excerpt: Beverly Hills school board candidate Kim Lifschitz faced allegations of antisemitism after screenshots appeared to show her mocking trustee Russell Stuart's visit to Jerusalem's Western Wall. (Russell...
articles.body_text:
Beverly Hills school board candidate Kim Lifschitz faced allegations of antisemitism after screenshots appeared to show her mocking trustee Russell Stuart's visit to Jerusalem's Western Wall. (Russell Stuart)

Beverly Hills school board candidate Kim Lifschitz faced accusations of antisemitism this week after screenshots surfaced appearing to mock a trustee's visit to Jerusalem's Western Wall, while a separate controversy involving her husband's comments featured on a livestream by Twitch streamer Hasan Piker resurfaced.

The screenshots show messages labeled with Lifschitz's name responding to a Beverly Hills Standard article documenting Beverly Hills Unified School District Board of Education member Russell Stuart's New Year's Day visit to the Western Wall, one of Judaism's holiest sites.

One message attributed to Lifschitz appeared to ridicule his kippah, a traditional Jewish head covering. "Maybe he can bust out the kippah from his dress up trunk," the message said.

Another message attributed to Lifschitz appeared later in the conversation, continuing the joke about Stuart's religious head covering, saying, "He probably used it to store his complimentary in-flight nuts."

RIHANNA'S BEVERLY HILLS HOME TARGETED IN BRAZEN DAYLIGHT SHOOTING

Beverly Hills Unified School District trustee Russell Stuart condemned the alleged remarks about his religious observance, telling Fox News Digital that mocking his visit to Jerusalem's Western Wall crossed the line from political criticism into religious ridicule. (Russell Stuart)

Stuart, whose family is Jewish, condemned the messages in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying political disagreements do not justify ridiculing religious practices.

"I found them deeply offensive," he said. "My visit to the Western Wall was personal and meaningful to me. Seeing a kippah described as something from a 'dress up trunk' turns Jewish religious observance into a costume and a punchline."

"Anyone is welcome to challenge my votes, my positions or my work on the school board. Mocking my religious observance crosses a very different line," he continued.

Lifschitz pushed back against the allegations in a statement to Fox News Digital, acknowledging that the nearly year-old messages came from a private group chat while arguing that her criticism concerned what she described as Stuart's use of Jewish religious symbols to gain political support.

"I said nothing antisemitic at all. In fact, I criticized Russell Stuart for disrespecting Jewish culture and observance," she said. "He was treating a kippah like a costume used in a performance, and he afforded it the same amount of respect one would give a container for airplane snacks."

"I didn’t 'attack' Russell Stuart for wearing a kippah or visiting the Western Wall," Lifschitz continued. "I expressed disgust that he turned those things into internet content."

EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE LA'S HOMELESS HELLSCAPE — UNLIKELY CRITICS BLAST DEMS AS GOP HOPEFUL TOURS SKIR ROW

Beverly Vista Middle School on Monday, Feb. 26, 2024 in Beverly Hills, CA. (Jason Armond / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

California GOP Jewish Engagement Chair and attorney Elizabeth Barcohana, who has publicly criticized Lifschitz's candidacy, also condemned the school board hopeful, accusing her of being "prejudiced, rude, and unserious about education or the well-being of children."

Lifschitz, who identified herself as Jewish, also pointed to her personal experiences with antisemitism when explaining why she questioned Stuart's intentions.

"As a Jewish woman who has experienced plenty of antisemitism in her lifetime and who has a son who cannot protect himself from it, it's hardly surprising that I assumed the worst about his intentions, given the evidence available to me," Lifschitz said.

A newly circulated screenshot shows a group-chat message labeled with Lifschitz's name appearing to ridicule BHUSD Board Vice President Sigalie Sabag for discussing Holocaust survivors. According to the Beverly Hills Standard, the remark concerned Sabag's discussion of survivors who had spoken with district students.

"Love that Sigalie is talking about holocaust survivors like she collected the most Pokémon," the message said.

Stuart characterized the comments concerning his religious observance as antisemitic and called on Lifschitz to address them directly.

"I consider the remarks attributed to her antisemitic because they ridicule Jewish religious observance and an identifiable symbol of Jewish faith. I cannot speak to what was in her heart, but I can speak to the words," Stuart said.

HASAN PIKER POINTS THE FINGER AT AIPAC AS DEMOCRATS SPEAK OUT AGAINST HIM

Lifschitz's husband is also drawing criticism over Twitch streamer Hasan Piker praising him in 2025.  (Sam Barnes/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images)

The controversy comes as Lifschitz competes for one of two seats on the BHUSD Board of Education in the Nov. 3 election. During an October interview with the Beverly Press, she emphasized combating discrimination and modeling appropriate behavior for students.

"You have to be a role model," she said. "You have to model the conduct that we are expecting from our children."

The allegations follow previous scrutiny involving Lifschitz's husband, Daniel Lifschitz, who wrote on Instagram that a clip of him had been featured on far-left streamer Hasan Piker's livestream after publicly criticizing the district's antisemitism resolution, according to a screenshot posted by Barcohana on X.

"I just wanted to make some MAGA folks on the school board feel bad and now I'm on [Hasan Piker's] livestream..." Daniel Lifschitz said in an Instagram post.

During a September 2025 livestream, Piker replayed a Fox 11 Los Angeles report by Chelsea Edwards concerning the district's decision to reverse a proposal to display Israeli flags during Jewish American Heritage Month. The footage featured Daniel Lifschitz criticizing the original resolution.

Piker praised Lifschitz's comments and compared displaying Israeli flags to displaying Nazi flags during a hypothetical German-American heritage commemoration.

Kim Lifschitz previously disputed claims that her husband appeared as an invited guest on Piker's program, explaining that the streamer had independently replayed television footage featuring his public remarks.

She also defended the private nature of the group-chat conversation, accusing Stuart and his supporters of seeking out critical remarks and using them to portray her negatively.

"Adults are allowed to dislike each other and talk about it amongst themselves in private chats," she said. "Seeking out the opinions of those you know dislike you, and then painting them as monsters when you 'catch' them doing what you expected them to do, is the equivalent of putting a stick through the wheel of your own bicycle."

Barcohana criticized the district's previous leadership and teachers' union, arguing that Beverly Hills parents had pushed for greater accountability over school spending and education policy.

"Parents in Beverly Hills worked very hard to take control of their children’s education back from the teachers’ union and other special interests, who allowed taxpayer money to be squandered without proper oversight," Barcohana told Fox News Digital.

"Once that happened, incompetent and unpopular school principals, teachers, and the superintendent were fired and replaced; student test scores and academic achievement improved, budgets got under control and teacher pay increased to record highs, and enrollment increased," she said.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

articles.body_text:
The trailer for 20th Century Studios' "Whalefall" starring Austin Abrams, Josh Brolin, John Ortiz and Elisabeth Shue. Directed by Brian Duffield.

Josh Brolin starts his mornings with a commitment to sobriety.

The "Dune" star said he joins a recovery meeting on Zoom every morning at 6 a.m. sharp, making the daily commitment a cornerstone of his life after years of struggling with drinking.

"Drinking got boring in the end," Brolin told The Telegraph when asked how long he had been sober.

JOSH BROLIN WATCHED MAN GET BIT BY LION WHILE GROWING UP ON WILDLIFE RANCH

Josh Brolin said he worked as a stock trader full-time in his 30s, when his Hollywood career was floundering. (Getty Images)

He recalled waking up on the sidewalk outside his house once again, a moment that prompted him to question the direction of his life.

"Which way was I going to go for the rest of my life?" he said.

Brolin said he attends the daily meetings as part of his recovery, insisting sobriety has brought him more enjoyment than drinking ever did.

ZACH BRYAN ADMITS HE DRANK '15 BEERS A DAY' AS PART OF 'PERFECT ROUTINE' BEFORE QUITTING ALCOHOL

Josh Brolin attends the 2025 Arlington Artist Award ceremony in Santa Barbara, Calif. (Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images for Santa Barbara International Film Festival)

"I love being sober. I’m having way more fun now than I ever did drinking, and I never end up in jail, which is a real bonus," he said.

The candid admission highlights how Brolin has embraced a daily routine to maintain his sobriety.

Brolin has also opened up about another addiction he has struggled to overcome — nicotine.

'EVERYBODY LOVES RAYMOND' STAR PATRICIA HEATON REVEALS THE MORTIFYING MOMENT THAT MADE HER QUIT DRINKING

During a 2024 appearance on the "WTF with Marc Maron" podcast, the actor revealed that nicotine pouches had become a near-constant presence after he gave up chewing tobacco. He said he kept the pouches "all over the house" and sometimes used them without even realizing it.

"My wife would hear this in the middle of the night," Brolin said before mimicking a chewing noise. "I don't even know I'm doing it. I'm asleep. I have a pouch in my lip, and I'm not f---ing lying — 24 hours a day."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Josh Brolin and wife Kathryn were married in 2016 and have two children. (Lisa O'Connor/Getty Images)

"Then I started taking them out and putting them on the bedside table," he said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Brolin detailed his addiction journey in his memoir, "From Under the Truck." (Getty Images)

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, nicotine pouches contain nicotine, flavorings and other ingredients, with nicotine absorbed through the gums and lining of the mouth. The agency says nicotine is highly addictive and that more research is needed to understand the products' short- and long-term health effects.

Brolin's comments underscore the challenges he has faced with nicotine even as he celebrates his sobriety from alcohol.

Brolin has spoken openly about his past struggles and his decision to turn his life around. In his 2024 memoir, "From Under the Truck," he explored the personal experiences that shaped his relationship with addiction and recovery.

The actor, known for roles in "Avengers: Endgame" and "No Country for Old Men," stars alongside Austin Abrams and Elisabeth Shue in "Whalefall."

articles.title: Texas Tech’s $30 million roster runs into a buzzsaw as Cincinnati delivers Sorsby revenge in Top-10 upset
articles.excerpt:

Even ...
articles.body_text:
The College Football Playoffs are set to expand from 12 to 24 teams starting next season, and Craig Carton asked former Heisman trophy finalist and CFB analyst Ryan Leaf his take on the change.

Even though former quarterback Brendan Sorsby was obviously not on the field today for No. 8 Texas Tech, the Cincinnati Bearcats had this game circled on the calendar for nearly an entire year.

Call it a revenge game for what had taken place leading up to the 2026 season, or the Red Raiders finally running into a team that could present a viable challenge, this expensive roster that was assembled through the transfer portal ran into a buzz saw on Saturday afternoon.

The reality check for this Texas Tech football team took place in the first half, trailing 24-6 as both teams ran into the locker room after what was an eye-opening performance by the Red Raiders offense with two turnovers and just six points.

Cincinnati would end up winning 37-24, in a game that never truly felt close after the opening 10 minutes.

And, for a squad that could not afford a Big 12 loss like this with how BYU and Utah are currently playing, the uncomfortable truth is that head coach Joey McGuire had to rely on quarterback Will Hammond to lead this football team after Brendan Sorsby was ruled ineligible for the season due to his gambling situation.

But most importantly, the Red Raiders are just not as explosive as what we saw in 2025.

For a lot of college football fans, they will look at this result as karma for making their Big 12 colleagues file a federal lawsuit in order to scare Texas Tech enough to end the charade surrounding Sorsby suiting up for the Red Raiders this season.

BIG 12 FILES LAWSUIT AGAINST TEXAS TECH SEEKING COURT APPROVAL TO SANCTION SCHOOL OVER BRENDAN SORSBY

Joey McGuire of the Texas Tech Red Raiders looks on during the first half of a game against the Cincinnati Bearcats at Nippert Stadium on Oct. 24, 2026, in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Getty Images)

But there was no denying what type of beating we all witnessed on Saturday in Cincinnati, where the Red Raiders looked like a mediocre football team that had spent more than $35 million on their roster this season in hopes of competing for a CFP title.

Well, unless the Big 12 sees an absolute meltdown over the next 45 days, Texas Tech will undoubtedly be looking back at this performance on the road as the culprit for its season taking a drastic turn.

Following the 2025 season, the former Bearcats quarterback decided it was in his best interest to enter the transfer portal and cash in on his play on the field.

It was no secret within the college football world that Texas Tech had all but officially signed Sorsby towards the end of last season.

TEXAS TECH QB BRENDAN SORSBY ENTERING TREATMENT FOR GAMBLING ADDICTION AMID NCAA INVESTIGATION

So, when the Bearcats athletic department decided to sue Brendan for a buyout tied to a contract signed with Cincinnati, it was clear that his former team was not going to make the transition to Lubbock an easy one.

Future Texas Tech quarterback Brendan Sorsby shouts during the first half of the game between the Houston Cougars and Texas Tech Red Raiders at United Supermarkets Arena in Lubbock, Texas, on Jan. 24, 2026. (John E. Moore III/Getty Images)

Turns out, just a few months after arriving at Texas Tech, Sorsby was embroiled in an NCAA investigation tied to thousands of bets placed during his college career, with a number of them coming while he was on the roster at Indiana. These bets were flagged by law enforcement officials, who then turned them over to the NCAA.

BRENDAN SORSBY GAMBLED ON HIS OWN TEAM, YET THE NCAA IS SOMEHOW THE BAD GUY IN THIS CASE

Just before summer officially got underway, Sorsby filed a lawsuit against the NCAA in Lubbock district court, where an injunction was granted that would have allowed him to suit up this season for the Red Raiders. Then came the backlash from across college athletics, with the Big 12 conference searching for ways in which it could possibly punish Texas Tech.

Things had gotten so tense around the situation between the Red Raiders and its conference that Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sent a letter to Big 12 officials, warning them that if the conference were to punish the school for playing Sorsby, the state would take them to court in return.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Big 12 was prepared to file a federal lawsuit in order to enforce its own rules, which obviously scared Texas Tech enough to finally fold its hand and make the decision to not continue pushing for Sorsby to play thanks to a court order.

But through all of the nonsense around the school and conference, it was Cincinnati that still had a lawsuit against its former quarterback.

TEXAS TECH CANNOT PLAY THE VICTIM IN BRENDAN SORSBY SAGA, IT COULD’VE DEALT WITH PR MESS MONTHS AGO

Lyviel Waters No. 85 of the Cincinnati Bearcats scores a touchdown against the Texas Tech Red Raiders during the first half at Nippert Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio, on Oct. 24, 2026. (Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Thanks to plenty of teams sitting atop the conference currently, with No. 14 Houston facing No. 10 Utah tonight, and No. 2 BYU making a major statement over the past seven weeks, the Red Raiders would ultimately find themselves on the outside looking in.

A roster that mega-booster Cody Campbell touted in the offseason now finds itself staring down the barrel of a season that doesn’t involve the CFP, unless the Red Raiders can find themselves playing for a conference title.

Could Texas Tech stay in contention within the Big 12?

Sure, given the toughest game on paper will come next week against Arizona.

But, the Red Raiders are now in very dangerous territory with an expensive roster.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

Michael Douglas is opening up about the "art" of filming sex scenes, revealing that the intimate moments require extensive communication and trust between actors.

During a recent appearance on "Happy, Sad, Confused" with Josh Horowitz, the 82-year-old actor reflected on filming sex scenes earlier in his career, before intimacy coordinators became commonplace on movie sets.

"There’s an art to sex scenes in films. It’s not easy to do things like shadowing people when you’re on top and this and that," Douglas said.

MICHAEL DOUGLAS REVEALS HE MADE FIVE PHONE CALLS TO FIVE WOMEN THE DAY HE CHOSE CATHERINE ZETA-JONES

Michael Douglas gets candid about the "art" of filming sex scenes. (Getty Images)

"But the big thing with sex scenes is trust," he continued. "And as long as the lady is trusting me — obviously I trust her — it’s like a dance. You’re taking the lead."

Douglas explained that actors carefully discuss each movement before filming begins.

BILLY BALDWIN ADMITS HE REFUSED TO KISS CO-STAR AFTER WEEKS OF TENSION ON SET

"You just talk it out slowly. ‘Kiss, kiss, bite. Looking at you. Is it all right to touch your breasts?’ ‘Yes.’ ’All right, I'm touching your breasts. Kiss. Kiss,'" he said. "You do it, and it’s just like choreographing a fight scene."

Michael Douglas and Sharon Stone are seen on the set of "Basic Instinct." (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

"You start very slowly … and then action. It makes it look like it really happens," Douglas added.

'TEACHER'S PET' STAR MAMIE VAN DOREN SAYS SHE FELT 'USED' AS YOUNG ACTRESS NAVIGATING HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE

The "Wall Street" star also emphasized the importance of making female performers feel comfortable on set, particularly when they are surrounded by a predominantly male crew.

"It’s awkward enough for ladies, in terms of being mostly surrounded by a male crew and everything, especially in those days, to make sure that they were as comfortable as possible," he said.

Douglas also compared acting to working as part of an ensemble, explaining that he has always prioritized the overall quality of a project over the size of his own role.

"I've always thought your role is one small part of the whole," he said. "And so what you really need … is better actors around you. You want the best you can get because it’s the whole thing that matters."

"I’d rather be good in a little movie than lousy in a big part," Douglas added.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Michael Douglas, seen with Sharon Stone in "Basic Instinct," said that he's always seen his acting roles as being "one small part" of a much bigger project. (TriStar/Getty Images)

In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," Douglas pulled back the curtain on the most explosive moments of his life, both in front of the camera and behind the scenes.

Douglas detailed his volatile relationship with his late father, Kirk Douglas, his son Cameron’s addiction and imprisonment, and the Stage 4 cancer diagnosis that forced him to confront his own mortality.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Michael Douglas detailed the complicated relationship with his father, Kirk, in his recent memoir. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images for AFI)

At one point, while filming "Adam at 6 A.M." early in his career, Douglas wrote that he and his married co-star, Lee Purcell, became romantically involved.

"As filming progressed, my relationship with Lee changed and we became lovers," he wrote. "Our intimate relationship was complicated by the fact that she was married, and we had to keep it a secret from the cast, crew, the people in the town we were filming in, and of course her husband. It was a passionate affair that lasted through filming."

Purcell disputed Douglas’ account in a statement to Fox News Digital.

SHARON STONE SAYS SHE 'NEARLY DIED' AFTER 'BASIC INSTINCT' OPENED THE DOOR TO HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE

"This story came as a complete surprise to me. I have fond memories of Michael and our time together. However, our recall appears to differ," she said. "First, I remember the process of searching for his character of Adam after having already been hired by Steve McQueen for the role of Jerri Jo. Secondly, we had a strictly professional relationship during filming. The personal one came much later."

In his memoir, Michael Douglas revealed that he broke up with five women before embarking on a romance with wife Catherine Zeta-Jones. (David M. Benett)

Years later, while making "Romancing the Stone," Douglas also wrote that he had an affair with screenwriter Diane Thomas, who wrote the film. He said he and his first wife, Diandra, were both involved in extramarital relationships as their marriage deteriorated.

Heritage Foundation Chief Economist EJ Antoni analyzes why cruise stocks, like Royal Caribbean, are rising. They discuss how cheaper fuel from potential Middle East energy flows boosts profitability.

A cruise scheduled to sail to the sunny Bahamas this week took a northward turn for the worse when it got rerouted to chilly Canada instead.

More than 5,000 passengers boarded Royal Caribbean’s Oasis of the Seas in New Jersey on Oct. 18, expecting a seven-day cruise to Florida and the Bahamas. But forecasts of stormy weather off the East Coast prompted the cruise line to change the itinerary, sending the ship north to Halifax, Nova Scotia, according to reports.

The ship stopped in Halifax for about 24 hours, giving passengers time to explore ashore, shop and take harbor rides. It departed Wednesday evening and is scheduled to return to New Jersey on Sunday after three days at sea.

OUTRAGED CRUISE PASSENGERS SOUND OFF ABOUT 'IMMENSE DISAPPOINTMENT' AFTER ABRUPT CANCELLATION

The line announced the changed itinerary the evening before the ship sailed, according to reports, leaving passengers with little time to adjust.

Royal Caribbean replaced the Oasis of the Seas’ planned Florida and Bahamas stops with a call in Halifax after forecasts of stormy weather off the East Coast. (iStock)

"My husband said to me, 'This is a joke, right?'" New Jersey resident Marie Durning told CTV News. "I have my winter hat and earmuffs, but I forgot my scarf," she said, adding that she was left scrambling to repack.

Daytime temperatures hovered in the upper 40s to low 50s this week in Halifax, with overnight lows in the 30s, according to weather reports.

ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS SAY FRUSTRATING ISSUE SHOULD HAVE BEEN DISCLOSED BEFORE BOOKING

For some, the surprise destination was a chance to make the most of an unfamiliar city.

"I’m grateful and I’m going to make the best of it," Jim Matthews, who lives near Paterson, New Jersey, told the outlet. "And I have found out that Halifax is a beautiful city."

Passengers (not pictured) had only hours’ notice before their Bahamas-bound cruise was redirected to Nova Scotia. (iStock)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"I am already from Canada, and I wanted to go to the Bahamas," Nicholas Meli, who drove seven hours with his family from Toronto to New Jersey to board, told CTV News.

Online, commenters in Reddit’s r/canada thread expressed sympathy for the passengers but also shared their fondness for Halifax.

One commenter called it their favorite Canadian city to visit, but said they would be "bummed" to end up there while expecting a Bahamas beach vacation.

Halifax was the cruise’s only port stop, giving passengers about 24 hours ashore before three days at sea. (iStock)

Another summed up the change more bluntly, writing, "Halifax is gorgeous, but it is not the Bahamas."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

PEOPLE reported that passengers received a 50% travel voucher and refunds for shore excursions.

Weather and other circumstances can prompt Royal Caribbean to alter or substitute ports, according to its website, and it is not necessarily required to refund fares or provide compensation.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Royal Caribbean for comment.

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

Larry the Cable Guy says corporate America has a double standard when it comes to choosing which entertainers are too controversial for advertising campaigns.

The comedian went on a tirade against DirecTV, suggesting the satellite-TV provider missed an obvious advertising opportunity – "Larry the Cable Guy has switched to DirecTV" – because of concerns about his image.

During an appearance on "The MeatEater Podcast," Larry recalled seeing a DirectTV commercial with an actor "back in the day," and said, "The first thing I thought was, why don't they get me? ‘Larry the Cable Guy is switching to DirecTV.’"

JEFF FOXWORTHY REVEALS HOW 'REDNECK' INSULT INSPIRED DECADES OF COMEDY

Larry the Cable Guy criticized what he sees as a double standard in corporate advertising, arguing that brands embrace entertainers he considers more controversial than himself. (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images)

A podcast host agreed with the idea. "Oh, dude, that would have been genius,"

The comedian agreed, "It would have been huge!"

Larry said he believed the company's concern was that his Southern accent and edgy humor might appeal to only one slice of America and make him too controversial for a national advertising campaign.

"At the time, ‘Well, Larry the Cable Guy is only really for one part of the country, you know, ’cause of the Southern accent, sometimes he says things that are a little controversial,'" he explained of the general sentiment then.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The comedian said DirecTV missed a major advertising opportunity by not tapping him for a campaign that would have played off his famous stage name. (Getty Images)

But the comedian rejected that reasoning.

"Meanwhile, you got freaking rappers singing about killing cops" and making degrading remarks about women, he argued. "They're getting all kinds of corporate stuff. I'm like going, 'How am I controversial when you got … you know what I mean?"

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

He singled out Snoop Dogg, who has appeared in major advertising campaigns, including Super Bowl commercials. Larry emphasized that he did not fault the rapper for accepting those opportunities.

Snoop Dogg has appeared in major advertising campaigns, including Super Bowl commercials, but Larry the Cable Guy questioned why corporations embrace entertainers he considers more controversial than himself. (James Wiltshire/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

"I got nothing against Snoop Dogg," he said. "God bless Snoop Dogg."

He later added, "There's a lot of hypocrisy in corporate, who they get and who they don't get. Look, I've had a good career. I ain't worried about it. But I'm just saying, that DirecTV pissed me off."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

He said again that he doesn't have any issue with Snoop Dogg, explaining, "I love everybody, and I'm happy for everybody's career. I'm not mad at them, I'm upset at the corporations that would say ‘you're too controversial,' but then they'll put somebody else that's even way more controversial.’"

Larry the Cable Guy questioned corporate America's approach to celebrity endorsements during an appearance on "The MeatEater Podcast," accusing companies of hypocrisy. (Isaiah Vazquez/Clarkson Creative/Getty Images)

Larry, whose real name is Daniel Whitney, built a national following with the Blue Collar Comedy Tour, alongside Jeff Foxworthy, Bill Engvall and Ron White.

His signature catchphrase, "Git-R-Done," and blue-collar comedy persona helped launch a career that has included stand-up, comedy albums, movies and television.

articles.title: Thousands gather at new Albanian antigovernment rally
articles.excerpt:
Protesters have clashed with police in rallies in the Albanian capital of Tirana, with police firing tear gas and water cannon to disperse crowds.

Several government buildings were attacked, dozens o...
articles.body_text:
Protesters have clashed with police in rallies in the Albanian capital of Tirana, with police firing tear gas and water cannon to disperse crowds.

Several government buildings were attacked, dozens of demonstrators arrested, and more than 300 protesters and police injured, authorities said Saturday.

Protesters and police have routinely clashed since a significant wave of protests started in mid-October over poor conditions in schools and the cost of living in the small Balkan country.

While the protests in Tirana had calmed in recent days, Saturday’s demonstration escalated the situation again, with police deploying water cannon, tear gas and rubber bullets against crowds.

Thousands of people had heeded calls from organisers for students and others around Albania to attend the rally. Various groups, including university professors, artists and opposition parties, announced their support or attendance.

The country’s Ministry of Education has become a focal point of rallies, and Saturday’s gathering saw some in the crowd throwing stones and rolling burning bins at the building.

Police had introduced heightened security around the capital on Saturday, with checks being carried out on cars heading to the city, local media reported.

Albania has seen intermittent antigovernment protests since May, when news emerged of a luxury hotel project linked to United States President Donald Trump’s family.

Since then, public anger has turned into a broader push against corruption and the high cost of living, with protesters calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama.

Rama has blamed “foreign actors” for the violence and accused both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation.

The prime minister has called for dialogue, and on Saturday red cushions were laid outside the government headquarters in a symbolic gesture for talk and dialogue. Protesters later set the cushions on fire.

Protesters have blamed the entire political class for the crisis, with some also seen holding signs decrying Rama’s opposition, centre-right leader Sali Berisha.

articles.title: Dream, Valkyries stay off court for fourth WNBA Finals national anthem as some fans remain seated
articles.excerpt: Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries players left the floor moments before the national anthem in Game 4 of the WNBA Finals, while many fans remained seated. Both teams returned seconds after it e...
articles.body_text:
Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries players left the floor moments before the national anthem in Game 4 of the WNBA Finals, while many fans remained seated. Both teams returned seconds after it ended.

ATLANTA – The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries were off the court for the national anthem before Saturday’s Game 4 of the WNBA Finals at State Farm Arena, marking their fourth straight absence in the series.

Some fans also remained seated during the performance, including spectators who kept their hats on.

The foul line stands empty during the national anthem before Game 4 of the WNBA Finals at State Farm Arena. The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries remained off the court for the fourth straight Finals anthem. (San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)

I attempted to observe what Atlanta’s players do after leaving the court, but arena staff told me my credential did not grant access to that area and escorted me back to my assigned media seat.

WNBA PLAYERS, COACHES REFUSE TO EXPLAIN NATIONAL ANTHEM ABSENCES AMID MOUNTING CRITICISM

An employee inside State Farm Arena told OutKick that Dream players stand in a hallway after leaving the court before games. OutKick asked the Dream to confirm whether players remain there during the national anthem and explain what they do during the performance. The team did not immediately respond.

Players from both teams said Friday that staying off the court during the anthem has been their practice for years.

In the first three games, both teams left shortly before the anthem and returned seconds after it ended. Games 1 and 2 were played at Chase Center in San Francisco on Oct. 17 and 19. The series moved to Atlanta for Game 3 on Oct. 21.

Atlanta entered Saturday with a 2–1 lead in the best-of-seven series after winning Wednesday’s Game 3, 97–71.

The anthem absences have drawn criticism from President Donald Trump, who urged fans to stop watching the WNBA at an Oct. 22 rally in Iowa. Vice President JD Vance also called the absences "disgraceful."

Atlanta coach Karl Smesko was asked Friday why his team left the floor for the anthem and whose decision that was.

"We’re just kind of focused on the Finals," Smesko said.

Asked whether he had any further comment about the anthem and his team’s absences on the league’s biggest stage, Smesko said, "No."

An Atlanta public relations representative then moved to the next question.

Dream guard Rhyne Howard was asked Friday about calls to exclude players from Team USA if they do not stand for the national anthem during the WNBA season.

Riley Gaines and former Georgia state Rep. Vernon Jones have argued that anthem conduct should carry consequences when athletes seek to represent the United States internationally.

"I don’t think I’ve been on the floor for the national anthem for any of my tenure in Atlanta, so if that’s what people are gonna look to nitpick for then so be it," Howard said. "But as far as competing for your team, when I go put on USA jersey I’m out for the national anthem every time, there’s no doubt about it."

"Yes, I love the country that I play for and I love what we have here," she added.

Angel Reese, left, and Rhyne Howard celebrate Team USA’s World Cup gold medal in September. Critics have called for WNBA players who stay off the court during the anthem to be barred from the U.S. Olympic team. (NBAE via Getty Images)

Howard and Dream teammate Angel Reese represented the United States at September’s FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup, where both stood for the anthem. Golden State had no players on that U.S. roster, although Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase served as an assistant coach.

OutKick followed up with Howard: "Is there a reason you’re not on the court for the anthem?"

Howard and an Atlanta public relations representative both responded, "Next question."

During Friday’s media availability in Atlanta, OutKick asked Nakase whose decision it was for Golden State to stay off the court and why.

"We’re two years in," Nakase said. "That’s been part of our pregame."

Asked again who decided and why, she said, "I really don’t know."

"I understand your question," Nakase added. "I’m not trying to, you know, not answer your question. It’s just part of our pregame."

OutKick followed up: "What do you do during those 90 seconds that you’re off the court?"

"I’m with my staff, so I’m focused on my plays," Nakase said.

Golden State’s public relations staff then moved to the next reporter. OutKick did not get an opportunity to ask why those preparations needed to happen during the anthem rather than before or afterward.

OutKick also asked Valkyries forward Gabby Williams whether the anthem absences are meant as a protest.

Asked why the team was off the court, Williams responded: "That’s been the routine for like, seven years now."

A Valkyries public relations representative then said, "Next question."

Williams was born in Nevada, holds U.S. and French citizenship and represents France internationally. She joined Golden State this year after playing for Chicago from 2018–20 and Seattle from 2022–25.

Williams’ reference to roughly seven years would reach back to her time in Chicago and span the three WNBA teams she has played for, though she did not explain whether each followed the same routine or how it began.

There is a history of WNBA teams staying off the court as a demonstration. During the 2017 Finals, Los Angeles Sparks players voted to remain in the locker room in solidarity with Black Lives Matter, according to reporting at the time.

Atlanta also published players’ union messaging in its Aug. 2, 2020, game notes. It said "the anthem does not represent freedom, justice and liberty for all Americans" and that players would "continue to protest" in various forms.

Williams denied that the absences are a protest, but the pregame routine explanation still did not identify who established the practice or why it coincides with the anthem.

The WNBA’s 2026 official rulebook says players, coaches and trainers are to "stand and line up in a dignified posture" along the sidelines or on the foul line during the national anthem.

The Associated Press reported Oct. 20 that the league suspended its anthem protocols in 2017. The provision remains in the 2026 rulebook.

OutKick has asked the WNBA to clarify its current requirements and enforcement, whether discipline is planned or under consideration, and whether teams have received instructions about being on the court.

The league has not answered multiple requests for comment.

Friday’s interviews were OutKick’s first opportunity to put the anthem questions directly to players and coaches. OutKick had attended all 13 formal press conferences during the first three Finals games without being called on.

Crystal Renee Hayslett performs the national anthem before Game 4 of the WNBA Finals at State Farm Arena. The Dream and Valkyries were off the court for the fourth straight Finals anthem. (Getty Images)

The emailed inquiries began after Game 1 on Oct. 17. OutKick followed up with the WNBA, Dream and Valkyries on Oct. 18 and again Oct. 20, asking about the absences, the teams’ plans for subsequent games and any league instructions.

OutKick also contacted NBA Executive Vice President and Chief Communications Officer Mike Bass on Oct. 20.

The inquiry asked about the NBA’s role in enforcing the WNBA provision, whether Commissioner Adam Silver or other NBA officials had discussed the absences with WNBA leadership, and possible exemptions or discipline.

The WNBA, NBA and both teams’ front offices have not responded to OutKick’s repeated emailed requests for comment about the anthem absences. Friday’s responses came from players and coaches during media availabilities.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Four games, two arenas and a week of questions later, both teams are still leaving the floor for the anthem.

And no one has given a good answer as to why.
