While he may have seen some similarities, Rhys-Davies told Fox News Digital he doesn't "see Pierce there" when working with Paris.

"I think this man is already his own man. It's always very hard to come out under the shadow of a giant," he said. "What I see is a vulnerability and an innocence and a willingness ... an openness to evolve, adapt, and become. He's still defining what he really is and what he wants. And I think it's fascinating to watch. All credit to Pierce and his mum for bringing him up so well. But I think he's his own man."

Paris also touched on his decision to become an actor despite his father trying to deter him from going down that path, noting he always interpreted his dad's words not as a way of discouraging him from acting, but saying, "unless you love it, and you want it, then don't pursue it … just because it's on the table."

He explained he came into the industry with a love for it and revealed that his father has always preached about how much work it takes to be an actor.

"Go to class, read, learn from the greats. He's given me countless books on it," Paris said. "So I think he just means if you want it, you have to study it, and you have to earn your way and pave your own way."

articles.title: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
articles.excerpt:
Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola pa...
articles.body_text:
Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.

The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.

“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water bills
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Angela Eagle tells utility bosses next price review ‘must focus on value for money for customers’

Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies priorit...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Angela Eagle tells utility bosses next price review ‘must focus on value for money for customers’

Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows.

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat.

Sources at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan, which will follow next week’s budget, would hand the government more robust powers to lower bills and direct local investment. But sources close to Eagle said there also needed to be immediate action as companies began to make decisions before the next price-setting process, expected to conclude in 2029.

There has never been government intervention in the five-year review process. It is run by Ofwat, which analyses companies’ business plans and determines how much can be charged to customers in their bills to fund investment and running costs.

Eagle has written to regulators and water company chief executives, saying that the process must meet specific government priorities, including offering bill payers much better value for money – though stopping short of demanding bill cuts.

The letter to companies and regulators says they must be focused on investment in new technology to save money, and early intervention on leaks and sewage. It also called for far better communication and decision-making power handed to local communities and leaders.

The first priority must be affordable bills, the letter says, adding: “Affordability means a laser focus on value for money for customers.”

The letter says the public is clear about what the objectives for the industry should be. “They want clean rivers. They want reliable water services. They want to know that their money is being spent wisely, and that bills are kept affordable. And they want confidence that the system is working in their interests.”

The letter warns company bosses that it will “not be a business-as-usual price review … it is the beginning of a long-term transition to a different model for the water sector”.

Defra sources said Eagle intended it to be the first in a series of changes that will be announced in the coming months on the water industry, calling it “one of the clearest symbols of public frustration with Britain’s infrastructure”.

A Defra source said the intervention by Eagle was a down payment on bigger changes that would come in the 10-year plan. The source said: “Angela will take a much more bullish approach to telling water companies and regulators what is expected from them. This is the start of a journey to a very different water system and one that delivers for the public.

“There are also things we want regulators and companies to be doing now and so Angela is using the levers she’s got to influence their investment decisions at an early stage and make sure they’ve got no excuses. As well as looking at ownership structures, there are other ways we can go further than what came before.”

The new intervention from Eagle comes as the government continues to explore more radical options for the stricken company Thames Water. The Guardian reported earlier this week that Burnham had told officials to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that meant spending taxpayer money and going to court.

Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames Water – which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn – but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.

The outcome of the last price review process in 2024 led to highly controversial bill rises, after Ofwat authorised a £104bn modernisation programme, funded in large part through progressive annual rate increases that will see average water bills surge by 36% over the second half of the decade. The biggest increase was allowed for Southern Water, whose customers will pay 53% more by 2030, at an average of £642 per year.

Over the summer, several major suppliers requested permission to charge billions more to cover mounting capital costs and debt obligations, sparking fury from campaigners and from politicians, including Burnham.

The prime minister criticised the decision, warning that bill payers must no longer be treated as a “blank cheque” or a “bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures”, saying ordinary households were being forced to plug massive corporate balance-sheet deficits.

However, campaigners for public ownership have warned the move will do little in practice to reduce bills or the environmental impact of sewage or leaks. Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “These proposals are yet more reshuffling of the deckchairs on the Titanic, and fall far short of Burnham’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.

“This government should be intervening on behalf of households to stop bill hikes. If water companies can’t function without siphoning more and more money out of our pockets, then this government should let them go bust.

“From there, we can bring water affordably into public hands. ⁠Under public ownership, we can put people and the environment ahead of the interests of faraway shareholders and hedge funds.”

articles.title: Finland nearing opening of world’s first permanent nuclear waste repository
articles.excerpt:
Finland has granted an operating licence for the world’s first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel.

The government handed Onkalo, in western Finland, the licence on Thursday, wast...
articles.body_text:
Finland has granted an operating licence for the world’s first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel.

The government handed Onkalo, in western Finland, the licence on Thursday, waste management company Posiva said.

Although the move does not allow the opening of the facility, it is expected to start operations soon, the firm said. However, 22 years after construction began, no exact date has been decided yet.

“This is a great and historic day for both Posiva and Finland,” the company’s Chief Executive Officer Ilkka Poikolainen said in a statement.

“Before final disposal begins, Posiva will finalise the commissioning stage, carrying out the necessary tests and inspections which STUK [the Finnish Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority] also needs to verify and approve.”

With space for 6,500 tonnes of uranium, Onkalo, which means “cave” in Finnish, will provide permanent storage for spent fuel from Finland’s five nuclear reactors.

The fuel will be enclosed in copper canisters that are highly resistant to corrosion inside the geological repository. The canisters will then be lowered into holes drilled into the bedrock, which will be filled with bentonite clay and finally sealed with a steel-reinforced concrete plug.

The waste will remain highly radioactive for tens of thousands of years. After about 100,000 years, the levels will be about the same as the uranium ore of which the fuel is made, according to Posiva.

Countries have been wrestling with what to do with dangerous nuclear by-products since the first plants were built in the 1950s. Currently, most of it is in temporary storage.

Final repositories are being built in other countries, including neighbouring Sweden and France, but Finland is expected to be the first to open its underground storage facility.

The cost of the Onkalo site has been estimated at $1.16bn.

articles.title: Dembele to miss Ballon d’Or event as PSG game moved amid protests in France
articles.excerpt: Paris Saint-Germain’s home Ligue 1 game against Lyon scheduled for this Sunday has been postponed until Monday, the French league announced, following a request by police amid a wave of violent protes...
articles.body_text:
Paris Saint-Germain’s home Ligue 1 game against Lyon scheduled for this Sunday has been postponed until Monday, the French league announced, following a request by police amid a wave of violent protests in the French capital.

The decision means the reigning Ballon d’Or, Ousmane Dembele, will miss Monday’s awards ceremony in London, for which he and a number of his PSG teammates have been nominated.

The 29-year-old French international forward was once again among the favourites to win the award, having helped his nation to the FIFA World Cup 2026 semifinals while leading PSG to their defence of the UEFA Champions League crown.

“The LFP takes note of the police decree prohibiting the staging of the game between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais on Sunday at 8:45 pm [19:45 GMT] … and has decided to reschedule the match for Monday at 8:30 pm,” the French league said in a statement on Friday.

French authorities are braced for another weekend of protests in Paris and across the country, after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago.

Defending champion PSG and Lyon were level on 14 points at the top of Ligue 1 heading into this weekend’s eighth round of games

Monday’s match will clash with the Ballon d’Or awards ceremony in London, where several PSG players are on the men’s shortlist: holder Dembele of France, Morocco’s Achraf Hakimi, Georgia’s Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Brazil’s Marquinhos, Nuno Mendes, Joao Neves, and Vitinha of Portugal, Willian Pacho of Ecuador, and Fabian Ruiz and Ferran Torres of Spain.

French officials will mount a “massive” security operation for protests planned on Saturday, with troops reinforcing police, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Tuesday, after rioting and looting swept through Paris and other French cities on October 17.

The PSG-Lyon game is among several high-profile sporting events scheduled in the French capital area this weekend.

The Pittsburgh Steelers are due to face the New Orleans Saints in an NFL regular-season game at the Stade de France on Sunday, an event expected to require a significant police deployment.

Separately, Toulouse’s Ligue 1 home match against Troyes has already been pushed back from Saturday to Sunday at the request of local authorities, the LFP said on Wednesday.

articles.title: Kenya’s marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir provisionally banned by AIU
articles.excerpt: Kenya’s world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for the banned blood booster EPO in a sample taken before her Sydney Marathon victory, the Ath...
articles.body_text:
Kenya’s world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for the banned blood booster EPO in a sample taken before her Sydney Marathon victory, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said.

The AIU added that the out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO (erythropoietin), which boosts the production of red blood cells.

“I can only say that I feel terrible about what happened and I think it’s only right that an athlete who uses performance enhancing drugs should be disqualified,” her agent Gianni Demadonna said in an emailed statement.

Sydney Marathon organisers said they were “extremely disappointed” to learn about Jepchirchir’s provisional suspension.

“Jepchirchir is entitled to due process and we will make no further comment on the case until that process has concluded,” organisers said in a statement on social media.

“Our commitment to clean sport is unwavering. Every athlete who lines up in Sydney deserves to race on a level playing field and every participant and spectator deserves to trust the result they see at the finish line.

“That conviction is why, alongside our fellow Abbott World Marathon Majors, we have invested in increased out-of-competition testing in partnership with the AlU, and why we will keep standing firmly with the athletes who compete cleanly.”

The 33-year-old is a former Olympic champion and half-marathon world record holder, as well as a four-time World Marathon Majors winner.

She won gold at the Tokyo Games in 2021 and has also claimed major marathon victories in New York (2021), Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney (2026).

Jepchirchir dominated the women’s race in Sydney in August, pulling clear of the field to finish in 2:18:31, more than three minutes ahead of second-placed compatriot Irine Cheptai.

Last year, Kenya’s women’s marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich was banned for three years after admitting anti-doping rule violations involving hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), a prohibited diuretic, though her world record of 2:09:56 remained on the books because it was set before her positive test.

articles.title: White House says Melania Trump ‘secured a ceasefire’ in Ukraine’s Oleshky
articles.excerpt: The White House has said First Lady Melania Trump has “secured a ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since February 2022....
articles.body_text:
The White House has said First Lady Melania Trump has “secured a ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since February 2022.

Neither Russia nor Ukraine immediately confirmed the statement on Friday, which comes as the administration of US President Donald Trump has renewed diplomacy aimed at ending the war.

The approach has included upping pressure on Ukraine and handing several recent concessions to Russia.

“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster,” Melania Trump said in a statement released by the White House.

“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she said.

The First Lady added that her representatives worked directly with “Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire” and that civilian leaders from both countries will work together to grant humanitarian access to civilians in the city.

Oleshky, which had a population of 24,000 people before the war, sits along the southeastern front of the conflict. It was captured by Russia during the first day of the invasion in February 2022 and experienced heavy shelling.

While most residents have fled, those who remain have faced dire food and medical shortages. Both sides have accused the other of staunching the flow of supplies.

In her statement, Melania Trump said those of the estimated 2,000 remaining residents who wish to be evacuated will be transported to their “preferred destination”, she said, adding, “I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine”.

The first lady added that “an impartial American media organisation” will accompany both Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground. She did not identify the organisation.

“This will play a significant role in ensuring that the wishes of each family are faithfully respected,” she said.

Melania Trump had previously worked to reunify children seized by Russia during the war.

The announcement comes after the Kremlin said it had agreed to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine as early as next month, although both sides remain far apart on terms of a possible deal.

The Trump administration has upped rhetorical pressure on Ukraine while simultaneously offering several concessions to Russia.

The administration has said those concessions, which include purchasing diesel from Russia and waiving some sanctions, are aimed at reducing high fuel costs spurred by the US-Israel war with Iran.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has complained of disruptions to its Starshield military satellite system, upon which it relies for much of its air defence. Ukrainian Prime Minister Volodymyr Zelenskyy has since said an agreement has been reached to resolve the issues.

Starshield is a version of the Starlink system operated under billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

Go have an incredible weekend. We'll be in Columbus for the Ohio Junior High Cross Country State Championships. Can Screencaps Jr. run in the 11:20s or maybe even the 11:19s at one of the fastest courses of the season? The weather should be just about perfect. Stay tuned.

Joe Kinsey is the Senior Director of Content of OutKick.

articles.title: Trump to rally in Florida after stoking Ramaswamy ad furor – US politics live
articles.excerpt:
Trump to campaign for gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, who has distanced himself from president; Trump doubled down on support for Ramaswamy

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of US ...
articles.body_text:
Trump to campaign for gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, who has distanced himself from president; Trump doubled down on support for Ramaswamy

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of US politics. Donald Trump is travelling to Florida today to speak at another rally as midterm election day races nearer.

The president will stump for gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds. Whether Donalds regards this as helpful remains to be seen after he removed mentions of the president from his website and has barely uttered his name during the race for governor.

My colleague Richard Luscombe has more on that race:

Last night, Trump further stoked the controversy over an attack ad by Vivek Ramaswamy, featuring the mother of his Democratic rival, Dr Amy Acton – telling supporters at a rally that he personally told the Republican candidate for Ohio governor to keep running the spot.

Acton’s mother lost custody of her daughter at age 12 because her husband was charged with raping the young girl. Trump told the rally in Iowa: “I said, ‘You’ve got to ride with it.’”

Trump looks increasingly out of step with his own party over the ad after yet another Republican denounced the ad on Thursday. Iowa Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson broke with the president by denouncing the attack ad, saying: “I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down.”

Most likely voters say they will trust the results of the midterm elections, according to the latest poll from the New York Times and Siena University.

While 74% of those surveyed said they would have confidence in the outcome, 23% said they would not.

Notably, 50% of voters said that that the Democratic party is “too far to the left”, while 51% feel that the GOP is “too far to the right”.

Meanwhile, the latest polling also shows that a majority (53%) are not confident that Republican candidates will accept the results of the midterm elections if they lose. This is compared to 28% of those who feel the same about Democrats’ response to the results.

Almost half of those surveyed said that they are worried about the possibility of Republicans trying to overturn the results if they lose. Only 31% had the same fear about Democrats.

With only 11 days until the midterm elections, and with more than 20m early votes cast, we’re watching the key races that will ultimately decide who controls the Senate in the new Congress.

My colleagues John Farrell, Hazel Tang, Karif Wat and I have put together a video breaking down the candidates, stakes and issues in these four battlegrounds.

A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade.

The trove reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.

The AfD became a home for anti-immigration voters after 1.2 million refugees arrived in Germany in 2015 and 2016. It entered the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, in 2017 with 12.6% of the vote, came second in the February 2025 federal election with 20.8%, and now leads national polls at about 30%. In September it won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and it is now trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the second world war.

Trump hailed the win in Saxony-Anhalt in a post on his Truth Social, concluding his message with a German version of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”

Germany’s domestic intelligence agency monitors the party as a suspected rightwing extremist organisation, and state agencies classify five of its regional branches as confirmed extremist.

The leaked documents show AfD officials quickly moving to requests for support from the White House on policy issues when he first won the 2016 election.

Others show a burgeoning political courtship between senior figures including the AfD’s now leader Alice Weidel and key Trump ideologue Steve Bannon.

The data, provided to reporters by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), covers more than 420,000 emails, along with documents and personnel records, from the party’s foundation in 2013 to the present, with most coming before 2019.

The ongoing slowdown to Ukraine’s access to Starshield – the modified military-grade version of the Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network – reached fever pitch this week.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the Donald Trump had asked Musk to restore the service, with Trump later told reporters the system was “back”.

However, the president refused to comment on whether he had spoken to Musk, but appeared to suggest the ultimate power to limit the service rested with the SpaceX founder and CEO. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk.

This comes after a protracted series of disruptions for Ukraine accessing the network – a key defense tool against Russian strikes.

Despite Trump’s insistence, Ukrainian officials said on Friday morning that speeds remained capped, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.

Trump will begin his day in Washington, before his midterms blitz continues in Florida. A reminder that today is his fifth day of campaign rallies this week. He’ll deliver remarks at 2pm ET in Fort Myers.

We mentioned the key gubernatorial race in the Sunshine state earlier – where Republican congressman Byron Donalds will face off against Democrat David Jolly. But there is also a key contest that we’re watching in Florida too.

This is the special Senate election, where the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, is facing a challenge from progressive Democrat Angie Nixon – who defied odds and won her primary earlier this year.

Americans heading to the polls for next month’s midterm elections are not just choosing whom to send to Washington, or their state capitols. There are also 145 statewide measures on ballots across 39 states, polling voters on actions from a novel wealth tax on California’s billionaires to requiring Alabama’s public schools to broadcast or perform the first stanza of the national anthem each week.

Voters in Idaho, Nevada and Virginia are asked to protect abortion rights; voters in Missouri are asked to give those rights back. Property tax issues appear on dozens of state ballots. Several state referendums ask voters to bar trans athletes from competing in women’s sports, or bar gender-affirming medical care for minors.

Voters like referendums, in principle, as a tool of direct democracy. “Polls in every state show at least 2-to-1 support for having an initiative process,” said John Matsusaka, a business professor at the University of Southern California (USC) and executive director of the Initiative and Referendum Institute.

Here are the big topics voters are being asked to decide this year:

Ashley Hinson’s criticism of the ad came after similar condemnation by Ohio governor Mike DeWine triggered a swift rebuke from Donald Trump.

Speaking to ABC News, Hinson said: “It’s terrible. I think about it as a mom and you think about your kids surviving childhood sexual abuse and having to relive that trauma on TV again.”

Hinson also criticised vice-president JD Vance for striking “absolutely the wrong tone” when he said he was “disgusted” by Republicans “whining” about the ad.

double quotation mark“Iowans want - and probably Ohioans want – someone who’s going to be an empathetic leader, and I think it sends absolutely the wrong message.

“And I would bet that Amy Acton and I probably don’t agree on anything, either. But like the last thing I would want as someone who’s running against is to force them to relive the childhood trauma. So, I think, again, I think it’s wrong, and it should come down.

My colleague Richard Luscombe has more on that race:

articles.title: Macron to meet student groups: Where are France’s protests heading?
articles.excerpt:
Paris, France – President Emmanuel Macron plans to meet with high school student representatives as the country braces for further protests over the weekend.

The meeting on Friday marks the first tim...
articles.body_text:
Paris, France – President Emmanuel Macron plans to meet with high school student representatives as the country braces for further protests over the weekend.

The meeting on Friday marks the first time the French leader has held talks with the student groups that have been calling for an overhaul of the education system since September.

Students have called for more demonstrations to maintain the pressure while Jean-Didier Berger, the minister delegate to the interior minister, said the police presence on the streets would be increased by 20 percent.

Last weekend, largely peaceful demonstrations gave way to violent riots. Authorities were accused of failing to prepare adequately and are taking no chances before further protests expected on Saturday.

A curfew in Paris will limit movement while protest bans are in place in Marseille and Lyon.

High school students have made their demands clear: better-funded schools, more teachers and a greater say in decisions affecting their future.

With protests showing little sign of abating, a government weakened by political deadlock and mounting debt faces a difficult question: What can it do to bring young people off the streets?

“For years, we’ve been given promises that were never kept,” said Soumaya Sarre, an 18-year-old student and a leading figure in the Federation of High School Students from Working-Class Neighbourhoods. “What we want is for promises to be backed by concrete results. We want to see real change in our high schools.”

Since mid-September, high school students have been protesting against teacher shortages; overcrowded classrooms, sometimes with more than 40 students; and dilapidated school buildings.

Their grievances have grown into a nationwide movement at a tense moment for France as it gears up for its presidential election in six months.

“Let’s be clear: Our demands are not all impossible to meet,” said Nathanael Combary, 18, president of the board of directors of the student organisation Renouveau Lyceen.

He identified two priorities: a comprehensive overhaul of Parcoursup, the university admissions system, which many students consider discriminatory, and a 1.5-billion-euro ($1.7bn) emergency plan to improve school infrastructure before winter and summer.

Other student organisations and unions are calling for an additional 10 billion euros ($11.2bn) for education, more teachers on permanent rather than precarious contracts and 250,000 additional university places.

“My primary goal is to provide very concrete solutions,” Combary said.

So far, the government has announced 3,000 additional substitute teachers and an online consultation while its 2027 budget allocates an extra 1.1 billion euros ($1.2bn) to national education.

But beyond these practical demands, one message emerged repeatedly in interviews with students: They want to be heard.

“It is clear that this crisis points to one thing: a breakdown in dialogue between the government – and politicians in general – and young people,” Combary said. “We need a government that listens to us and is capable of responding to our demands.”

Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste is not considering abolishing Parcoursup, calling the idea “pure demagogy”, but he said he was ready for “profound changes”.

After a meeting with student organisations on October 7, the Union etudiante, a national student union federation, said the minister could not give them any guarantees. Another meeting is set for Monday at which the government said it will present a first set of decisions on staffing, teacher replacements and Parcoursup.

Some observers doubted that these measures alone can address the deeper causes of the unrest: a sense of anxiety linked to a diploma that no longer guarantees a job, an ever-increasing cost of living and a sense that the state is not capable any longer of providing services.

“Young people’s prospects depend on the social status and wealth of a family. This is the root cause of these protests, and it can’t be fixed with a few measures, such as improving heating in schools and toilets,” said Jacques Reland, a senior research fellow at the Global Policy Institute.

“The wealthy family has replaced the welfare state,” he said.

On top of that, students and unions are asking for a level of support that the government can’t give, even if it wanted to.

On a political level, Macron has a minority in parliament, which makes it impossible to pass any meaningful reforms.

But the biggest obstacle for any concessions to the protesters is finances.

France has long spent on a generous welfare system.

Macron offered a cheque of 10 billion euros ($11.2bn) in tax cuts to quell the ‘yellow vest’ movement, which ripped through France in 2018. A similar response may be more difficult this time.

Public debt is projected to reach 121.7 percent of France’s gross domestic product in 2027, up from 119.3 percent this year, according to the government’s budget bill.

“They are demanding things that the government is not in a position to satisfy unless they increase the deficit, or touch social security –  two aspects that would push people in the streets,” Reland said.

articles.title: Government won’t put together ‘shopping list’ for public to stockpile for emergency – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Ministers have repeated several warnings in the last 18 months about the threat of hybrid attacks from overseas

As Wes Streeting and James Murray have been recommending in the last 24 hours, the Gove...
articles.body_text:
Ministers have repeated several warnings in the last 18 months about the threat of hybrid attacks from overseas

As Wes Streeting and James Murray have been recommending in the last 24 hours, the Government is advising people to stockpile supplies for three days.

Have you been persuaded to follow this advice? The Guardian would like to speak to you about what you have in your cupboard, and what other items you have in case of emergency.

Andy Burnham has been meeting armed forces veterans and Royal British Legion Poppy Appeal collectors to mark the start of the year’s campaign.

Burnham welcomed them to Number 10 North’s office in central Manchester, contrary to the usual convention of making a donation to the cause on the steps of Number 10 in Downing Street.

Good morning from London, where we’re less than a week from Andy Burnham and John Healey’s first budget, and the Government has been telling people to build up 72 hours of supplies in case of a disaster. We’ll be bringing you updates throughout the day. I’m Harry Taylor.

The Government has said that will not be putting together a “shopping list” for the public to buy in anticipation of a disaster, despite launching a campaign on Thursday which told people to stock up on supplies.

Treasury minister James Murray has been on the broadcast round this morning where has been asked about the announcement yesterday that people should assemble three days of supplies.

It’s come after repeated warnings in the last 18 months about cyber-attacks from overseas that could affect key systems.

It’s also timely as 32 Government services were taken offline yesterday after millions of attempts to exploit a weakness in numerous’ websites coding.

However Murray told Times Radio this morning: “This is not about the Government sending out a shopping list to everyone in the country.

“This is about putting the right information there on the government website, having an information campaign so that people are aware about it and then people taking the right choices for themselves about what they need to make sure they have supplies of at home.”

Meanwhile it’s five days until Healey’s budget, and Murray was asked on BBC Radio 4 whether he would be reducing red tape for business.

He said cutting “pointless bureaucracy” was “at the heart of what the Chancellor is going to be thinking about”.

Healey said the Treasury would aim to cut £800m of red tape for businesses at the budget, including reduced reporting requirements.

articles.title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
articles.excerpt:
Taiwan is bracing for Champi's worst effects on Saturday

Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.

Sc...
articles.body_text:
Taiwan is bracing for Champi's worst effects on Saturday

Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.

Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday.

One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate.

Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far.

On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) .

After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island.

Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan,

However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches.

Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said.

Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains.

Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island.

Taiwan's $5tn (£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather.

Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual.

In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company.

More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines.

Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan.

Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties.

Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane.

While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea.

This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms.

The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El Niño - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons.

articles.title: LeBron shrugs off Trump blast in home debut win for Philadelphia 76ers
articles.excerpt:
The Philadelphia 76ers erased a 29-point deficit to stun the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 on Thursday in NBA superstar LeBron James’s first home game since landing in Philly as a free agent.

The victo...
articles.body_text:
The Philadelphia 76ers erased a 29-point deficit to stun the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 on Thursday in NBA superstar LeBron James’s first home game since landing in Philly as a free agent.

The victory came only hours after LeBron was slammed by US President Donald Trump, who accused the NBA legend of disrespecting their national anthem in a game earlier this season.

Tyrese Maxey scored 32 points and Joel Embiid added 24 – including a jump shot with 6:54 left to play that gave the Sixers their first lead of the night – one they wouldn’t relinquish on the way to an epic comeback.

Former Celtics star Jaylen Brown, the Sixers’ other big off-season acquisition, scored 21 points and pulled down eight rebounds and four-time NBA champion James added 17 points, 10 rebounds and five assists to help the 76ers author their biggest comeback of the play-by-play era that started in 1996.

It was also the biggest comeback of James’s storied career. The league’s all-time leading scorer called it a good win – but not a position he wants to be in often.

“You don’t want to rely on that,” he said. “I think it’s great to know (that) deep down we’re not going to have that quit mentality. You never want to look around and say guys gave up.

“But you don’t want to put yourself in too many of those situations.”

Al Jazeera have requested a response from the Philadelphia 76ers to Trump’s criticism of their star, who appeared to practice basketball and golf shots during the anthem ahead of Tuesday’s game at New York Knicks.

LeBron has not made any statement or offered any response himself.

Cleveland, disappointed not to land hometown hero James after he announced he was leaving the Los Angeles Lakers after eight seasons, appeared to be on a mission to show him what he missed.

Donovan Mitchell scored 22 of his 32 points in the first half as the Cavs seized control against a 76ers team struggling to find a rhythm and protect the ball.

Philadelphia centre Joel Embiid looked creaky, and James had five of the Sixers’ 15 first-half turnovers – which led to 22 Cavs points and provoked boos from Philly fans whose hopes of a title run have been raised by the arrivals of James and Brown.

The boos turned to raucous cheers as the re-energized 76ers opened the third quarter on an 11-0 run. They cut the lead to single digits on back-to-back baskets from Maxey that pulled them within 80-73.

The Cavs were struggling to regroup. Maxey reduced the deficit to two points with a running finger roll layup with 2:33 left in the third before Cleveland reeled off six straight points to take a 90-82 lead into the fourth quarter.

But the 76ers, who beat the reigning champion New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, kept coming. They outscored the Cavaliers 60-37 in the second half, clamping down defensively and giving up just two turnovers.

Evan Mobley scored 18 points for Cleveland but had just three in the second half. Jarrett Allen scored 14 but was held scoreless after the break.

“We stayed together, that’s the main thing,” Sixers guard VJ Edgecombe said. “When it got worse we could have given up, we didn’t. It’s an early season test, early season adversity, and we overcame it.”

In Oklahoma City, the Thunder pulled away late for a 96-84 victory over the Denver Nuggets, despite a rough shooting night for two-time reigning Most Valuable Player Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who saw his streak of games with at least 20 points end at 141.

Gilgeous-Alexander missed all seven of his first-half shots and was just two-of-13 from the floor through three quarters. Nevertheless Oklahoma City, led by Jalen Williams’s game-high 21 points, took a 70-64 lead into the fourth quarter.

Gilgeous-Alexander connected on four of his six attempts for 10 points in the final frame for a respectable total of 17 points — his first regular-season contest with less than 20 since October 30, 2024, when he scored 18 against San Antonio.

Denver’s three-time MVP Nikola Jokic also had a quiet night, connecting on five of 19 attempts for 13 points with seven rebounds and five assists. Aaron Gordon led the Nuggets with 20 points.

articles.title: Starlink access for Ukraine limited after Trump’s claims satellite service restored, officials say – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
The satellite service was still operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences

In Vienna this morning, Austria’s foreign ministry has announced it is kicking out another four Russian dipl...
articles.body_text:
The satellite service was still operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences

In Vienna this morning, Austria’s foreign ministry has announced it is kicking out another four Russian diplomats over “activities incompatible ⁠with their diplomatic status” – a euphemism usually for espionage.

Three of them worked at the Russian embassy while the other worked at the Organization ​for ​Security and Cooperation in Europe) in arms control, Die Presse is reporting.
 
 
 They had all been monitored for some time by the Austrian security authorities.

You have to wonder how many Russian diplomats are left in Vienna – Europe’s espionage capital since the cold war, as my colleague Jon Henley puts it. Just a few months ago, Austria also expelled three Russian embassy staff on spying allegations, after a “forest of antennae” was detected at the Russian mission.

Austria has expelled now 18 Russian diplomats since 2020.

A quick update from what the Ukrainian and Russian officials are saying this morning on overnight attacks:

Ukraine says Russia targeted energy sites in six different regions. Currently more than 500,000 people are without power.

Russia’s defence ministry confirmed strikes on Vilkovo port in Odesa, a railcar depot in Poltava and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

A war of words has erupted between the Trump administration, officials in Kyiv and Elon Musk over who is to blame for limiting Ukraine’s access to Space X’s military-grade version of Starlink.
 
 
 The restrictions to Starshield have rendered many of the drones used by Kyiv to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and hampered air defence systems that stop Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian officials.
 
 
 The US president said on Thursday that the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
 
  
  What has Trump said?

Trump initially denied any responsibility for the changes to Starshield, telling reporters last Friday: “I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” referring to Musk, SpaceX’s CEO.

Trump’s cabinet backed him up, with secretary of state Marco Rubio saying on Wednesday: “What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made.”

Rubio, however, also made a comment that threw suspicion on to Musk, the world’s richest man.

The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk. That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the US president had asked Musk to restore the service, with Trump later telling reporters the system was “back”.

He refused to comment on whether he had spoken to Musk, but appeared to suggest the ultimate power to limit the service rested with the SpaceX CEO. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk.

However, John Cornyn, a Republican who is in his final weeks as the US senator for Texas, told US media that he didn’t believe Musk would have acted “without at least the acquiescence of the White House”.
 
 
 What about Musk?
  
  Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced and has been highly critical of the Ukrainian president. However, he was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”.

Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.

Musk – one of the Republican party’s biggest donors and a Trump ally – continued to deny responsibility for the changes. However, on Tuesday the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk made the order to slow down Starshield, with the paper’s sources in disagreement over whether this was made in concert with Trump.

Vice-president JD Vance backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.

So I don’t think this is about Elon. I think it’s fundamentally what is America’s policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be.

Amid the war of words, civilian casualties in Ukraine have surged, and the question over who is ultimately responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access has remained unanswered.

Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where we’ll begin in Ukraine.

Local authorities reported explosions overnight in Lutsk, a city not far from the Polish border, and in the central Poltava and southern Sumy regions. Russia this morning has also claimed strikes on ships in the Black Sea.

Both sides engaged in heavy strikes yesterday with Russia bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sending swarms of drones to Moscow.
 
 
 Trump has declared that Starlink is once again running at full speed across Ukraine after the service was throttled last week -but Ukrainian and European officials say they haven’t seen that speed and functionality resume.

The satellite service was still only operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences and limiting mid-range strikes, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent after Trump’s comments. “Overall, nothing has changed anywhere,” the paper quoted the unnamed official saying.

Elsewhere we’re watching this continued wave of student-led protests across Europe. From Rome to Athens, Madrid and Paris, young people are venting their anger over the lack of resources in schools as well as wider housing and cost-of-living concerns. They’ve often been joined by their teachers in these ralies.

Fearing another weekend of street marches descending into violence and looting, French authorities have banned some protests over the coming days. President Emmanuel Macron, just returned from his mid-week tour to the Gulf states, is due to meet with student leaders around lunchtime in Paris.

It’s Frances Mao today in London, covering for Jakub, stay with me for all the developments.

articles.title: Severe flooding in eastern Spain, while UK hit by first named storm of winter
articles.excerpt:
Storm Adam brings heavy rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen gusts strike England and Wales

Storm Adam brought torrential rain to eastern Spain earlier this week. In Pego,...
articles.body_text:
Storm Adam brings heavy rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen gusts strike England and Wales

Storm Adam brought torrential rain to eastern Spain earlier this week. In Pego, Alicante, 632mm fell in 36 hours with 430mm of this falling in just six hours, while the Valencian town of Olivia received 600mm in 24 hours. As a result, 145 municipalities, approximately 850,000 people, across Valencia and Alicante were placed in a temporary lockdown on Monday due to the severe flooding.

At least five people have died and 500 have been rescued and 2,100 evacuated. The storm also affected the Balearic Islands, with more than 130 incidents recorded in Ibiza including standing water at the airport, which caused some flights to be diverted or suspended. Although the worst of the storm has passed and conditions improving across Valencia and Alicante, local disruption is expected to continue.

The first named storm of the winter for the UK is currently tracking through the Channel. Storm Austen is bringing damaging winds not only to south-west England and Wales, but also south-west Ireland and northern France. Gusts are expected to be around 50-60mph, but some exposed north-western coasts of France could experience winds of up to 80-90mph.

Following quickly on from Storm Austen is another deep low pressure system, Storm Boelo, which is expected to track across northern Scotland on Saturday into Sunday. Much of the UK and Ireland will see very unsettled conditions with further damaging winds and heavy and prolonged rain. Western Scotland will face the strongest gusts, but the rest of the UK and Ireland will see 40-55mph winds. Western parts of Ireland will experience 50-60mph winds with up to 70-80mph in exposed parts of north-west Ireland, similar to western Scotland. Again, heavy rain associated with Storm Boelo will reach 10-20mm with as much as 30-60mm in western parts of Ireland, Wales and south-west England. This, on top of the rainfall from Storm Austen, will increase the risk of flooding.

Super Typhoon Champi is headed towards China and Japan over the weekend after passing north-eastern Taiwan on Friday. While it has weakened since Wednesday, it is still a significant typhoon with the equivalent strength of a category 5 hurricane, producing 185mph gusts and sustained winds of 121 mph.Following torrential rain associated with the typhoon this week, up to 900mm of rain is forecast to fall in the mountainous regions of northern and eastern Taiwan from Tuesday to Saturday. As a result, there are school closures, cancelled flights and six-metre waves, with more impacts to come over the next few days.

articles.title: Two suspected gunmen killed after shooting wounds 5 Israelis in West Bank
articles.excerpt: Five Israelis were wounded, including two critically, in a shooting in the southern West Bank on Friday, prompting a security response in which Israeli forces killed two suspected attackers, according...
articles.body_text:
Five Israelis were wounded, including two critically, in a shooting in the southern West Bank on Friday, prompting a security response in which Israeli forces killed two suspected attackers, according to officials.

Five people were wounded, including two critically, and two suspected gunmen were killed in a shooting Friday in the southern West Bank, officials said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) reported that it responded to a shooting in the Judea Junction area Friday and killed two people it identified as "terrorists."

A blockade was established while the agency continued to search the area, the IDF said.

INSIDE ISRAEL'S MISSION TO TRAIN CIVILIANS TO STOP THE NEXT OCT 7-LIKE TERROR ATTACK

Israeli forces stand guard near a shooting scene in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (REUTERS/Ammar Awad)

Five Israelis were wounded in the shooting, according to The Times of Israel.

Two people were critically wounded and three were in light-to-moderate condition, first responders told the outlet.

ISRAELI COMBAT MEDICINE SLASHES IDF DEATHS AFTER OCT 7, DRAWS US MILITARY INTEREST

Israeli authorities responded to a shooting in the southern West Bank on Friday that left five people wounded and two suspected attackers dead. (REUTERS/Ammar Awad)

Magen David Adom, Israel's emergency medical service, said it treated two people in critical condition at the scene of the attack.

The identities of the suspected gunmen were not immediately released.

Israeli security forces investigated the scene of a shooting near Judea Junction in the West Bank that left five Israelis injured. (REUTERS/Ammar Awad)

This is a developing story; check back for updates.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

articles.title: Trump's MAGA faithful send warning to Republicans ahead of high-stakes midterm elections
articles.excerpt: Some of President Donald Trump's loyal supporters still have has back, but outside of his rally in Sioux City, Iowa, they want to see change come soon from him and Republicans heading into a crucial m...
articles.body_text:
Some of President Donald Trump's loyal supporters still have has back, but outside of his rally in Sioux City, Iowa, they want to see change come soon from him and Republicans heading into a crucial midterm election.

SIOUX CITY, Iowa — President Donald Trump’s loyal base of supporters still have his and Republicans’ back in Iowa, but some are growing concerned over lingering issues, like the economy and gridlock in Congress, as Election Day nears.

Trump and Republicans ran on a platform of lowering inflation, halting "forever wars" and repairing an economy that they say was wrecked by former President Joe Biden and his administration. But prices are still high, and the war in Iran is still ongoing, causing a spike in fuel prices that have stuck around heading into Nov. 3.

Outside of Trump’s rally in Sioux City, Iowa, where the president was set to rile up support for Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, in a tightening Senate race against Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, his supporters who spoke with Fox News Digital still backed Republicans but expressed hope that change would soon come.

VOTERS PREPARE TO WEIGH-IN ON TRUMP'S ECONOMY AS COSTS CONTINUE TO SURGE

President Donald Trump greets supporters during a campaign rally at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kan., on Oct. 19, 2026. (Getty Images)

Beth Fitzl, an Iowa voter, said of Trump that she didn’t "agree with everything he does, but in the end, he's here for us."

"This is the way I see it," Fitzl told Fox News Digital. "He's like the Packers, OK? They may be getting in deep, but they always pull it off in the end, and I truly think he's going to do something to turn it around. I really think he's going to pull something to turn it around."

Chuck Jones, a veteran and Purple Heart recipient who made the trek from Minnesota for the Iowa rally, was frustrated about the divisive, tribal nature of politics.

He told Fox News Digital that "these politicians, they're fighting for one thing on one side, and other people are fighting for something on the other side, but there's nobody sitting at the table in the middle."

TRUMP VOTERS REVEAL THEIR BIGGEST FEAR HEADING INTO MIDTERMS — AND IT'S NOT RISING PRICES

When asked if Republicans and Trump needed to do something different should they hold onto control of Washington, D.C., after the election, Jones said, "Well, I think it's time that we're going to have to show some difference, because people aren't happy with the way things have been in the last few years."

"And we're going to have to do something about it and decisively show the American public that you can get it done and get it done correctly," he said. "They're going to have to work together instead of fighting each other."

Hinson’s race is one of six toss-ups that Republicans in the Senate are trying to hold onto. She and Turek are vying for Sen. Joni Ernst’s, R-Iowa, seat after she opted to retire from the upper chamber last year.

Their race, like others during this cycle, has become surprisingly close, given that Trump won the state in 2024 by roughly 13 points and has won it each time he’s been on the ballot.

THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES

Republican nominee for Senate Ashley Hinson, right, speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for Senate Josh Turek at WHO 13, on Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (Charlie Neibergall/AP Photo)

Dawn Stanley, an Iowa voter who has voted for Trump in each of the last three elections, still planned to support him and Hinson. She told Fox News Digital that Turek hadn’t "showed up" for Iowa and noted that he’d been absent from the state legislature "42% of the time" — Turek missed 261 votes between January and May of this year while on the campaign trail.

Still, her biggest frustration with Republicans was their inability to pass the SAVE America Act, voter ID and election security legislation that has been consistently blocked by Senate Democrats.

"I really do think it comes down to the SAVE Act," Stanley said. "I really do, because we can't have all these Democrats in there and bringing over all these illegals who are going to vote for those people and have chaos. That's what it is."

"The United States is in chaos and I really believe it's because of the illegals and the Islamic terrorists that are coming over," she continued. "And just look at what's going on in France. I mean, it's terrible. And I don't want that for our country, and that's what Trump can stop. And that's why we need to bring in all the conservatives that we can."

Others were concerned about Democrats regaining power and feared that Republicans may not show up on Nov. 3 to support GOP candidates.

"We need to get the people out to vote," Kurt, who traveled from South Dakota for the rally, told Fox News Digital. "Republican people need to get out the vote. They stay home too much. This is a war to be won with the Left, as far as I'm concerned."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

articles.title: Nigeria and Kenya Ebola patients may have crossed paths at Uganda airport, officials say
articles.excerpt:
Health officials are investigating if both patients contracted the virus at the aiport

Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Nigeria and Kenya may have crossed paths at Uganda'...
articles.body_text:
Health officials are investigating if both patients contracted the virus at the aiport

Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Nigeria and Kenya may have crossed paths at Uganda's main airport earlier this month.

Both travelled through Entebbe airport on 3 October and investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established.

Nigeria is battling its first Ebola case in more than a decade, while Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including one death.

The Nigerian patient, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman who lives in Abuja, is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

She is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Nigeria, Switzerland's foreign ministry has confirmed. Her husband, who accompanied her on a trip to Uganda, is also in isolation but has not developed symptoms.

The woman returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda, travelling through Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, where she had a two-hour stopover.

She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October.

Health officials are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus and whether her movements overlapped with those of the Kenyan patient.

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

The Kenyan man had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He later died, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death ever.

Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact.

"One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.

Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source.

The WHO said it was too early to determine where the patient in Nigeria became infected.

"The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.

He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.

Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help investigators understand whether the infection is related to other cases.

"The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria.

Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business, where the current Ebola outbreak began.

However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country.

Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there.

Meanwhile, Africa CDC said Nigeria had identified additional people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially reported.

"Most of those contacts, they are from the healthcare workers in different facilities where this case has been receiving treatment. We have also some few family members," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.

He said Nigerian authorities were working to identify and quarantine those considered at high risk, but declined to give an updated figure before the government released its findings.

"The position of the country [is] to bring those high-risk contact and put them on quarantine," he added.

Dr Ursu said the woman was receiving a high standard of clinical care and that her condition was stable.

In Kenya, the first group of people quarantined after possible exposure to Ebola will begin returning home on Sunday after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms.

Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission.

"We are not out of the woods," he warned, urging the public to remain vigilant but not panic.

He said the remaining eight patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.

The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between the DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.

Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points.

The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.

Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu.

The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms.

Health authorities say tracing contacts quickly, isolating suspected cases and providing early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected

Why Uganda is winning the battle against Ebola as virus spreads in DR Congo

Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.
