articles.title: Comedian Heather McMahan cries sexism while reflecting on firing from Ryder Cup for 'f--- you Rory' chants
articles.excerpt: U.S. team captain Brandt Snedeker and golfers Jacob Bridgeman, Sam Burns, Russell Henley and Cameron Young speak with OutKick's Dan Zaksheske about how their Christian faith strengthens relationships ...
articles.body_text:
U.S. team captain Brandt Snedeker and golfers Jacob Bridgeman, Sam Burns, Russell Henley and Cameron Young speak with OutKick's Dan Zaksheske about how their Christian faith strengthens relationships and helps them keep golf in perspective.

Aside from Team Europe dominating the Americans over the course of the first two days of the 2025 Ryder Cup, one of the wilder moments from the biennial event involved comedian Heather McMahan and chants of "f--- you Rory" ringing out across the first tee at Bethpage Black.

Now, a year removed from helping lead the vulgar chants, McMahan is claiming that if she were a man, the consequences that followed never would have happened.

Ahead of Saturday's foursomes matches, McMahan, who was hired as an MC for the event, attempted to fire up the crowd on Long Island. While it's an admittedly awkward job for anyone to start chanting things into a microphone at sunrise in front of tens of thousands of rowdy golf fans screaming their own obscenities, McMahan made a mistake that immediately cost her.

2025 Ryder Cup at Black Course at Bethpage State Park Golf Course on September 27, 2025 in Farmingdale, New York. (Photo by Michael Reaves/PGA of America/PGA of America via Getty Images) (Michael Reaves/PGA of America/PGA of America via Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

As fans in the stands started a "fâ you Rory" chant for Team Europe leader Rory McIlroy, McMahan joined in and started shouting the chant into her microphone. The following day, the PGA of America issued a statement explaining that McMahan had extended an apology to McIlroy and had stepped down from her role. McMahan recently told Oona McCaughan of Barstool Sports that she was "immediately fired" after joining in on the chants.

During a recent sit-down with The Hollywood Reporter, McMahan reflected on nearly being "cancelled" after the incident while pinning the blame on golf not knowing its identity, whatever that means.

"The Ryder Cup has always been known to be heavily competitive between Europe and America," McMahan told the outlet. "But it's always been in good fun? I think [having it in Long Island], the already the weird animosity that America was having to outsiders, I don't think they were set up for success that year. And, I'll fall on the sword. I did not help the cause. It's just really wild.

"What does golf want to be? Is it all buttoned up like The Masters? Is it trying to be Happy Gilmore? I do think golf needed to like shake off the cobwebs, quit being as stuffy, but it doesn't know where it wants to go."

RIDICULOUS USA TODAY COLUMN PROVES THAT THE DEMAND FOR MISOGYNY IN SPORTS FAR EXCEEDS THE SUPPLY

Actress/comedian Heather McMahan performs onstage during the 2025 GCAPP EmPower Party at Atlanta History Center on November 13, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Paras Griffin/Getty Images) (Paras Griffin/Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOWâUNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

After explaining that she's only planning on attending LPGA events from now on, McMahan claimed that her being a woman played a role in the backlash and firing.

"I went to the Masters and got to see him win again. I'm still a huge fan," McMahan said, referring to McIlroy winning the green jacket in April. "It's not the players. They're doing their thing. It's just this kind of weird environment with some of the male fans these days. And again, I apologized, but I do think, had a male comedian been in my shoes, we would have never had this conversation. They wouldn't have given a sât. Dudes being dudes. Set it on fire, man."

GOLF CHANNEL ANALYST CALLS LONG ISLAND FANS 'A STAIN ON THE GAME' AFTER US OPEN INCIDENTS

Heather McMahan at the 76th Emmy Awards at the Peacock Theater on Sunday, Sept. 15, 2024 in Los Angeles. Mandatory Credit: Kevork Djansezian-USA TODAY (Kevork Djansezian-USA TODAY)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

It's extremely hard to find a modicum of truth in what McMahan is implying.

If anyone who is hired to MC one of the largest events in golf grabs a microphone and joins in on "fâ you" chants directed at a player in the event you're being paid to be a part of, that person is undoubtedly being fired, regardless of gender.

When it comes to the idea that McMahan should have been cancelled for the chant, that's equally as absurd.

The 2025 Ryder Cup was three full days of American fans shouting obscenities at every European player, but fans aren't held to the same standard as a paid employee of the event, as McMahan was presumed to be.

Mark Harris is a writer for OutKick. Follow him on X @itismarkharris.

articles.title: Germany target of 'intensive' espionage, Merz says after suspected Russian spy arrest
articles.excerpt:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Russian intelligence activity in Germany remains 'at a consistently high level'

Germany is the target of "intensive" espionage activity, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has s...
articles.body_text:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Russian intelligence activity in Germany remains 'at a consistently high level'

Germany is the target of "intensive" espionage activity, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said after a Ukrainian national was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia.

Officials said the suspect, named as Vadym Y., had allegedly collected military-related intelligence from Germany.

Merz called the uncovering of the case a "success", but warned "let us not delude ourselves - the activities of Russian intelligence services in Germany remain at a consistently high level".

Several people alleged to be acting on behalf of Russia and other foreign powers have been arrested in Germany this year. Germany has been one of the leading European suppliers of weapons to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

The German Federal Prosecutor General's Office said on Thursday that Vadym Y., as he was  identified under German privacy law, had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025.

It also said the Ukrainian man had collected information including "on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition, and explosives".

He is due to appear before an investigating judge on Friday.

In January, a woman was arrested in Berlin suspected of gathering information for an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy.

Other arrests this year included a Romanian woman and a Ukrainian man accused of spying on an individual supplying drones from Germany to Ukraine, according to the prosecutor's office.

UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham in Berlin

Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal

Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid

And, the former German spy chief August Hanning was arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power earlier this month. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.

Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.

Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D and accused him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents in exchange for money.

Speaking at the sidelines of a conference in Montenegro on Thursday, Merz said: "We will likely see more such cases in the coming months and years."

Merz reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier this month, including tackling hybrid attacks and hostile activity.

The talks between the two leaders came after Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport in September.

Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Russia.

articles.title: Jillian Michaels urges parents to fight back against Big Tech's 'addictive' grip on kids
articles.excerpt:
Health advocate and best-selling author Jillian Michaels hosts 'Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink,' now streaming on Fox Nation.

Fitness trainer and media personality Jillian Michaels is urging pare...
articles.body_text:
Health advocate and best-selling author Jillian Michaels hosts 'Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink,' now streaming on Fox Nation.

Fitness trainer and media personality Jillian Michaels is urging parents to "keep the pressure on" social media companies, warning about the platforms' allegedly "addictive" algorithms and content.

Michaels made the comments during an appearance on "The Faulkner Focus" while promoting her new Fox Nation documentary, "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink." Michaels advised parents to limit their children's access to online activities.

"You have to do everything you can," Michaels said. "And that means putting parental controls on your kid's phone, period. Take the phone away at night, limit the sites that they can access, have communications with them regularly about the content that they're seeing online. But you also have to be realistic about what they're going to do when they're not with you."

CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS

Concerns about children's excessive screen time are explored in Fox Nation's "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink." (iStock)

"This is the part where we also have to continue putting pressure on the social media companies to make their algorithms safer for kids," she said. "They created an addictive product, they know it, and we need to keep the pressure on."

In the documentary, Michaels examines the risks she says children face in the modern age, including excessive screen time, mental health issues and over-medicalization.

"The truth is, a lot of parents probably don't realize the scale of what kids are dealing with today," she said. "From day one, the fragile little bodies and brains of the tiniest and most vulnerable among us are being targeted, treated and toxified from all angles."

NATION'S SECOND-LARGEST SCHOOL DISTRICT MOVES TO LIMIT KIDS' SCREEN TIME

Michaels is joined by several experts in "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink," including psychology researcher Jean Twenge, who argues that individuals who begin using smartphones at an early age are more likely to experience mental health issues later in life.

"In some of the best design studies, the heaviest users of social media are about twice as likely to be depressed as lighter non-users," Twenge said. "Even in other studies, you see at least often a 40% or a 50% increase in depression from not using social media to being a heavy user of social media."

Apps like WhatsApp, with over 2 billion users, face scrutiny over how private chats really are. (Photo by Anna Barclay/Getty Images)

"Gen Z and Gen Alpha know how bad these technologies can be for them," Twenge added. "They're the ones who came up with phrases like 'chronically online,' which make it sound like a disease, 'brain rot,' that it's bad for your attention span and your focus."

FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15

Social media companies have faced increasing pressure to be regulated and be held accountable for the potential effects of their platforms. In August, Meta agreed to pay as much as $17.1 billion and implement restrictions on teen accounts to settle claims that it designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children and misled the public about the platforms' safety. Meta denied the allegations.

Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg leaves a Los Angeles courthouse after testifying in a trial over allegations that Meta and Google's YouTube harmed children's mental health through addictive platforms on Feb. 18, 2026. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

For more on the potential risks personal tech and other issues pose to young children, make sure to watch "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink," now streaming on Fox Nation.

Fox Nation programs are viewable on demand and from your mobile device app but only for FOX Nation subscribers. Go to Fox Nation to start a free trial and watch the extensive library of your favorite FOX Nation personalities.

Benji Ferraro is a recent University of Maryland grad and new digital production assistant, with a focus on channel coverage and culture stories. He can be reached at benji.ferraro@fox.com for any story tips.

articles.title: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
articles.excerpt:
Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro in the second round of voting on Sunday

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requ...
articles.body_text:
Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro in the second round of voting on Sunday

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.

In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.

In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.

The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.

It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.

A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.

It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts".

"Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read.

Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally.

Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted.

Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula.

Pro-Lula supporters gathered outside Meta's office in São Paulo on Monday, accusing the company of interference in the Brazilian electoral process

Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office.

Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.

On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network".

The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election.

Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power".

He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes.

Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.

articles.title: Reader Q&A: What’s next for France after a weekend of riots? Ask our Europe columnists
articles.excerpt: At 3pm BST / 4pm CEST Friday 23 Oct, Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in France. Send your ques...
articles.body_text:
At 3pm BST / 4pm CEST Friday 23 Oct, Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in France. Send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com, or join the discussion on Friday

After weeks of protests and a weekend of riots in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured, the repercussions for France – for its society and its economy – continue. Allegations of police brutality surfaced, and the violent protests unnerved investors, resulting in a debt sell-off, with borrowing costs rising higher than for Greece. All of this ahead of a hotly contested presidential election that’s now just six months away.

The French government’s escalating financial problems were covered by the Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley who wrote: “France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.”

Columnist Paul Taylor commented that “Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel (Marine) Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy.”

And the Guardian’s editorial noted that “In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.”

What are your views on the riots, their causes and their aftermath? Are they paving a path to the presidency for Le Pen? In his final months in charge, can embattled incumbent Emmanuel Macron meaningfully address the situation in which France finds herself?

France-based Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live here at 1500BST on Friday 23 October to answer your questions on what happened, why, and where France goes from here.

Comments will open at 0900BST on Friday, but you can send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com

articles.title: Biden-appointed judge blocks voter-fraud probes in battleground states just days before midterms
articles.excerpt: Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter discusses the DOJ lawsuit against California over voter rolls. McCotter details efforts to crack down on noncitizens registered to vote and ensure electio...
articles.body_text:
Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter discusses the DOJ lawsuit against California over voter rolls. McCotter details efforts to crack down on noncitizens registered to vote and ensure election integrity.

A Biden-appointed federal judge in California ruled Wednesday that the Department of Homeland Security must halt certain investigations into suspected illegal voting, citing concerns over voter intimidation.

U.S. District Judge Araceli MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­n, the jurist in question, was born in Mexico and nominated to the federal bench by President Joe Biden in 2022. Before becoming a federal judge, MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­n spent about six years at the American Civil Liberties Union, a progressive civil rights organization, where she worked on women's and immigrants' rights issues.

The activist groups suing DHS "demonstrate[d] that they are likely to succeed in their claim that Defendants have run afoul of the Voting Rights Actâs prohibition of intimidating voter assistance and mobilization," according to MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­n.

DOJ OFFICIAL DEFENDS TRUMP'S NONCITIZEN VOTER PROBE ON '60 MINUTES,' ACCUSES SHOW OF EDITING OUT HER ANSWERS

The Department of Homeland Security has directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to deport undocumented immigrants who vote in American elections. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

The publicâs "interests in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation, far exceed (the governmentâs) purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens," she added.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, maintained that noncitizen voting in federal elections is a crime and that DHS has statutory authority to investigate suspected violations. MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­n did not find investigating noncitizen voting as itself unlawful, but instead argued that DHSâ methods likely violate the law as it used unreliable source data and sent armed agents to homes to conduct interviews, which could constitute intimidation.

STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS

Members of Homeland Security Investigations listen as FBI Director Kash Patel speaks during a press conference on Oct. 23, 2025 in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

Lawyers representing the federal government conceded that some American citizens may have been looked at in connection with DHSâ investigations, but contended that in-person interviews were "expressly designed to resolve the discrepancies."

Noncitizen voting is rare, but cases of illegal voting have been documented. News broke earlier this year, for example, that New Jersey erroneously placed over 6,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls. The Justice Department announced charges against 16 individuals in September, including noncitizens accused of voting illegally in federal elections, and brought additional election-related charges in October.

NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION

US President Donald Trump (R) speaks as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (L) looks on before he signs an executive order in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on March 31, 2026. President Donald Trump on March 31 signed an order seeking to crack down on mail-in voting, escalating his push to restrict a popular way of casting ballots in US elections. Trump's executive order follows repeated attacks by the 79-year-old Republican on US elections, based on his disproven conspiracy theories about supposed cheating by his Democratic opponents. It was unclear whether Trump has authority to impose the measures and legal challenges were almost certain, with a possible final decision being left to the Supreme Court. (Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images)

MartÃ­nez-OlguÃ­nâs order blocks DHS from carrying out certain field investigations into suspected illegal voting involving U.S. citizens in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. Several of those states are led by Democrats who have opposed the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies, and some face high-profile elections in November.

Cracking down on illegal voting has been a priority for the second Trump administration, though it has yet to produce evidence of widespread noncitizen voting.

The judge delayed enforcement of her order until Friday, giving the Trump administration time to appeal, and set the restrictions to expire on Election Day unless otherwise ordered.

"DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders," a spokesperson for the department told Fox News Digital. "We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."

articles.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
articles.excerpt:
Nate Foy reports from Park City, Kansas, where President Donald Trump campaigns for Sen. Roger Marshall in a crucial bid to retain Republican control.

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic chal...
articles.body_text:
Nate Foy reports from Park City, Kansas, where President Donald Trump campaigns for Sen. Roger Marshall in a crucial bid to retain Republican control.

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night.

The hourlong showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932.

The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall â a topic touched on during the debate.

Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate.

SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, left, and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, right, faced off in a Kansas U.S. Senate debate Wednesday night ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. (Getty Images)

The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates.

Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills.

"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."

Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse.

Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation.

FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS

"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."

Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week.

"And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd.

Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda.

"No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump.

President Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally at the Oncenter, on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, in Syracuse, N.Y. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP)

Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports.

"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."

Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate.

The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are.

"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls."

"There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded.

TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR

The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports.

Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females.

"I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight."

Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology."

Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people.

Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.

"We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said.

But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer.

"You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers.

Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement.

"This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best."

BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH

This split image shows then-President Biden and migrants at the southern border. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP Photo)

Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle."

The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed.

"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders."

"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."

Hamilton also reiterated during the debate that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats capture control of the chamber.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

articles.title: BBC News to axe education editor role in cost-cutting move
articles.excerpt:
Fears over lack of scrutiny for key sectors as health editor position also to go in cuts aimed at saving £5.5m

The BBC will no longer have a dedicated education editor as part of a cost-cutting drive...
articles.body_text:
Fears over lack of scrutiny for key sectors as health editor position also to go in cuts aimed at saving £5.5m

The BBC will no longer have a dedicated education editor as part of a cost-cutting drive in which 100 jobs are to go across BBC News under a plan that school leaders described as “deeply regrettable”.

BBC staff have been told that the roles of education editor and social affairs editor are to be combined into a single position as part of a round of changes that will save £5.5m. However, prominent unions and campaigners are saying the reform will dilute scrutiny of two specialisms that are too important to go without a dedicated BBC role.

The education editor at BBC News is Branwen Jeffreys and the social affairs editor is Alison Holt.

In a message to staff seen by the Guardian, Richard Burgess, the director of news content, said he was proposing the change after a review of on-air editor roles. He said the review looked at “audience demand, editorial requirements and how we ensure these roles remain relevant in a changing news environment”.

There will also be no health editor title at the BBC when the current incumbent, Hugh Pym, leaves in the spring. That job will be incorporated into the role of medical editor, currently held by Fergus Walsh.

“These are difficult decisions, but I have given the changes careful consideration, taking into account levels of audience interest and editorial demand, as well as how we can work as efficiently as possible across the department,” Burgess said.

It appears BBC executives have opted to combine the education and social affairs jobs as they attempt to reduce duplication and cut wage costs. Sources said experienced education and social affairs specialists would remain at the BBC, but others inside the corporation have been left puzzled by a change that will leave the world’s oldest national public service broadcaster without a dedicated education editor.

School leaders and teaching unions questioned the move. “On the face of it, this announcement suggests that the BBC is proposing to dilute leadership of its education coverage,” said James Bowen, the assistant general secretary at the school leaders’ union NAHT. He urged the BBC to rethink the plan.

He said: “This would be a deeply regrettable move by our national broadcaster, which plays a vital role in shining a light on important issues affecting the education sector and holding the government and Department for Education to account.”

Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union, said the move would “diminish the public’s understanding of education matters in this country”. Matt Wrack, the general secretary of the NASUWT teachers’ union, said: “At a time when schools are grappling with rising child poverty, crumbling buildings, teacher shortages and major funding cuts, the public needs to hear from strong public interest reporting in the sector.”

Nadra Ahmed, the co-chair of the National Care Association, said she was concerned that the lack of a social affairs editor meant the sector could lose attention at a critical time with the prime minister drawing up social care reforms.

One BBC insider said combining the education and social affairs editor roles “further erodes our ability to give sufficient coverage to the breadth and depth of two materially distinct topics”.

However, others inside the BBC said the issues of education, social affairs and health all had dedicated teams of journalists that would ensure proper coverage. A BBC spokesperson said: “The BBC remains committed to covering education, and will continue to do so both at editor level, and with its team of expert reporters and producers.”

Burgess said that alongside the editor role changes the job requirements of on-air editors would be reviewed to place “greater emphasis” on making an impact on social media and digital platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.

The BBC is making renewed efforts to boost its presence on those platforms as it attempts to reach younger audiences who are increasingly using the sites for news.

The new head of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, used one of her first memos to staff to tell them that the department’s target of finding £51m in savings could be increased “given the BBC’s financial pressures”.

articles.title: How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain a massive flaw in internet technology, after AI discovered issues that could be exploited by hackers.

Developers of ...
articles.body_text:
Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain a massive flaw in internet technology, after AI discovered issues that could be exploited by hackers.

Developers of the PHP platform - which powers more than 70% of websites, including Wikipedia and digital shopping sites - rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

Cyber-security firm Wiz described the issue as the "most severe" ever detected, while OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

But how did AI discover a massive cyber-security risk in the internet, and what does it mean for you? The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy reports.

Read more on the cyber-security threat here.

Nancy Mace said: ‘This ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season’

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of US politics. We’re less than two we...

Nancy Mace said: ‘This ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season’

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of US politics. We’re less than two weeks out from the midterm vote and the campaigns are getting even more nasty.

Condemnation continues of Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign in the Ohio governor race after his team put out an attack ad, featuring the estranged mother of his Democrat rival Amy Acton criticising her daughter and calling her a liar.

Acton’s campaign has called it a despicable ad after putting out the clarification that Acton was sexually abused by her stepfather and removed from her mother’s custody at age 12.

Ramaswamy’s team however has dug in behind the ad, and were backed by Veep JD Vance yesterday who condemned Republican criticism. He said Ramaswamy “had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls ​it out like it is”.

However South Carolina congresswoman Nancy Mace joined the chorus of Republican critics saying:

double quotation markThis ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season.

double quotation markI just can’t believe that this is what passes for decency in this election.

Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington, before traveling to Sioux City, Iowa for another campaign rally, as part of his week-long midterm blitz.

He’ll stump for Ashley Hinson, the Republican congresswoman and nominee for the state’s open US Senate, who is trailing in the polls against her opponent, Democratic state legislator Josh Turek.

The president will also campaign on behalf of Zach Lahn, a businessman and the GOP nominee for governor, who is facing a tough competition against Democratic state auditor Rob Sand in November.

Iowa’s has become an unexpected battle ground this midterm cycle, with voters particularly frustrated about the impact on the war in Iran – namely the high cost of fuel and fertiliser. Democrats are hoping for an upset in a state where they haven’t won a US Senate set since 2008.

Trump will take the stage at 7pm ET, and we’ll bring you the latest lines.

New polls shows the super-tight race in Texas where Democratic candidate James Talarico is challenging Republican Ken Paxton in the US Senate race. Earlier this week, Talarico also won the endorsement of George W Bush’s brother.
 
 
 New polling from Emerson College shows Talarico at 48%, just in front of Paxton at 46% – with about 5% undecided.
 
 
 Neil Bush, a son of former president George HW Bush and a lifelong Republican, announced on Tuesday that he crossed party lines to vote for Talarico.

In a Facebook post, Neil Bush said he chose to vote early for Talarico over Ken Paxton, the current Texas attorney general, because he was “deeply troubled” by Paxton’s conduct and was “enormously impressed” by Talarico’s principles.

As a moderate Republican, Neil Bush’s statement on the competitive Senate race in Texas reflects views from a faction of the party that often disagrees with Donald Trump while holding traditional conservative views.

double quotation markI have been deeply troubled by Paxton’s conduct as Texas attorney general, particularly his decision to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election in other states in an effort to help Donald Trump remain in power.

The former president’s son and brother of George W Bush expressed concern about Paxton’s past controversies, including Paxton’s 2023 Texas state legislature impeachment and acquittal, as well as Paxton’s loyalty to Trump.

double quotation markI have been a Republican for most of my life, and I still believe deeply in many traditional Republican principles. But character matters more than party affiliation. Our democracy depends on leaders who respect our institutions, tell the truth, accept accountability, and seek to unite rather than divide.

Multiple protesters were removed from Donald Trump’s rally at South Carolina’s Clemson University on Wednesday, including one who was apparently punched by a rally attender – to the US president’s delight.

“That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that. I watched that,” Trump said. “That was incredible. Wow. That was unbelievable. Is everybody OK?

“Who’s the guy that threw that punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield,” referring to the former heavyweight champion, who was also in attendance at the rally.

“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally,” he said. “He got whacked.”

The president was interrupted at least nine times by hecklers. One protester who was removed by security was followed by a rally attendee, who appeared to slap the demonstrator on the head.
 
 
 Trump was in South Carolina to support Darline Graham, the sister of late senator Lindsey Graham who died suddenly in July from a heart condition. Graham, elected to her brother’s seat in a special election, is facing Democratic challenger Annie Andrews in her bid for a full six-year term.

Responding to the ad yesterday, Amy Acton told a group of voters that her mother was not well and Ramaswamy shouldn’t have “exploited her”.

Earlier in the week, her brother had called Ramaswamy’s attack ad a “despicable low” in a statement released by Acton’s campaign:

double quotation markIt’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point.

double quotation markAfter he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died. This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”

The ad, which had circulated among conservatives on social media, featured Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, urging Ohioans to not vote for her daughter.

The Ohio gubernatorial campaign between Acton and Ramaswamy is regarded as one of the uglier contests in the 3 November midterm elections.

Acton has refused to debate Ramaswamy, who she has called a “chronic liar” and has also criticized him for airing an ad which features a woman married to a registered sex offender.

articles.title: Chiricahua monument in Arizona is now the 64th US national park
articles.excerpt:
New designation of the Land of Standing-Up Rocks, known for its historic rock spires, passed with bipartisan support

An area of towering rock spires in south-eastern Arizona known among Native Americ...
articles.body_text:
New designation of the Land of Standing-Up Rocks, known for its historic rock spires, passed with bipartisan support

An area of towering rock spires in south-eastern Arizona known among Native Americans as the Land of Standing-Up Rocks has become the nation’s newest national park.

Legislation to create Chiricahua national park was sent to the White House and Donald Trump signed it on Tuesday. It passed Congress with bipartisan backing and is now the 64th US national park.

The 19-sq-mile (49-sq-km) site is within the historical territory of the Chiricahua Apache tribes. It was designated a national monument in the 1920s to preserve hundreds of pinnacle-shaped rocks formed from an ancient volcanic eruption.

For centuries the site of the proposed park was home to the Apache, nomadic tribes who often resisted European newcomers to North America. They clashed with settlers until surrendering to US troops in 1886 and being forcibly removed to the San Carlos Apache reservation.

“Chiricahua’s towering rock spires, rich Apache heritage and remarkable biodiversity make it one of America’s most extraordinary landscapes,” said Doug Burgum, the interior secretary. “This new designation will shine a national spotlight on one of Arizona’s hidden gems, creating opportunities to welcome more visitors, strengthen local economies and share this incredible landscape with more Americans.”

The bill creating Chiricahua national park preserves tribal access for traditional ceremonies. It allows temporary public closures within the park to protect those cultural uses, although Juan Ciscomani, a US representative from Arizona, said specifics have not been decided.

Early settlers called the site Wonderland of Rocks. The name Chiricahua comes from the surrounding mountains.

“This is a win for the communities in southeastern Arizona and for everyone who worked to protect this extraordinary place so our kids and our grandkids can enjoy it,” said Mark Kelly, a senator from Arizona.

The area has evidence of thousands of years of human use, according to the park service. That spans from prehistoric people to Buffalo soldiers – US troops who were Black and stationed at the monument site after the civil war, during a government campaign against Apache leaders Geronimo and Cochise.

Calvin Coolidge named the site a national monument in 1924 under the federal Antiquities Act. Franklin D Roosevelt expanded the site in 1938.

It gets roughly 60,000 visitors annually.

“While its name is changing, our commitment remains the same: protecting this remarkable landscape and its cultural heritage while providing opportunities for visitors to experience and enjoy it for generations to come.” said Jessica Bowron, comptroller and acting director of the National Park Service.

The park service has undergone deep cuts to its workforce under Trump. Maintenance projects at many sites – including Chiricahua – were ranked “low priority” by officials who have instead focused on projects wanted by the White House, including repairs to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: ‘Nunchucks’ wielded by agitated man in Hannah Beazley’s office may have been drumsticks, court told
articles.excerpt:
John Lawrence Smart charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear but Perth lawyer expresses concern for mental health

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A man accus...
articles.body_text:
John Lawrence Smart charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear but Perth lawyer expresses concern for mental health

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A man accused of making threats while armed with “improvised nunchucks” at a Western Australian MP’s electorate office could have been holding a musical instrument, not a weapon, a court has been told.

John Lawrence Smart appeared on Thursday in the WA magistrates court where his lawyer expressed concern for his mental health. He was not required to enter a plea.

Smart was accused of making verbal threats at the office of state Labor MP Hannah Beazley in the inner-Perth suburb of Victoria Park on Wednesday afternoon.

He was charged on Thursday with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making an unlawful threat and possessing cannabis. Police alleged Smart “made verbal threats while in possession of an improvised martial arts weapon (nunchucks)”.

During the court hearing, the highly agitated 56-year-old held his head in his hands and said he had been a musician for 20 years and he was holding claves.

“People, they don’t understand what I’m going through,” he said from the dock. Smart claimed people had “destroyed” his head.

Prosecutors said Smart entered Beazley’s office physically agitated and screaming, and holding two pieces of wood tied together.

He had a second similar implement attached to his belt, the police prosecutor said.

Smart allegedly demanded to see the politician while raising one of the implements above his head in a threatening manner before leaving the premises.

Smart’s lawyer said he was known to carry percussion sticks in the community and play drums.

The magistrate Heidi Watson suggested to the prosecutor that Smart might have been holding “drumsticks”.

The court heard Smart had previously been involuntarily admitted to hospital with schizophrenia and displayed delusional persecutory beliefs. He believed he had the “devil inside him”.

Watson ordered that Smart remained in custody for further medical assessment.

Beazley earlier said two of her staff were present in the electorate office when Smart allegedly entered.

“It was confronting,” she said in a social media post. “My staff did an amazing job and did everything right.”

No one was injured in the alleged incident, which comes after federal member for Indi Helen Haines was struck by a 4WD vehicle outside her electorate office in northern Victoria on Monday.

That incident sparked a nationwide debate about whether public officials were sufficiently protected from threats against their safety.

The WA premier, Roger Cook, said state parliament had been shocked by both incidents.

“We have got to start to turn the temperature down,” he said.

Cook said discussions were under way about potential upgrades to security measures to protect parliamentarians and their staff.

“Everyone deserves to feel safe at work, at home and in their communities,” he said.

“It’s not OK for people to take out their aggressions, their disagreements on staff in a politician’s office.”

Cook said security measures could be improved at state parliament, but they must be balanced with the need to maintain public access.

The Labor leader said he would support making an allowance available to MPs for security upgrades at their homes.

Beazley is the Labor state minister for local government and the daughter of former federal Labor leader Kim Beazley.

Smart was scheduled to return to the same court next Thursday.

articles.title: Macron condemns ‘seditious acts’ by ‘ultra-left’ and says he will seek to ban some protests – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
French government will show ‘absolute’ determination to stop the riots, Macron says

Macron begins by acknowledging there were some “shortcomings” in response to last weekend’s protests, with “an elem...
articles.body_text:
French government will show ‘absolute’ determination to stop the riots, Macron says

Macron begins by acknowledging there were some “shortcomings” in response to last weekend’s protests, with “an element of surprise.” He says the government needs to learn from that and apply it to this weekend’s events.

He says that local authorities have been empowered to adopt local measures, such as bans on gatherings, and the judicial system is “fully mobilised” to respond to events.

The president backs the justice ministry’s call for seeking harsh punishments for those involved in the riots.

He then makes it very clear what he makes of the riots:

“We witness both political and even seditious acts carried out by organised ultra-left groups aiming to bring down the Republic - acts that these groups themselves openly claim, characterised by extreme, intense violence.”

German chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was not surprised by the arrest back at home, as “Germany is a target of intensive espionage activity” all the time, as he welcomed the news that the authorities uncovered the alleged spy.

“But let us not delude ourselves: the activities of Russian intelligence services in Germany remain at a consistently high level.”

Speaking from Montenegro, where he is taking part in the Berlin process summit, Merz also said “the western Balkans must not ‌become a theatre where ​major powers vie for influence,” as he repeated his support for further EU enlargement.

Appearing alongside Montenegro’s Milojko Spajić and Austria’s Christian Stocker, Merz also responded to this week’s talks between Ukraine and the US, reiterating that Berlin is “committed to advancing this process,” but with a clear principle that “there will be no lasting peace in Ukraine without Europe.”

“We are doing everything in our power to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible. Any format for dialogue that serves this goal is welcome. But a lasting solution cannot be reached over the heads of the Ukrainians.”

Now, having covered the important stuff first, can we also take a moment to pause and consider what is surely the strangest press conference arrangement by the pool I have seen in years?

We are also receiving news from Germany, where a Ukrainian national has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, local prosecutors in Karlsruhe have announced.

The man, identified in a press statement only as Vadym Y., is suspected of having been “in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary” for over a year, collecting “relevant military information.”

This is alleged to have included “information about the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition, and explosives, as well as personnel and military facilities at sites securing Nato’s eastern flank.”

The man is due to appear in court tomorrow.

Meanwhile, the Paris prefecture has approved the proposed route of the main Parisian demonstration on Saturday, from Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation.

But a separate demonstration organised by the students collective Interfac and the so-called “yellow vests,” which wanted to go from Bastille to Place de l’Opera, will be blocked, the local authorities decided, as quoted by Le Monde.

It’s a strong political response from Emmanuel Macron as he seeks to draw a clear line between legitimate demonstrations organised by recognised trade unions and the looser, often spontaneous gatherings called by the “ultra-left” that descend into rioting and street violence – and show the state’s determination to fight back against the latter.

The signal he wants to send is very clear – but in the age of social media, can top-down regulation actually work? And will authorities have enough resources on the ground to respond to every banned demonstration?

Macron declares the government will show “absolute” determination to stop the riots, with a “multi-pronged” approach in response to the events to restore order.

He says that legitimate demonstrations held by trade union groups will be “reviewed in accordance with our laws” and allowed to go ahead in a way ensuring they can go ahead safely, with potential changes to their routes and subject to additional conditions.

But he says any other protests, not organised by trade unions, will “wherever possible” be “prohibited entirely”.

On substance, he says that PM Lecornu will meet with student organisations next week to work on “legitimate requests and grievances”.

He ends by saying that he will hold further meetings with relevant authorities tomorrow.

He says that local authorities have been empowered to adopt local measures, such as bans on gatherings, and the judicial system is “fully mobilised” to respond to events.

The president backs the justice ministry’s call for seeking harsh punishments for those involved in the riots.

He then makes it very clear what he makes of the riots:

“We witness both political and even seditious acts carried out by organised ultra-left groups aiming to bring down the Republic - acts that these groups themselves openly claim, characterised by extreme, intense violence.”

France’s Macron is speaking now after this morning’s security council meeting on protests across the country.

I’m listening and will bring you the key lines here.

The international criminal court and its officials have been awarded the prestigious 2026 EU Sakharov human rights prize, the European parliament’s speaker Roberta Metsola just announced.

“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” Metsola said.

It’s the latest recognition for the ICC as it finds itself under growing pressure from its critics, primarily the US president, Donald Trump, and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu.

“I also want to use this moment to recognise Tundu Lissu from Tanzania, and Taraneh and Romina Rahimi on behalf of all those persecuted by the Iranian Islamic Regime,” Metsola added.

The award ceremony will take place in December.

Officials have banned “all protests” in France’s third-biggest city of Lyon on Saturday, ahead of nationwide demonstrations that day following rallies last weekend that descended into widespread street violence, AFP reported.

The prefecture for the Rhone region said on Thursday in a statement to media that, “given the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to ban by decree all protests in the city of Lyon this Saturday, 24 October”.

Lyon, like Paris and other French cities, suffered clashes and looting when masked youths took to city centre streets on the sidelines of mass rallies protesting high inflation.

The mayor of Lyon, Grégory Doucet, has said that his city experienced hours of “chaos” during the riots, with between 150 and 200 shops looted and a tourist office torched. Police arrested some 200 people.

As we are waiting for Macron, first details of the planned police response to this weekend’s protests are emerging.

Junior interior minister, Jean-Didier Berger, said that the police presence will be “20% higher” than last weekend, with reinforcements from the army, elite police forces and gendarmerie.

But French media are reporting that some shopkeepers do not seem to be convinced, and they reinforce their own security measures, closing and boarding up some of their shops.

As lorry drivers’ protests bring much of southern Italy to a standstill amid food and fuel shortages, with businesses warning they are on the brink of collapse, Italian authorities have launched a police crackdown on road blockades.

The interior ministry said on Wednesday that 1,339 protesters had been identified, 71 reported to judicial authorities and 242 fined over what it described as “illegal road blockades”. Police escorted hundreds of vehicles carrying goods, including 500 in Campania alone, while the interior minister, Matteo Piantedosi, warned of possible infiltration by criminal groups.

Industry associations in Campania and Puglia warned that businesses were on the brink of collapse, prompting the prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, to convene an emergency cabinet meeting.

“The truckers’ dispute requires an immediate response,” said industry associations representing Naples and other parts of Campania and Puglia in a joint statement. “Production has ground to a halt due to a lack of supplies. The strike must end; otherwise, the damage to consumers and businesses, which is already significant, will become unsustainable.”

The protests began last week, with lorry drivers blocking roads and slowing traffic across the country, particularly in the south, following strikes and sit-ins by farmers and fishers.

The disruption has left supermarket shelves empty in several regions. Stocks at some supermarket chains have reportedly fallen to 50% of normal levels.

Italy’s air traffic management agency, ENAV, said on Wednesday that Crotone and Reggio Calabria airports had run out of jet fuel because of supply disruptions.

According to estimates gathered by Confcommercio Sicilia, the five-day disruption to freight transport has caused between €40m and €50m in losses in Sicily alone, affecting supermarkets and the wider fresh food supply chain.

The protests threaten to deepen the crisis facing Meloni’s government, which is struggling to contain the unrest. Measures announced so far by Rome appear to have done little to appease lorry drivers, prompting the government to take the controversial step of attempting to quell the protests through a police crackdown.

And as we wait for Macron, we have an update for you from Italy on lorry drivers’ protests there.

I am keeping an eye on France, where Emmanuel Macron is set to speak shortly after this morning’s emergency security council meeting ahead of more protests expected this weekend.

I will bring you the key lines when he shows up.

Meanwhile, we are getting more lines from Ukraine, with Belarusian state news agency reporting that Russia and Ukraine exchanged bodies of their war dead today.

Moscow handed over 252 corpses, and received 25 bodies in return, it said.

We will no doubt hear about this from the official channels later.

Meanwhile, French health authorities said they had detected ⁠the Shamonda ⁠virus ​usually affecting livestock in a human for the first ⁠time in a patient who later died, while adding that ⁠they saw no risk to ​the general ‌population at ‌this stage.

Shamonda virus is an insect-borne ‌Orthobunyavirus primarily affecting livestock, particularly cattle, and transmitted by biting midges, Reuters explained.

First identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, it has since been detected sporadically ‌in animals in Africa and Japan. It has been ​spreading among several European countries this year.

The virus had until now been considered non-transmissible to humans, ⁠the French government said.

Italy and Spain have dropped mutual border controls introduced in the aftermath of the Ceuta border crisis.

We covered that scenario on the blog last week (Europe Live, Friday).

In a statement, the Italian interior ministry said the two interior minister held “a cordial telephone” and “agreed that the suspensions of Schengen in force … will not be extended further.”

“The decision, which came after a careful analysis of the situation, will be accompanied by a strengthening of the exchange of information to ensure the full security of the Schengen common area,” the statement said.

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded to overnight attacks on Kyiv with a dig at US peace envoy Steve Witkoff’s comments lauding Russia’s Vladimir Putin as “a humanitarian”.

“Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles. Unfortunately, numerous sites across the city have been hit and damaged: ordinary residential buildings, energy facilities, infrastructure at one of the railway stations and the metro, shopping malls, and businesses. Even a monastery is among the damaged sites. Our emergency services are working at all the affected locations. Twelve of our regions came under Russian attack overnight.”

He said that at least two people died and 34 people were injured, including five children, in Kyiv.

“Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening. It is important to keep trying to find the right solutions to end this war. But when Russia responds to negotiations with ballistic missiles, real pressure on Russia is needed to bring about different steps – steps toward ending the killing.”

Thailand has advised its citizens to postpone non-essential travel to parts of Europe rocked by protests, while Malaysia also warned its nationals about visiting France, AFP reported.

“Those travelling from Thailand to Europe must closely monitor the situation as it is changing rapidly and France remains a concern as the situation is still ongoing,” Thai foreign minister Sihasak Phungketkeow told reporters late Wednesday during a trip to Italy.

He cited concerns about protests in Italy, noting his Italian counterpart had to cancel their bilateral due to an urgent government cabinet meeting on the unrest, adding: “We are also worried about Spain.”

“If it’s not necessary, with everything going on in those countries, I think it’s better to delay the trip for a while.”

The Malaysian embassy in Paris had on Sunday advised Malaysians in France “to exercise caution and remain vigilant” due to the protests.

China warned its citizens travelling to France to take safety precautions, state broadcaster CCTV reported Monday, after town halls and shops were looted and set on fire at the weekend.

French president Emmanuel Macron is back from his tour of the Gulf and convening a meeting with relevant ministers and intelligence services to figure out what can be done to prevent unsavoury scenes on the streets of French cities as more protests are planned for this Saturday.

“The government must hold its nerve,” Macron told reporters earlier this week.

He is expected to speak after the meeting, so once to watch.

Later today, French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a separate meeting with party leaders to discuss their concerns, including about policing and the next year’s presidential campaign.

Over in Ukraine, there are no signs of Russian attacks stopping anytime soon, after a night of “massive strikes” on port infrastructure facilities in Odesa region and on Kyiv.

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andii Sybiha commented on the attacks, saying:

“Kyiv residents heard what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centers, and residential areas. Other cities across Ukraine came under attack as well.

Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.”

No prizes for guessing who he may be addressing these comments to.

I will also bring you the latest from Serbia where the last day of campaigning begins before this Sunday’s closely contested parliamentary election.

It’s Thursday, 22 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Americans could be detained for years in popular travel destination, officials warn
articles.excerpt:
A U.S. State Department advisory highlights potential dangers for Americans visiting China, prompting travel expert Bobby Laurie to discuss ways tourists can protect themselves.

Americans traveling t...
articles.body_text:
A U.S. State Department advisory highlights potential dangers for Americans visiting China, prompting travel expert Bobby Laurie to discuss ways tourists can protect themselves.

Americans traveling to China are being warned about the possibility of detention, electronic surveillance and restrictions that could keep them from returning home â with a travel expert sharing critical information for people to know before they go.

The U.S. State Department issued an updated Level 2 "Exercise Increased Caution" advisory for mainland China this week, citing concerns about wrongful detention and restrictions on leaving the country.

Travelers are told to be aware that routine professional, academic and personal activities â which carry no risk in Western countries â may be treated as criminal offenses under China's broad security laws.

STATE DEPARTMENT ISSUES TRAVEL ADVISORY AS ARRESTS AND EXIT BANS HIT POPULAR DESTINATION

The advisory also raises concerns about private communications, warning Americans that emails, texts and social media activity could be monitored by Chinese authorities.

"Assume that China's security services can read your emails, texts and social media posts if you send them to or from China," the Oct. 19 advisory states.

Americans traveling to China are being warned about the risk of detention and restrictions that could prevent them from returning home. (Ju Huanzong/Xinhua via Getty Images)

The State Department said some people have been detained or deported over private messages considered critical of Chinese authorities, even when those messages were sent outside China.

The risks extend beyond electronic communications.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The State Department elaborated on possible detention without justification.

"The U.S. Department of State has determined that Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention by the Government of China," the advisory states.

Travelers could face restrictions that prevent them from leaving the country â even if they haven't been detained. (iStock)

Those detained could spend years behind bars with limited contact with family members or U.S. officials, according to the department.

Travelers could also face restrictions that prevent them from leaving the country, even if they have not been detained.

Chinese authorities have used the "exit bans" during investigations and business or civil disputes. Exit bans have also affected relatives of people under investigation, including children, according to the advisory.

Some travelers may not know they're prohibited from leaving until they try to fly home.

"U.S. citizens might only become aware of an exit ban when they attempt to depart China," the State Department said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Some bans have lasted for years â and officials warn there may be no clear way to challenge them in court.

Americans who plan to visit China are advised to travel with a U.S. passport and valid Chinese visa, enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program and arrange regular check-ins with family members or an employer.

Some travelers may not even realize they're banned from leaving the country until they try to fly home from China.  (Wu Yongbing/VCG via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. State Department for further comment.

"Be aware of your surroundings. Think before you take a picture," advised Bobby Laurie, a longtime travel expert and former flight attendant.

"This is one of those situations where maybe you were spotted taking pictures of law enforcement on the street, or you were somewhere you shouldn't have been. Maybe you were inadvertently near a protest â¦ on the streets," he added.

"Then you realize you're actually not allowed to fly home."

"Then as your trip comes to an end, you head to the airport. You scan your boarding pass, ready to get through immigration to fly home. And then you realize you're actually not allowed to fly home. There has been an exit ban placed on you."

He said anyone traveling to China should go with "a cell phone or electronic device that is really stripped down just to what you need for your trip."

Leave confidential information at home, he also urged.

Kelly McGreal is a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. She and the team cover travel, food and drink, health, relationships and more. She also produces the weekly American Culture Quiz and handles other special projects.

articles.title: Texas mom charged with manslaughter after allegedly driving 82 mph in crash that killed 2 recent college grads
