Regina Hickson, mother of 20-year-old Kiercy Hickson, shares heartbreaking memories of her daughter after she was tragically killed in a wrong-way DUI crash in Oklahoma. Hickson recounts Kiercy's dreams of cosmetology and travel, and her deep faith. She calls for justice for her daughter and other victims, urging awareness of drunk driving consequences.

A 22-year-old Texas mother accused of driving more than twice the speed limit with her two young children in the car faces manslaughter charges after a crash killed a couple who had recently graduated from college.

Aldrea Rogers, 22, was arrested and charged with two counts of manslaughter in connection with the deaths of Julian Harris and Madison Duren, Dallas County jail records reviewed by Fox News Digital show.

Rogers was allegedly driving 82 mph in a 35 mph zone when she crashed into the couple's vehicle, FOX 4 Dallas reported, citing a newly released arrest affidavit.

TEXAS WOMAN SENTENCED TO 7 YEARS IN PRISON, ANNUAL JAIL TIME DURING PROBATION FOR DEADLY DUI CRASH

Harris, 23, and Duren, 22, had recently graduated from Southern Methodist University, where they shared a passion for theater.

Aldrea Rogers, 22, was arrested Oct. 16, 2026, and charged with two counts of manslaughter in connection with a Dallas crash that killed recent Southern Methodist University graduates Julian Harris and Madison Duren. (Dallas County Jail)

Harris died at the scene, while Duren was taken to a hospital, where she later died.

LSU STUDENT AND FIREFIGHTER FIANCÃ MOWED DOWN NEAR CAMPUS, IMPAIRED UNDERAGE DRIVER ARRESTED

Rogers' two children were also in her vehicle during the crash. All three survived, authorities said.

A damaged red Hyundai is seen following an Oct. 6 crash in Dallas that killed Julian Harris and Madison Duren. Investigators allege the car's driver, Aldrea Rogers, was traveling 82 mph in a 35 mph zone before the collision. (FOX 4 Dallas)

Investigators said Harris was driving a Toyota Prius with Duren in the passenger seat when he attempted to turn left onto a major roadway.

WOMAN ACCUSED OF DEADLY REVENGE CRASH FACES JURY AS BOYFRIENDâS HOSPITAL ACCOUNT STAYS OUT OF TRIAL

The couple's car was struck by a Hyundai Elantra driven by Rogers, who investigators said was traveling at a high rate of speed before the collision.

Rogers was booked into the Dallas County Jail on Oct. 16, with bond set at $250,000 for each manslaughter charge, jail records show.

Madison Duren and Julian Harris share a playful moment while dressed in theatrical attire. The couple shared a passion for acting and were active in the Dallas theater community before their deaths. (Courtesy of Teatro Dallas via FOX 4 Dallas)

Her total bond was listed at $500,000 as of Wednesday afternoon.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Harris and Duren were active in Dallas' theater community after graduating from SMU, where they shared a passion for acting.

Two heavily damaged vehicles are seen following an Oct. 6 crash in Dallas that killed recent Southern Methodist University graduates Julian Harris and Madison Duren. Aldrea Rogers, 22, faces two counts of manslaughter in connection with the collision. (Credit: FOX 4 Dallas)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Their friends, Eli Barron and Emmet Overcarsh, described the couple to FOX 4 Dallas as curious, enthusiastic people who loved learning and connecting with others.

Overcarsh also expressed disbelief that Rogers, who was the same age as the victims, allegedly had her two young children in the car when the deadly crash occurred.

ulian Harris and Madison "Madi" Duren share an embrace outdoors. The couple, recent Southern Methodist University graduates, were killed in an Oct. 6, 2026, crash in Dallas. (Courtesy of Teatro Dallas via FOX 4 Dallas)

The couple had been leaving their apartment when the crash occurred.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Friends said the deaths have been difficult to comprehend, particularly because Rogers was the same age as the victims and allegedly had her two young children in the car.

Madison Duren and Julian Harris pose for a playful photo outside Southern Methodist University. The couple were killed in an Oct. 6 crash in Dallas. (Courtesy of Teatro Dallas via FOX 4 Dallas)

Fox News Digital has contacted the Dallas Police Department and Dallas County court officials to obtain a copy of the arrest affidavit and additional details about the crash investigation.

A memorial service for Harris and Duren is scheduled for Oct. 31 at Southern Methodist University.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors say
articles.excerpt:
Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’

Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton...
articles.body_text:
Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’

Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, faces a high risk of ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, according to an assessment by United Nations nature advisers.

About 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered, the assessment said, but when the expected impacts of global heating were added this rose to 96%.

Coral reefs are known as the rainforests of the sea. A quarter of all known marine species are found in and around them and they support hundreds of millions of people with food, as well as protecting shorelines and supporting tourism.

Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and global heating have already caused declines in the ecosystems over the past 50 years, measured by the loss of live coral as well as changes in fish populations, the assessment said.

But the scientists said while the prognosis was dire, the findings should serve as a “wake-up call” because reefs could survive with rapid cuts to fossil fuel use and strong conservation action at local levels.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

“The risk is real and very concerning,” said Dr Mishal Gudka, research director at CORDIO (Coral Reef Degradation in the Indian Ocean) East Africa and the scientific lead for the assessment.

“We stand to lose one of the most valuable ecosystems we have – the impacts of which will affect millions of people around the world.”

The assessment analysed the current status and future threat levels of 127 coral reef regions and was coordinated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), an international group that advises the United Nations.

The assessment assumed greenhouse gas emissions – mainly from burning fossil fuels – would follow a “middle-of-the-road” pathway, causing about 2.7C of global heating by the end of the century when compared with temperatures before the Industrial Revolution.

Current climate policies and targets adopted by countries around the world are likely to cause about 2.6C of global heating, one assessment finds.

The share of coral eco-regions considered critically endangered would likely be even higher, the IUCN said, but four regions did not have enough data to assess them and the coral reefs of the western Galápagos had already collapsed.

The critically endangered classification meant an “extremely high risk” of ecosystem collapse before 2075.

The group considers a coral reef ecosystem to have collapsed if the reef could not maintain itself because of a near or complete loss of living reef-building corals.

The assessment did not fully account for the impacts of the fourth global mass bleaching event from early 2023 to mid-2025 – the most widespread global mass bleaching event on record, the US government’s Coral Reef Watch has confirmed.

That global event was bookended by the worst mass bleaching event on record for reefs in Western Australia where a heatwave killed corals across 1,500 kilometres (930 miles).

Marine heatwaves can cause corals to separate from the symbiotic algae that provides them with colour and nutrient. While not always deadly, bleaching can weaken corals and make them more susceptible to disease.

Gudka said the results were a “wake-up call” and were “alarming, but certainly not hopeless”.

He said: “They should be seen as a call to action – an early warning sign before the worst outcomes eventuate.”

Dr Grethel Aguilar, the director general of the IUCN, said: “It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming.

“We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them.”

Four of Australia’s 17 reef regions were considered critically endangered. Five were endangered and five more were classed as vulnerable.

But all 17 regions, including the Great Barrier Reef, were critically endangered once the expected impacts of climate change were accounted for.

Dr Ben Fitzpatrick of the University of Western Australia Oceans Institute led the Australian assessment. He said even after accounting for the ability of some corals to adapt to warmer water, the rising heat “overwhelmed everything”.

“Reefs are like Picasso paintings underwater,” he said. “They have all these wonderful inhabitants in their millions. You can spend a lifetime trying to understand how all these weird critters go about their daily lives.

“To think we might lose that is devastating. There’s one message. We have to stop burning fossil fuels.”

The actor opened up to Fox News Digital about fatherhood and admitted he hopes to learn from both his own fatherâs strengths and mistakes while raising his children.

Chris Pratt is shedding light on the reality of raising four kids in Hollywood while keeping his Christian faith present in their lives.

During an interview with Fox News Digital ahead of the season 2 release of "Terminal List," Pratt said that his faith is how he starts and ends each day.

The new season of "Terminal List" premiered on Oct. 21, 2026 on Prime Video.

"Oh, God, you know, I'm for the most part, I'm always gonna be a man of faith. My faith is how I start my day, it's how I end my day. It's the most important thing that I'll be able to pass on to my kids," the actor began.

Chris Pratt keeps his faith at the center when raising his four kids in Hollywood. (Pablo Cuadra / Getty Images)

JACK CARR REVEALS WHY CHRIS PRATT WAS HIS PICK FOR 'THE TERMINAL LIST' FROM THE VERY START

"It's an incredible blessing to be a father. It's also a lot of hard work. And so I think I just want to teach them that... I don't know, I want to do my best. I basically want to get right everything my dad got right and get right everything my dad got wrong. And I'm sure I'll screw up both, you know?" Pratt continued.

"My faith is how I start my day, it's how I end my day. It's the most important thing that I'll be able to pass on to my kids."

Pratt is married to author Katherine Schwarzenegger, the daughter of actor Arnold Schwarzenegger and journalist Maria Shriver. The couple began dating in 2018, became engaged in January 2019 and married in June of that year.

Pratt and Schwarzenegger have three children together: daughters Lyla Maria, born in August 2020, and Eloise Christina, born in May 2022, along with their son, Ford Fitzgerald, born in November 2024.

Pratt also shares a son, Jack, with his former wife, actress Anna Faris. Jack was born in August 2012. Pratt and Faris married in 2009, announced their separation in 2017 and finalized their divorce in 2018. Pratt is now a father of four.

Katherine Schwarzenegger and Chris Pratt have three kids together. He also has a fourth child from a previous marriage. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Netflix)

Pratt was joined by his "Terminal List" co-star, Constance Wu, during the Fox News Digital interview.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Wu plays Katie Buranek, a seasoned war correspondent who helps Reece investigate the truth. As a journalist, Katie uses her reporting skills and connections to expose information surrounding the military conspiracy, becoming one of Reeceâs key allies. The series is based on Jack Carrâs novel of the same name and streams on Prime Video.

Wu told Fox News Digital that she's "never felt safer" on a television set before, due to all the veterans involved in the production.

"Yeah, you probably weren't," Pratt said. "We have 17 veterans on this in front of the camera, behind the camera. Writers, directors, tech advisors, safety coordinators, stuntmen, actors. So it was awesome."

Constance Wu stars in "The Terminal List." (Getty Images)

Wu explained that in season 2, her character Katie cares more personally for Pratt's character, Reece.

"I think for Katie, I think she cares more personally for Reese, whereas before she cared a lot about the truth and the story, but she also cares for him as a person a little more, which I think changes a lot of things," Wu said.

articles.title: Minister says 32 government services offline due to PHP code flaw – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Organisations around the world scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites

Some 32 government services are offline and four are partial...
articles.body_text:
Organisations around the world scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites

Some 32 government services are offline and four are partially unavailable while work is carried out to address potential cybersecurity issues, a minister has said.

As the Press Association reports, organisations around the world have been scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites.

Downing Street on Thursday said no large UK public-facing critical services have been affected, but some “limited” government websites have gone dark while issues are resolved. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) experts are working with OpenAI, whose technology was used to discover the vulnerabilities, and partners around the globe to address potential problems, a No 10 spokesperson said.

In the House of Lords, Liz Lloyd, the tech minister, said:

double quotation markThe information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable.

Lloyd said that “has largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied”.

double quotation markWork has already taken place across government to identify and fix potential exposures to our systems, and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue.

Here is our story about the global impact of the problems identified in the PHP programming language. It’s by Robert Booth and Aisha Down.

Yesterday Steve Witkoff, the property developer appointed by Donald Trump as his lead foreign policy envoy, described Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian”. Andrew Roth has more about that here, in a piece pointing out that this is an extraordinary lie.

Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, was giving interviews this morning. Asked if he agreed with Witkoff’s description on LBC, he was reassuringly blunt. He replied:

We see him as somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil.

So we simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.

In contrast, we are crystal clear that we stand foursquare behind Volodymyr Zelensky and the people of Ukraine in their battle for freedom.

At the No 10 lobby briefing, a No 10 spokesperson also argued that Witkoff had got it wrong. Asked about Witkoff’s comment, the spokesperson said:

double quotation markWe do not recognise that characterisation … Putin has killed thousands of people, Ukrainians and his own. He’s starving children and the elderly of heat and warmth and destroying critical national infrastructure.

The Conservative party seems to have missed the bit in the ONS report on the crime figures where it said “crime against individuals and households has generally decreased over the last 10 years”. (See 9.54am.) Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, has issued a statement saying:

double quotation markCrime is spiralling out of control under Labour. Record numbers of sexual offences, knife crime and shop theft show what happens when criminals know they can get away with it. This is a direct consequence of Labour cutting police numbers by 2,000 and letting thousands of prisoners out of jail early.

The Tories justify this claim by looking at the ONS report and picking out all the worst bits (a technique not unfamiliar in the world of journalism). Their briefing highlights four figures in particular. Here is an extract.

double quotation markSexual offences have reached the highest level on record under Labour, with the police now logging around 600 of them every single day. Police in England and Wales recorded 218,994 sexual offences in the year to June 2026, the highest annual total since the series began in 2002-03 …

Police are recording more rapes of women than at any point since records began, at a rate of around 142 every day. There were 51,731 recorded rapes of women aged 16 or over in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2004-05 …

More people are being caught carrying knives and blades than at any point since records began. Police recorded 30,216 offences of possessing an article with a blade or point in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2008-09 …

Thefts and robberies from shops have reached a record high under Labour, with more than 1,500 recorded every single day. Police recorded 519,516 shoplifting offences and 31,089 robberies of business property in the year to June 2026, a combined 550,605 and the highest total since the series began in 2002-03.

But these claims are highly selective – to the point of being misleading.

On sexual offences, and rape, the ONS report points out that much of the increase over time is due to more offences being recorded, and not necessarily more of them taking place. It says “there has been a general increase in police recorded sexual offences over the last decade, largely because of improvements in police recording practices”. And it includes a specific warning about drawing the wrong conclusions from the figures.

double quotation markPolice recorded sexual offences are not a good indicator of trends over time. Improvements in police recording practices, the introduction of new offences, and increased reporting by victims have contributed to the level of offences in recent years.

On knives, while more people may be carrying them, the Tories have ignored the figures suggesting fewer criminals are actually using them. The ONS says:

double quotation markKnife-enabled crime recorded by the police decreased by 6% in year ending (YE) June 2026 (to 48,615 offences), compared with YE June 2025 (51,567 offences). Levels remained 12% lower than YE March 2020 (55,170 offences).

And, on shoplifting, the Tories are again presenting the data in a misleading way. The ONS says:

double quotation markFollowing a period of increases in shoplifting, there has been a 2% decrease (to 519,516 offences) in YE June 2026 when compared with the previous year (530,336 offences).

The Tories have justified their “record high” claim by combining the shoplifing figures with the figures for robberies from business properties. They describe this as “shop crime” – even though many business properties are not shops. And the ONS has a caveat about these figures too.

double quotation markThe number of robbery of personal property offences fell by 7% (to 57,193 offences) compared with the previous year, however, overall robbery increased by 10% (to 88,282 offences) mainly because of improvements to recording practices for robbery of business property.

And the ONS says, with shoplifting, more offences are also now being recorded than in the past.

double quotation markRecent increases in police recorded shoplifting likely reflect both growth in offences and improved reporting resulting from closer engagement between police and retailers. Reporting rates for shoplifting are known to be very low and police are actively encouraging the reporting of all incidents and the submission of supporting evidence, such as CCTV, to strengthen intelligence, identify offenders, and link related offences.

The Office for National Statistics has also published a report on the gender pay gap. It says:

double quotation markThe gender pay gap for full-time employees has continued to decline in the UK. It was 6.8% in April 2026, down from 7.2% in April 2025. This compares with 9.4% a decade ago and 16.4% 25 years ago.

This chart shows the pay gap trend over time.

Patrick Maguire was not the only person to interview John Healey yesterday. Robert Peston, ITV’s political editor, spoke to the chancellor too, and he has written a blog about the most interesting points to emerge. This is what Peston says about Healey’s comments about the banks. (See 10.41am.)

double quotation markSecondly, I asked Healey whether he sees the banks as making excessive profits, which would be the coherent justification for him to increase the surcharge on bank profits – as he is expected to do in the Budget next week.

He said: “You know the banks are the engine of investment in this country. The banks are doing well at the moment and that is good to see.

“It’s good for Britain – and the budget is where I’ve got decisions to take across the economy, across the tax system. I will set those out on Wednesday next week.”

This sounded like he will increase the surcharge but doesn’t have an economic rationale for doing so.

There has been a “significant increase” in the proportion of adults in England and Wales who have experienced domestic abuse, the Press Association report. In its report on today’s crime figures (see 9.54am), PA says:

double quotation markSome 9.6% of people aged 16 and over are estimated to have been the victim of domestic abuse in the year to March 2026, or around 4.7 million people.

This is up from 7.8%, or around 3.8 million people, in the year ending March 2025.

The rise indicates “real change” in the prevalence of domestic abuse and is a “significant increase”, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS) which carried out the survey.

The jump has been driven by a rise in partner abuse, experienced by 7.9% of people aged 16 and over in the latest figures, compared with 6.1% in the previous year.

Some “minor changes” to the way the survey is carried out are likely to have influenced the size of the increase, the ONS said.

But their best assessment is there has been a genuine rise in the level of domestic abuse.

While there has been a jump in the prevalence of partner abuse, figures for family abuse are broadly similar, at 2.8% of adults in the year to March 2026, compared with 2.7% in the previous 12 months.

Meghan Elkin, ONS head of crime statistics, said: “While minor survey changes and the usual uncertainty around gathering data on this sensitive topic are likely to have affected these estimates, our assessment is that the rise in domestic abuse includes real change.

“More data points are needed to further understand the uncertainty and what this tells us about trends in domestic abuse.”

Kemi Badenoch has criticised the government for not sending a minister to address the Police Federation’s conference.

Addressing the federation this morning, she said she was “not scared to wade in” and not scared to “back the police”.

double quotation markToo often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service. Whether it’s hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they’re in trouble themselves.

It’s no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police.

I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour government has not sent anyone to address this conference – not the policing minister, not the home secretary.

But Badenoch also said she would not promise police officers a big pay rise.

double quotation markNow, I know that you would also like a massive pay rise as well.

I’m sorry that I can’t promise that just yet – at least not on day one.

I am not going to stand here and promise something without a plan to pay for it.

Too many politicians have done that, and it only leads to disappointment.

Offenders who refuse to face their victims’ families in court for sentencing could be stripped of privileges or kept in cells for weeks under government changes granting wider powers to judges in England and Wales, Geneva Abdul reports.

Kalyeena Makortoff is the Guardian’s banking correspondent.

CS Venkatakrishnan, CEO at Barclays, seems to have admitted defeat over bank tax hikes, which are expected to be a headline measure in Healey’s budget next week.

When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US - where it also has operations - as a result of higher taxes, Venkatakrishnan gave his full backing to the chancellor.

double quotation markI recognise that the chancellor and the government has been entrusted with an important duty by the public and the people. And they have to balance a host of considerations. He [Healey] is the man in the arena, and I deeply respect the responsibility he bears on his shoulders and wish him well.

His long term goal is the same as our long term goal, which is to get growth.

Second, we are already a bank, which makes, effectively, half of our money elsewhere [outside] the UK. And so this is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signaling. But as I said, I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.

Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget.

That includes JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon, who said earlier this year he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile to banks. News of the tower – which will house more than half of its 23,000 UK staff – was unveiled just days after former Labour chancellor Rachel Reeves spared the sector of further tax rises in her 2025 autumn budget.

Here are some more lines from Patrick Maguire’s interview with John Healey in the Times. This passage sums up the overall picture very well. Maguire writes:

double quotation markSo what is the chancellor now concentrating on? One could be forgiven for thinking him utterly unreconstructed: a party man and proud of it. There is no such thing as Healeyism, he says when the conversation turns to Anthony Crosland’s evangelism for the mixed economy: “I’m just Labour.”

“Just Labour” is exactly what the bond markets fear — and, indeed, it is what gives Kemi Badenoch hope of pulling off a comeback to rank alongside Lazarus and Bobby Ewing for utter implausibility.

As explained earlier, while not going into specifics, Healey was keen to present himself as someone reducing the burdens facing businesses – especially smaller businesses. (See 9am.) But here are some other lines.

Healey argued that his budget next week would refute the claim made by Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, about Labour not having the right policies to promote growth. In an article for the Financial Times, Haldane said Conservative policies were better for the economy, partly because they were more likely to support “cuts to business and employment taxes and regulation to unleash animal spirits”. In his write-up, Maguire says:

double quotation markIt was Haldane who also said, memorably and mercilessly, that the markets had concluded that this was a “traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”. At Westminster, this sort of criticism is at risk of curdling into thick and immovable consensus. What does Healey say to that? “I’d say to Andy Haldane,” he growls, fixing me with a cold stare, “speak to me next Thursday.” And, for the record, he speaks explicitly of “making an argument for how you bring welfare costs down” — albeit not via the “crude cuts” that were Starmer’s undoing.

Healey hinted that he was sympathetic to arguments that Labour should drop its plan to let younger workers qualify for the full national living wage. In his article Maguire says:

double quotation mark[Healey] is “acutely conscious”, too, of the “trade off” between an ever-increasing minimum wage — particularly for the youngest workers — and levels of employment.

He knows the many businesses who “want to employ young people” sometimes cite that upward ratchet as a reason they cannot.

Healey defended the part he played in bringing down Keir Starmer. Healey resigned from Starmer’s government over defence spending, and this contributed to the loss of support for Starmer in the parliamentary party that led to him standing down. Referring to this period, Healey said:

double quotation markThe country was ready for a change … Wherever you stood on the spectrum of the [parliamentary Labour party], there was a recognition that we needed a change.

He also argued that changing leader had been good for the party.

double quotation markWe have a very rare moment now. We’re in the middle of a parliament, the second half of a parliament, and we’ve got a chance of a new hearing. People are at least willing to listen again … the Labour party is actually quite determined and disciplined, and in any party, the second half of a parliament starts concentrating minds.

The Office for National Statistics’ latest report on crime figures is out. It covers crime in England and Wales in the year ending June 2026 and it starts:

double quotation markCrime against individuals and households has generally decreased over the last 10 years with some notable exceptions, such as fraud.

This chart shows some of the key figures. The crime survey figures are based on what people tell researchers about the crimes they have experienced; the other figures related to the crimes reported to the police.

At this stage of the budget process, John Healey has almost certainly made all his key decisions. But, just in case he hasn’t, he could try our budget interactive. It allows you to make a decision on some of the options facing the chancellor, and then it will tell you what the impact would be on budget headroom, and how the markets and the polls might react.

Good morning. A week today John Healey, the chancellor, will be doing a media round defending the budget he is presenting on Wednesday next week. Ahead of that, he has given an interview to Patrick Maguire from the Times. As you would expect, there is no real detail in it about the measures he will be presenting to MPs. But the big picture message is very clear – and quite surprising, coming from a chancellor serving a PM who in some respects is steering left compared to his predecessor. Healey says that he wants to be on the side of bloody-minded entrepreneurs who make a profit, he acknowledges that government has made their life harder over the past two years, and he suggests that cutting the ‘cost of living’ for business is just as important as cutting the real cost of living for families.

In the quote that gives the Times its splash headline, Healey says:

double quotation markI want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, and those entrepreneurs who, in the end, are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures …

If you’re not making a profit, you’ve got nothing to put back into the business. And for the people who start up these businesses, the ones who really thrive and grow, they have to make a profit — and they will be much more inclined to put it back into their own business. But we want it to grow here and stay here.

And this is what he says about the government has recently been putting “a lot of pressure” on business.

double quotation markIf you talk to any of the businesses that have come in and have either had one-to-ones or round tables with me, I have recognised that in recent times there’s been a lot of pressure: employment law, regulation, tax, input costs, supply chains.

And so when I talk about the cost of business, and recognising that in the same way as we’re recognising the cost of living pressures, I’m conscious of that as I go into the budget for both businesses and households.

All chancellors – including all Labour chancellors – say they want to help businesses make a profit. But many people in the business community suspect that, when they face fiscal pressure, Labour government will usually default to treating business as a cash machine.

Healey’s comments about wanting to be seen as “a chancellor who backs business” and about how tax rises and the Employment Rights Act have increased costs sound like an implicit rebuke to Rachel Reeves, his predecessor. In his interview Healey defends her decision to increase employer national insurance, saying she had to deal with the “dereliction of duty” of the last Tory government on the economy. But Healey still gives the impression of wanting to be seen as markedly more pro-business than Reeves.

In his interview Healey does not give details of how he will cut costs for business next week. But, in his write-up, Maguire says:

double quotation mark[Healey] is expected to use the budget to make significant cuts to regulation on businesses that one senior Treasury source described as “the sludge choking firms”. Reporting requirements are likely to be abolished for many smaller enterprises, The Times understands.

9.30am: The ONS publishes crime figures for England and Wales and – separately – annual gender pay gap figures.

10am: Ofgem chief executive Tim Jarvis and Department for Energy and Net Zero permanent secretary Jonathan Brearley give evidence to the Commons public accounts committee about achieving clean power by 2030.

10.15am: Kemi Badenoch gives a speech at the Police Federation’s annual conference.

Morning: Andy Burnham is in Manchester where he is getting a flu jab, and also holding a meeting with mayors at No 10 North about mayors retaining revenue from business rates.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Lunchtime: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, speaks at a lunch at the Commons hosted by lobby journalists.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.
